0.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Book of Leviticus
0.overview:
Leviticus is the book most Christians skip, full of blood, smoke, and the regulation of altars, animals and ailments. Yet here, more than anywhere in the Old Testament, we learn how a sinful people may dwell with a holy God. The book answers the question raised at the end of Exodus: when the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle so that even Moses could not enter (Exod 40:35), how shall defiled creatures come near? Leviticus is God's gracious answer, written in the language of sacrifice.

The dominating word is holy, the cry of the seraphim: "Holy, holy, holy" (Isa 6:3). Leviticus brands it on the conscience of a redeemed people: "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2).

Do these laws apply to Christians? Christians are not under the law of Moses as a covenant (Rom 6:14; Gal 3:24–25), but it remains Scripture, profitable for teaching (2 Tim 3:16). The Reformed tradition reads it in three strands. Its moral law, rooted in God’s character and creation and repeated in the New Testament, still binds (Rom 13:8–10). Its ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, clean and unclean, feasts) was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17; Heb 10:1). Its civil law governed Israel as a nation under God and ended with that theocracy, though its principles of justice still teach us.

Who wrote it? The book presents itself as what the LORD spoke to Moses (1:1, and throughout), and Jesus called a leper's offering what Moses commanded (Mark 1:44). Many modern scholars date its final form after the exile; others note that its world is the wilderness camp. This commentary holds that its substance is from Moses; the question is debated.

Why so many purity laws? Unclean is not the same as sinful: childbirth or burying the dead made a person unclean without any wrong done. The laws taught a whole nation, daily, that God is holy and that approach to him is a serious thing (Heb 9:9–10).

Did animal sacrifice really forgive sin? Leviticus says he shall be forgiven (4:26), and Hebrews says it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Heb 10:4). Both are true. The forgiveness was real, received by faith in God’s promise, but its ground was the sacrifice the animals pointed to: God passed over former sins in his forbearance until Christ came (Rom 3:25).

But Leviticus is not legalism. It stands inside grace: Israel has already been redeemed by the Passover blood and brought into covenant at Sinai. The sacrifices do not purchase God's love; they are the appointed means by which an already-loved people may live in his presence.

Above all, Leviticus is about Jesus. Every offering, priest and Day of Atonement points beyond itself to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, and Hebrews is the inspired commentary on it. Holy, holy, holy, and yet in Christ the holy God has made a way for us to come home.

1.title: The Burnt Offering: Wholly the Lord's
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of livestock from the herd or from the flock.<sup>3</sup>"If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD.<sup>4</sup>He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.<sup>5</sup>Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall bring the blood and throw the blood against the sides of the altar that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>6</sup>Then he shall flay the burnt offering and cut it into pieces,<sup>7</sup>and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire.<sup>8</sup>And Aaron's sons the priests shall arrange the pieces, the head, and the fat, on the wood that is on the fire on the altar;<sup>9</sup>but its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"If his gift for a burnt offering is from the flock, from the sheep or goats, he shall bring a male without blemish,<sup>11</sup>and he shall kill it on the north side of the altar before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>12</sup>And he shall cut it into pieces, with its head and its fat, and the priest shall arrange them on the wood that is on the fire on the altar,<sup>13</sup>but the entrails and the legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall offer all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or pigeons.<sup>15</sup>And the priest shall bring it to the altar and wring off its head and burn it on the altar. Its blood shall be drained out on the side of the altar.<sup>16</sup>He shall remove its crop with its contents and cast it beside the altar on the east side, in the place for ashes.<sup>17</sup>He shall tear it open by its wings, but shall not sever it completely. And the priest shall burn it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
1.overview:
Leviticus opens not with a command but with a calling. The God whose glory has just filled the tabernacle now speaks from within it, and his first word to a redeemed people is about how to draw near. The first offering is the burnt offering, the 'olah, "the offering that goes up": the only sacrifice in which the entire animal, apart from the skin, is burned on the altar.

It is an offering of total self-dedication; the worshipper is saying, in the language of fire, "All that I am I give to you." Its key gesture is the hand laid on the animal's head. Many understand that gesture to picture the worshipper's guilt passing to the animal, so that the innocent dies in place of the guilty. "A pleasing aroma to the LORD" means the sacrifice is accepted: it brings delight to the heart of God.

Christ is our whole burnt offering, the one who held nothing back, who gave himself entirely to the Father on our behalf, and could say, "I have come to do your will, O God" (Heb 10:7). Where our consecration is always partial and hedged with reservations, his was total, and in him we are acceptable.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: God calls from the tent, and his first word about offerings is a permission.

Verses 3-9: The burnt offering from the herd: the hand laid on its head, the worshipper killing it, the whole burned.

Verses 10-13: The same from the flock, with the identical result.

Verses 14-17: And from birds, again a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Leviticus Is For

God opens a way to come near to him, and prices it so that rich and poor alike can take it.
verseByVerse.examples: Three prices brought one and the same acceptance. No believer comes to God on a lesser footing than another, because all come through the same offering.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of livestock from the herd or from the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exodus ended with the glory filling the tabernacle so completely that Moses was not able to enter (Ex. 40:35). Leviticus opens with the next problem: God has moved in, and nobody can go near him.

That is what this book is for. It is not a legal appendix but the answer to the question Exodus left hanging: how do sinful people live next door to a holy God without being destroyed? Every sacrifice, washing and distinction between clean and unclean addresses that question.

And the first word about the offerings is a permission, not a demand. The Hebrew for any one of you is adam, a human being: not a priest, not even an Israelite, but a person. The door is opened as wide as the language allows before a single regulation follows.
verseByVerse.note: Leviticus takes its name from the Levites, the priestly tribe.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him. Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall bring the blood and throw the blood against the sides of the altar that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. Then he shall flay the burnt offering and cut it into pieces, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire. And Aaron's sons the priests shall arrange the pieces, the head, and the fat, on the wood that is on the fire on the altar; but its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Olah comes from the verb to go up: all of it goes up in smoke. Nothing is eaten by the priest or returned to the worshipper.

Verse 4 contains the whole logic of the system in one sentence. The gesture is not affection or ownership. A man presses his hand on a living animal and identifies himself with it, and then the animal is killed and he is not. The verse says what this achieves: accepted for him, atonement for him. The acceptance is God's provision, received, not earned. And the animal must be a male without blemish (v. 3), the standard Peter sees met in Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet. 1:19).

Then he kills it himself. Not the priest: whoever brought the animal cut its throat and watched it die. No worshipper was permitted to be sentimental about what sin costs.

The last phrase of verse 9 is the one the New Testament picks up: Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Eph. 5:2). Paul calls the cross a burnt offering: the whole given, nothing held back, and its smell acceptable to God.

Does God eat? If I were hungry, I would not tell you (Ps 50:12). “Food offering” and “pleasing aroma” mean that the offering is accepted. When Paul uses the words of Christ, he means that the Father accepted his Son's offering completely.
verseByVerse.note: Except for the skin (7:8), the whole animal was burned.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his gift for a burnt offering is from the flock, from the sheep or goats, he shall bring a male without blemish, and he shall kill it on the north side of the altar before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. And he shall cut it into pieces, with its head and its fat, and the priest shall arrange them on the wood that is on the fire on the altar, but the entrails and the legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall offer all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The same procedure for a sheep or goat, in identical terms, with the identical result, and the repetition is the point. The poorer man's offering is not a lesser atonement or a partial acceptance. It is the same phrase, word for word.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or pigeons. And the priest shall bring it to the altar and wring off its head and burn it on the altar. Its blood shall be drained out on the side of the altar. He shall remove its crop with its contents and cast it beside the altar on the east side, in the place for ashes. He shall tear it open by its wings, but shall not sever it completely. And the priest shall burn it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turtledoves or pigeons cost very little. Here the priest kills the bird rather than the worshipper, and the crop is thrown away beside the altar, a detail that is almost tender: a man too poor to bring a lamb is not asked to do the slaughtering, and the small indignities of a small offering are handled discreetly. And the chapter ends on the identical sentence.

Three times, at three prices, and the same acceptance every time. God builds the poor into the system on the first page, and refuses to describe their offering in weaker terms than anyone else's.

When Mary and Joseph presented their firstborn, they brought a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons (Luke 2:24), the offering Leviticus allows a mother who cannot afford a lamb (12:8). The mother of the Lord could not afford a lamb. She was carrying him.
verseByVerse.note: Turtledoves and pigeons were the offering the poor could afford.

1.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The laid-on hand and the slain animal teach that sin is dealt with not by human effort but by a substitute God provides, which is the heart of the cross.

Total consecration. The wholly consumed offering pictures the surrender Christ gave the Father, which the Spirit now works in us: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).

The pleasing aroma. What the burnt offering symbolised, Christ accomplished, and in him our worship rises acceptably.
1.examples:
Then: an Israelite pressed his hand on his own animal and watched it die and go up in flame: approaching God requires a substitute.

Now: we come through Christ's once-for-all offering, and give our whole selves to God not to be accepted but because we already are accepted in him.

2.title: The Grain Offering: The Labor of Our Hands
2.text: <sup>1</sup>"When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it<sup>2</sup>and bring it to Aaron's sons the priests. And he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour and oil, with all of its frankincense, and the priest shall burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>3</sup>But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.<sup>4</sup>"When you bring a grain offering baked in the oven as an offering, it shall be unleavened loaves of fine flour mixed with oil or unleavened wafers smeared with oil.<sup>5</sup>And if your offering is a grain offering baked on a griddle, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mixed with oil.<sup>6</sup>You shall break it in pieces and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering.<sup>7</sup>And if your offering is a grain offering cooked in a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil.<sup>8</sup>And you shall bring the grain offering that is made of these things to the LORD, and when it is presented to the priest, he shall bring it to the altar.<sup>9</sup>And the priest shall take from the grain offering its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>10</sup>But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.<sup>11</sup>"No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>As an offering of firstfruits you may bring them to the LORD, but they shall not be offered on the altar for a pleasing aroma.<sup>13</sup>You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.<sup>14</sup>"If you offer a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer for the grain offering of your firstfruits fresh ears, roasted with fire, crushed new grain.<sup>15</sup>And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it; it is a grain offering.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall burn as its memorial portion some of the crushed grain and some of the oil with all of its frankincense; it is a food offering to the LORD.
2.overview:
After the bloody burnt offering comes the bloodless grain offering, the minchah, a gift or tribute. Where the burnt offering speaks of atonement, the grain offering speaks of consecrated labour. Fine flour is the fruit of ploughing, sowing, reaping, threshing and grinding: a working life laid on God's altar. It often accompanied the burnt offering, joining the dedication of the self to the dedication of its labour. The God who redeems us claims not only our souls but our Mondays.

And here is Christ, the true bread offered to the Father: the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died (John 12:24), the bread of life (John 6:35), the only human life ever lived wholly without the leaven of sin. Many Christians have seen in the grain offering, ground fine and passed through fire, a picture of his perfect obedience offered up for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-3: Fine flour with oil and frankincense; a memorial portion is burned and the rest goes to the priests.

Verses 4-10: Oven, griddle or pan, with the same result.

Verses 11-13: No leaven or honey, but always salt.

Verses 14-16: The firstfruits, roasted and crushed.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Offering With No Blood in It

This is a gift of grain, kept free of leaven and seasoned with salt.
verseByVerse.examples: The offering fitted whatever kitchen the household had. God asks for what we have, not for what we lack.

verseByVerse.quote: "When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it and bring it to Aaron's sons the priests. And he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour and oil, with all of its frankincense, and the priest shall burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second offering has no blood in it at all. Minchah is used elsewhere for a gift brought to a superior, and what is brought is not a living animal but the product of work: grain sown, watched, harvested, threshed and ground by somebody's hands. A man who brought this handed over a portion of his own labour, from a harvest God had given.

A handful stands for the whole, and the rest belongs to Aaron and his sons. So the grain offering is also how the priesthood eats: Israel's worship and Israel's ministers are funded by the same act.
verseByVerse.note: The grain offering acknowledged God as the giver of the harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you bring a grain offering baked in the oven as an offering, it shall be unleavened loaves of fine flour mixed with oil or unleavened wafers smeared with oil. And if your offering is a grain offering baked on a griddle, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mixed with oil. You shall break it in pieces and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering. And if your offering is a grain offering cooked in a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil. And you shall bring the grain offering that is made of these things to the LORD, and when it is presented to the priest, he shall bring it to the altar. And the priest shall take from the grain offering its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary: Listing three ways of preparing it means the offering fits the household. A woman with an oven brings loaves; a family with only a griddle brings wafers. God specifies the flour and oil and leaves the kitchen arrangements to whoever is cooking, and every version is most holy.

verseByVerse.quote: "No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD. As an offering of firstfruits you may bring them to the LORD, but they shall not be offered on the altar for a pleasing aroma. You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two prohibitions and one requirement are the heart of the chapter.

Both banned substances probably share one property: they ferment. Leaven works through dough by souring it; honey ferments as it warms. Leaven is usually a picture of corruption in Scripture (1 Cor 5:8), though not always (Matt 13:33). Leavened loaves could still be brought as firstfruits (v. 12; 23:17), but never burned on the altar. Nothing that spreads by souring may go on the altar, which is the sense the New Testament gives it: a little leaven leavens the whole lump, so cleanse out the old leaven and keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:6-8). Paul grounds that call in what has already happened: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7).

Salt does the opposite of leaven. It preserves, and in the ancient Near East a covenant sealed with a shared meal of salt was a bond that did not spoil. Every offering in Israel carried a pinch of the thing that stops decay, and God calls it the salt of the covenant: his own faithfulness, seasoning their gifts.

Jesus handed the image to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth (Matt. 5:13), and Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another (Mark 9:50). Paul told the Colossians to let their speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col. 4:6). What was sprinkled on every sacrifice is now said of the people who bring them.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5 also speak of a “covenant of salt”.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you offer a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer for the grain offering of your firstfruits fresh ears, roasted with fire, crushed new grain. And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it; it is a grain offering. And the priest shall burn as its memorial portion some of the crushed grain and some of the oil with all of its frankincense; it is a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Firstfruits are the first of the crop to ripen, brought before the rest of the harvest is in. To give them away is to act on the belief that the remainder is coming, and coming from God: the offering of a man not yet certain of his year who gives anyway.

Paul uses the word for the resurrection: Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20). One sheaf brought in early guarantees a whole field standing behind it.

2.theology:
Consecrated work. The fruit of human labour, offered to God, becomes worship. For the believer no honest work is merely secular.

The exclusion of corruption. Nothing that spreads by souring may go on the altar. Christ alone was wholly free of sin's leaven, the sinless bread offered to God.

The covenant of salt. God's covenant faithfulness does not decay. Christ kept that covenant perfectly, and his people are called to be salt.
2.examples:
Then: the farmer brought the ground fruit of his fields, salted and unleavened, to the God who gave the increase.

Now: we offer our work and wages to God as worship, not to earn his favour but because he has given us everything, and we look to Christ, the grain of wheat that died to bring forth much fruit.

3.title: The Peace Offering: Communion Restored
3.text: <sup>1</sup>"If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he offers an animal from the herd, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And he shall lay his hand on the head of his offering and kill it at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>3</sup>And from the sacrifice of the peace offering, as a food offering to the LORD, he shall offer the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails,<sup>4</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>5</sup>Then Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar on top of the burnt offering, which is on the wood on the fire; it is a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>"If his offering for a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD is an animal from the flock, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish.<sup>7</sup>If he offers a lamb for his offering, then he shall offer it before the LORD,<sup>8</sup>lay his hand on the head of his offering, and kill it in front of the tent of meeting; and Aaron's sons shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>9</sup>Then from the sacrifice of the peace offering he shall offer as a food offering to the LORD its fat; he shall remove the whole fat tail, cut off close to the backbone, and the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>10</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>11</sup>And the priest shall burn it on the altar as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"If his offering is a goat, then he shall offer it before the LORD<sup>13</sup>and lay his hand on its head and kill it in front of the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>14</sup>Then he shall offer from it, as his offering for a food offering to the LORD, the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>15</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD's.<sup>17</sup>It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood."
3.overview:
The peace offering (in Hebrew shelamim, related to shalom, peace and wholeness; some translations call it the “fellowship offering”) is the offering of communion. It is the only sacrifice that ends in a feast: after God receives the fat and the priests their portion, the offerer and his household eat a sacred meal in God's presence.

It celebrates the reconciliation the other offerings make possible. The goal of sacrifice is not merely the removal of guilt but table-fellowship with the living God. Sin had banished man from God's presence; the peace offering brings him back to the table. Yet even in joyful fellowship God is God: the fat and the blood are his.

Christ made peace "by the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20), and Paul draws the comparison himself: Israel's worshippers who ate the sacrifices shared in the altar, and believers at the Lord's Table share in Christ (1 Cor 10:16–18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-5: The peace offering from the herd, shared between God, priest and worshipper.

Verses 6-11: The same from the flock, with the fat tail specified for God.

Verses 12-17: A goat, and two permanent statutes on fat and blood.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Only Sacrifice the Worshipper Eats

This is a meal shared with God, and the best portion is his.
verseByVerse.examples: The best cut was put before the host. Thankful worship still gives God the first and best, not what is left over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he offers an animal from the herd, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD. And he shall lay his hand on the head of his offering and kill it at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw the blood against the sides of the altar. And from the sacrifice of the peace offering, as a food offering to the LORD, he shall offer the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails, and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. Then Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar on top of the burnt offering, which is on the wood on the fire; it is a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shelamim is unlike the two offerings before it in one decisive respect. The burnt offering was entirely consumed; the grain offering fed the priests. This one is shared three ways: part to God on the altar, part to the priests, and part eaten by the worshipper and his family. It is the only sacrifice in Leviticus that the person who brought it gets to eat.

So this is a meal with God, in his presence. Nothing about it is solemn in the way the sin offering is solemn. It is dinner.

And it is not brought to fix anything. No guilt is named and no wrong put right. The peace offering is what you bring when things are well.
verseByVerse.note: Some translations call it the “fellowship offering.”

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering for a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD is an animal from the flock, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish. If he offers a lamb for his offering, then he shall offer it before the LORD, lay his hand on the head of his offering, and kill it in front of the tent of meeting; and Aaron's sons shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. Then from the sacrifice of the peace offering he shall offer as a food offering to the LORD its fat; he shall remove the whole fat tail, cut off close to the backbone, and the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. And the priest shall burn it on the altar as a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What goes to God is oddly precise, and in a fat-tailed desert sheep the tail is the choicest part, the store of energy, the piece anyone would want. It is specified for God by name.

Food offering is deliberately domestic. Scripture is emphatic that God does not eat: if I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine (Ps. 50:12). The language describes a shared table rather than a transaction, and the best cut is put before the host.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a goat, then he shall offer it before the LORD and lay his hand on its head and kill it in front of the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. Then he shall offer from it, as his offering for a food offering to the LORD, the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. And the priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD's. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with two permanent restrictions, and both will matter later.

The fat is God's because it is the best, and the rule guards against a natural drift: a man carving up his own peace offering, deciding the choice portion is wasted in smoke, and keeping it. The first thing to go, when worship starts to be managed rather than offered, is the best part.

The blood is God's for a different reason, given in full at 17:11: the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that makes atonement by the life. Blood is not food because blood is life, and life belongs to the one who gave it.

Hold the two halves of this offering together, because the New Testament does. A shared meal in God's presence, eaten in peace, with no guilt on the table: Israel had a category for that and seldom enough confidence to enjoy it. Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5:1). For he himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14).

Peace with God was always a thing to be sat down to and eaten, not merely believed. Among the last pictures Scripture gives of it is a supper table and a voice at the door: if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev. 3:20).

The ban on fat belonged to the altar: the fat was the LORD’s portion, and it ended with the sacrifices. The ban on blood is a harder question.

Does the ban on eating blood still bind? It was given to Noah before Israel (Gen 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it for the sake of fellowship with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29). But the New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Tim 4:4), and most Christians have concluded that the principle, reverence for the life God gives, remains, while eating meat that is not fully drained is not sin. The command concerns eating, not medicine; a blood transfusion gives life and does not break it.

3.theology:
Peace with God. Atonement leads to restored fellowship, the heart of shalom, fulfilled in Christ "who is our peace" (Eph 2:14).

The fellowship meal. The shared meal anticipates the Lord's Table, where the reconciled feast in God's presence.

God's claim on the best. God receives the choicest portion, not the leftovers.
3.examples:
Then: a reconciled family sat down to a joyful sacred meal in God's courts.

Now: at the Lord's Table we celebrate the peace Christ made by his blood, because the gospel's goal is not mere pardon but fellowship with our God.

4.title: The Sin Offering: Even Unintended Sin
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them,<sup>3</sup>if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people, then he shall offer for the sin that he has committed a bull from the herd without blemish to the LORD for a sin offering.<sup>4</sup>He shall bring the bull to the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD and lay his hand on the head of the bull and kill the bull before the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And the anointed priest shall take some of the blood of the bull and bring it into the tent of meeting,<sup>6</sup>and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle part of the blood seven times before the LORD in front of the veil of the sanctuary.<sup>7</sup>And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before the LORD that is in the tent of meeting, and all the rest of the blood of the bull he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>8</sup>And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall remove from it, the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>9</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys<sup>10</sup>(just as these are taken from the ox of the sacrifice of the peace offerings); and the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering.<sup>11</sup>But the skin of the bull and all its flesh, with its head, its legs, its entrails, and its dung—<sup>12</sup>all the rest of the bull—he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place, to the ash heap, and shall burn it up on a fire of wood. On the ash heap it shall be burned up.<sup>13</sup>"If the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally and the thing is hidden from the eyes of the assembly, and they do any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and they realize their guilt,<sup>14</sup>when the sin which they have committed becomes known, the assembly shall offer a bull from the herd for a sin offering and bring it in front of the tent of meeting.<sup>15</sup>And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands on the head of the bull before the LORD, and the bull shall be killed before the LORD.<sup>16</sup>Then the anointed priest shall bring some of the blood of the bull into the tent of meeting,<sup>17</sup>and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD in front of the veil.<sup>18</sup>And he shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is in the tent of meeting before the LORD, and the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>19</sup>And all its fat he shall take from it and burn on the altar.<sup>20</sup>Thus shall he do with the bull. As he did with the bull of the sin offering, so shall he do with this. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.<sup>21</sup>And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it up as he burned the first bull; it is the sin offering for the assembly.<sup>22</sup>"When a leader sins, doing unintentionally any one of all the things that by the commandments of the LORD his God ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt,<sup>23</sup>or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring as his offering a goat, a male without blemish,<sup>24</sup>and shall lay his hand on the head of the goat and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before the LORD; it is a sin offering.<sup>25</sup>Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out the rest of its blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering.<sup>26</sup>And all its fat he shall burn on the altar, like the fat of the sacrifice of peace offerings. So the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>27</sup>"If anyone of the common people sins unintentionally in doing any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt,<sup>28</sup>or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring for his offering a goat, a female without blemish, for his sin which he has committed.<sup>29</sup>And he shall lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill the sin offering in the place of burnt offering.<sup>30</sup>And the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar.<sup>31</sup>And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat is removed from the peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>32</sup>"If he brings a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, he shall bring a female without blemish<sup>33</sup>and lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering.<sup>34</sup>Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar.<sup>35</sup>And all its fat he shall remove as the fat of the lamb is removed from the sacrifice of peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar, on top of the LORD's food offerings. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.
4.overview:
Now the tone deepens. The burnt, grain and peace offerings were largely voluntary. The sin offering, the chatta't (many scholars translate it “purification offering”, because its blood cleanses the sanctuary as well as the worshipper), is required, and its first lesson is that it covers sins committed unintentionally. Sins we never noticed or meant also defile and require blood. We measure sin by our intentions; God measures it by his holiness.

The chapter is graded by rank (priest, congregation, leader, ordinary person), and the higher the office, the costlier the sacrifice.

Christ is the sin offering: "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Cor 5:21). He entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, bearing not one man's unintended sin but the sins, deliberate ones included, of a countless multitude. "He shall be forgiven", the most beautiful refrain in the chapter, is purchased for us at infinite cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — The Sin Offering: When the Anointed Priest Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-12: The sin offering for unintentional sin, beginning with the anointed priest: a bull, its blood brought inside the tent, its carcass burned outside the camp.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Unintentional Sin Needs Atoning

The priest's sin is priced at the same rate as the whole nation's.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priest's sin brought guilt on the people. Now: those who lead in the church carry a heavier responsibility, and need the same sacrifice as everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them, if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people, then he shall offer for the sin that he has committed a bull from the herd without blemish to the LORD for a sin offering. He shall bring the bull to the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD and lay his hand on the head of the bull and kill the bull before the LORD. And the anointed priest shall take some of the blood of the bull and bring it into the tent of meeting, and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle part of the blood seven times before the LORD in front of the veil of the sanctuary. And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before the LORD that is in the tent of meeting, and all the rest of the blood of the bull he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall remove from it, the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys (just as these are taken from the ox of the sacrifice of the peace offerings); and the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering. But the skin of the bull and all its flesh, with its head, its legs, its entrails, and its dung— all the rest of the bull—he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place, to the ash heap, and shall burn it up on a fire of wood. On the ash heap it shall be burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth offering deals with guilt that needs removing rather than devotion that needs expressing. The Hebrew shegagah means sin committed in error, without meaning to, and that raises the question a modern reader asks at once: why need atonement for something you did not know you were doing?

Because guilt in Scripture is not measured by the offender's awareness of it. A law broken unknowingly is still broken. Leviticus assumes what every honest person discovers: we are not reliable judges of our own record, and "I did not realise" is an explanation rather than an acquittal. David prayed out of the same conviction: Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults (Ps. 19:12).

The first case is the priest, with the most expensive animal and the most elaborate blood rite, inside the tent itself. His sin does not stay with him; it brings guilt on the people. And the same bull is required for the whole congregation, so a priest's private failure is costed at the rate of a national one. Leadership is weighted, and Scripture prices it accordingly.

The rest of the bull is burned outside the camp, the detail Hebrews reaches for: the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:11-12).

What about deliberate sin? The one who sins with a high hand, in open defiance, had no sacrifice (Num 15:30–31). Yet David, guilty of adultery and murder, was forgiven when he confessed (2 Sam 12:13; Ps 51:16–17). The sacrifices covered sins of weakness; deliberate sin was cast on God’s mercy alone. In Christ every sin confessed is forgiven: the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).
verseByVerse.note: “Unintentionally” means by mistake (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13-21 — When the Whole Congregation Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-21: When the whole congregation sins unawares, the elders lay hands on a bull for the people.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guilt Nobody Has Noticed

Once a community's hidden sin comes to light, one offering covers it.
verseByVerse.examples: A church, too, can share a blind spot no one has named. Because the sacrifice is already provided, it can afford to have that blind spot pointed out.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally and the thing is hidden from the eyes of the assembly, and they do any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and they realize their guilt, when the sin which they have committed becomes known, the assembly shall offer a bull from the herd for a sin offering and bring it in front of the tent of meeting. And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands on the head of the bull before the LORD, and the bull shall be killed before the LORD. Then the anointed priest shall bring some of the blood of the bull into the tent of meeting, and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD in front of the veil. And he shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is in the tent of meeting before the LORD, and the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And all its fat he shall take from it and burn on the altar. Thus shall he do with the bull. As he did with the bull of the sin offering, so shall he do with this. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven. And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it up as he burned the first bull; it is the sin offering for the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A nation can be guilty of something none of its members has noticed, and that hidden corporate sin is real enough to require the most expensive sacrifice in the system.

And dealing with it depends on discovery. Until the sin is recognised there is no offering, so the health of the arrangement depends on a community willing to have its blind spots pointed out, which is easier for a people who know a sacrifice is already provided.

The elders lay their hands on the bull for everybody. Representation runs right through this book: one animal, a few hands, a whole people covered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-35 — When a Leader or a Common Person Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-35: A leader brings a male goat and an ordinary person a female goat or lamb, and each is forgiven.
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness Stated as Fact

When atonement has been made, forgiveness is pronounced.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the offering shrank with the offender's rank, and every offender heard the same words of forgiveness. Now: Christ's blood does what the blood of goats only promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a leader sins, doing unintentionally any one of all the things that by the commandments of the LORD his God ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt, or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring as his offering a goat, a male without blemish, and shall lay his hand on the head of the goat and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before the LORD; it is a sin offering. Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out the rest of its blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering. And all its fat he shall burn on the altar, like the fat of the sacrifice of peace offerings. So the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven. "If anyone of the common people sins unintentionally in doing any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt, or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring for his offering a goat, a female without blemish, for his sin which he has committed. And he shall lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill the sin offering in the place of burnt offering. And the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar. And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat is removed from the peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven. "If he brings a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, he shall bring a female without blemish and lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering. Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar. And all its fat he shall remove as the fat of the lamb is removed from the sacrifice of peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar, on top of the LORD's food offerings. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offering shrinks with the rank of the offender: the reverse of how most societies price wrongdoing, where the powerful make things go away more cheaply than the poor.

One small difference in wording is pointed. For the priest and the congregation the text says if; for the leader it says when. Scripture does not entertain the possibility that a man in authority will get through his term without needing this.

And every paragraph after the priest's ends with the same formula, four times (vv. 20, 26, 31, 35): atonement made, and he shall be forgiven. Not "he may hope to be", nor "he shall feel" forgiven. It is stated as accomplished fact, to a man who did not know he had done wrong until somebody told him. Hebrews observes that the mechanism had to keep running because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Heb. 10:4). The forgiveness announced here was real, underwritten by a payment not yet made.

4.theology:
The gravity of unintentional sin. Guilt is measured by God's holiness, not by our awareness, and that leaves no room for self-righteousness.

Graded accountability. The higher the office, the costlier the offering (cf. James 3:1).

'They shall be forgiven.' This is the chapter's refrain of grace. Christ the sin offering secures the forgiveness the bulls and goats could only foreshadow (Heb 10:4).
4.examples:
Then: an Israelite, suddenly aware of a sin committed unawares, brought a goat, laid his hand on it, and heard the priest pronounce him forgiven.

Now: we are guiltier than we know, but in Christ more loved than we dared hope. This is no call to anxious, endless self-searching: the believer who cannot name every hidden fault may rest in the One who knows them all and has paid for them all (1 John 3:20).

5.title: The Guilt Offering: Forgiveness and Restoration
5.text: <sup>1</sup>"If anyone sins in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, and though he is a witness, whether he has seen or come to know the matter, yet does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity;<sup>2</sup>or if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether a carcass of an unclean wild animal or a carcass of unclean livestock or a carcass of unclean swarming things, and it is hidden from him and he has become unclean, and he realizes his guilt;<sup>3</sup>or if he touches human uncleanness, of whatever sort the uncleanness may be with which one becomes unclean, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and realizes his guilt;<sup>4</sup>or if anyone utters with his lips a rash oath to do evil or to do good, any sort of rash oath that people swear, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and he realizes his guilt in any of these;<sup>5</sup>when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed,<sup>6</sup>he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed, a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin.<sup>7</sup>"But if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering.<sup>8</sup>He shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer first the one for the sin offering. He shall wring its head from its neck but shall not sever it completely,<sup>9</sup>and he shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar, while the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar; it is a sin offering.<sup>10</sup>Then he shall offer the second for a burnt offering according to the rule. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>11</sup>"But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two pigeons, then he shall bring as his offering for the sin that he has committed a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil on it and shall put no frankincense on it, for it is a sin offering.<sup>12</sup>And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take a handful of it as its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, on the LORD's food offerings; it is a sin offering.<sup>13</sup>Thus the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed in any one of these things, and he shall be forgiven. And the remainder shall be for the priest, as in the grain offering."<sup>14</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>15</sup>"If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation, a ram without blemish out of the flock, valued in silver shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, for a guilt offering.<sup>16</sup>He shall also make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>17</sup>"If anyone sins, doing any of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, though he did not know it, then realizes his guilt, he shall bear his iniquity.<sup>18</sup>He shall bring to the priest a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the mistake that he made unintentionally, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>19</sup>It is a guilt offering; he has indeed incurred guilt before the LORD."
5.overview:
The guilt offering, the 'asham (also called the reparation offering), overlaps with the sin offering but adds restitution. Where sin has caused measurable loss, to God's holy things or to a neighbour, the guilty party must repay in full and add a fifth. Forgiveness does not float free of repair. Grace does not excuse us from making things right; it enables us to.

The chapter opens with cases that still use the sin offering, and there confession, the open naming of sin before God, is required (5:5). Zacchaeus, giving back fourfold (Luke 19:8), is a son of the guilt offering, made a maker of restitution by the grace that found him first. And Christ is the One who not only forgives but restores, rebuilding what sin demolished: restoring to God a glory greater than Adam lost, and to us a sonship richer than Eden.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-13 — The Sin Offering Scaled to the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-6: A silent witness, an unnoticed uncleanness and a rash oath, each dealt with once the guilt is realised.

Verses 7-13: The offering scaled to poverty, down to a tenth of an ephah of flour.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Sin Offering of Flour

The sinner confesses, and the offering is priced so that everyone can afford it.
verseByVerse.examples: The way back is open the moment a person admits the wrong, and no one is too poor to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone sins in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, and though he is a witness, whether he has seen or come to know the matter, yet does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity; or if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether a carcass of an unclean wild animal or a carcass of unclean livestock or a carcass of unclean swarming things, and it is hidden from him and he has become unclean, and he realizes his guilt; or if he touches human uncleanness, of whatever sort the uncleanness may be with which one becomes unclean, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and realizes his guilt; or if anyone utters with his lips a rash oath to do evil or to do good, any sort of rash oath that people swear, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and he realizes his guilt in any of these; when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed, a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of three cases is not an action at all. A man who knows something, is publicly asked, and says nothing: no lie told, he simply keeps quiet while an injustice proceeds. Leviticus files that under sin requiring blood. Silence in a courtroom is treated as an act, and the guilt is the witness's own.

The second is touching something unclean without noticing; the third, a rash oath made and forgotten. Words spoken carelessly are still words spoken.

All three end in the same place: when he realizes his guilt, he confesses and brings his offering. Israel's remedy for sin begins the moment a man admits he has a problem, and the remedy is already waiting for him when he does.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. He shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer first the one for the sin offering. He shall wring its head from its neck but shall not sever it completely, and he shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar, while the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar; it is a sin offering. Then he shall offer the second for a burnt offering according to the rule. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven. "But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two pigeons, then he shall bring as his offering for the sin that he has committed a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil on it and shall put no frankincense on it, for it is a sin offering. And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take a handful of it as its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, on the LORD's food offerings; it is a sin offering. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed in any one of these things, and he shall be forgiven. And the remainder shall be for the priest, as in the grain offering."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the provision that makes this chapter remarkable: birds for those who cannot afford a lamb, and for those who cannot manage birds, a sin offering of flour.

Hebrews sums up the system, without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness (Hebrews 9:22), and is careful to say that under the law almost everything is purified with blood, perhaps with exactly this case in mind. The destitute are forgiven by bringing a bag of flour, the text insists on calling it a sin offering, and it closes with the same formula: he shall be forgiven.

Two details keep it honest. No oil or frankincense, unlike the grain offering of chapter 2: this is not a gift but a substitute. And the priest burns it on top of the blood sacrifices already burning. The poor man's flour goes into a fire that blood has already lit. His forgiveness is not bloodless; it is borrowed.

Which is the position of everyone who has ever been forgiven. Nobody's atonement is self-funded. The Israelite carrying a bag of flour to the altar is the plainest picture in Leviticus of being saved by a payment somebody else made.
verseByVerse.note: A tenth of an ephah was roughly two litres of flour.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-19: The guilt offering for a breach of faith: restitution plus a fifth, even when the offender did not know.
verseByVerse.theology:
Repentance With an Arithmetic

The offender brings a ram, restores the loss and adds a fifth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: worship was no substitute for putting something right. Now: a forgiven Christian pays back what he took, gladly, because his own debt has been paid.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation, a ram without blemish out of the flock, valued in silver shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, for a guilt offering. He shall also make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering, and he shall be forgiven. "If anyone sins, doing any of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, though he did not know it, then realizes his guilt, he shall bear his iniquity. He shall bring to the priest a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the mistake that he made unintentionally, and he shall be forgiven. It is a guilt offering; he has indeed incurred guilt before the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The asham deals not merely with sin but with damage, and alongside the ram the offender must restore what he took and add a fifth.

Repentance here has an arithmetic. The wrong is repaid in full, plus twenty per cent, and only then is the sacrifice offered. Israel could not use worship as a substitute for putting something right.

The closing case stretches the principle to its limit: a man who did something forbidden though he did not know it has indeed incurred guilt. He did not know; he is guilty. Neither cancels the other, which is why the sacrificial system exists: not to make people feel proportionate to their offence, but to deal with what is actually true about them.
verseByVerse.note: The “shekel of the sanctuary” (v. 15) was the standard weight for payments to the sanctuary.

5.theology:
Confession. Sin must be named openly before God, the gateway to forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

Restitution. Grace does not bypass repair; it enables it, and true repentance pays back more than it took.

Christ our restorer. Isaiah says the Servant's soul "makes an offering for guilt" (Isa 53:10): he is himself the 'asham, paying far more than the added fifth and giving back what he never took away (Ps 69:4).
5.examples:
Then: an Israelite who had defrauded God or a neighbour confessed, repaid with a fifth added, and brought a ram.

Now: resting in Christ, the guilt offering who cancelled our debt, we make things right where we have wronged others, by the Spirit who makes a forgiven person generous. Where our repair falls short, his covers it.

6.title: Laws for the Priests: The Fire That Never Goes Out
6.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"If anyone sins and commits a breach of faith against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in a matter of deposit or security, or through robbery, or if he has oppressed his neighbor<sup>3</sup>or has found something lost and lied about it, swearing falsely—in any of all the things that people do and sin thereby—<sup>4</sup>if he has sinned and has realized his guilt and will restore what he took by robbery or what he got by oppression or the deposit that was committed to him or the lost thing that he found<sup>5</sup>or anything about which he has sworn falsely, he shall restore it in full and shall add a fifth to it, and give it to him to whom it belongs on the day he realizes his guilt.<sup>6</sup>And he shall bring to the priest as his compensation to the LORD a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering.<sup>7</sup>And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD, and he shall be forgiven for any of the things that one may do and thereby become guilty."<sup>8</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>9</sup>"Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the burnt offering. The burnt offering shall be on the hearth on the altar all night until the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it.<sup>10</sup>And the priest shall put on his linen garment and put his linen undergarment on his body, and he shall take up the ashes to which the fire has reduced the burnt offering on the altar and put them beside the altar.<sup>11</sup>Then he shall take off his garments and put on other garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place.<sup>12</sup>The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and he shall arrange the burnt offering on it and shall burn on it the fat of the peace offerings.<sup>13</sup>Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.<sup>14</sup>"And this is the law of the grain offering. The sons of Aaron shall offer it before the LORD in front of the altar.<sup>15</sup>And one shall take from it a handful of the fine flour of the grain offering and its oil and all the frankincense that is on the grain offering and burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>16</sup>And the rest of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place. In the court of the tent of meeting they shall eat it.<sup>17</sup>It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it as their portion of my food offerings. It is a thing most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering.<sup>18</sup>Every male among the children of Aaron may eat of it, as decreed forever throughout your generations, from the LORD's food offerings. Whatever touches them shall become holy."<sup>19</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>20</sup>"This is the offering that Aaron and his sons shall offer to the LORD on the day when he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half in the evening.<sup>21</sup>It shall be made with oil on a griddle. You shall bring it well mixed, in baked pieces like a grain offering, and offer it for a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>22</sup>The priest from among Aaron's sons, who is anointed to succeed him, shall offer it to the LORD as decreed forever. The whole of it shall be burned.<sup>23</sup>Every grain offering of a priest shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten."<sup>24</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>25</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the LORD; it is most holy.<sup>26</sup>The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. In a holy place it shall be eaten, in the court of the tent of meeting.<sup>27</sup>Whatever touches its flesh shall be holy, and when any of its blood is splashed on a garment, you shall wash that on which it was splashed in a holy place.<sup>28</sup>And the earthenware vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken. But if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, that shall be scoured and rinsed in water.<sup>29</sup>Every male among the priests may eat of it; it is most holy.<sup>30</sup>But no sin offering shall be eaten from which any blood is brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it shall be burned up with fire.
6.overview:
Chapters 6 and 7 turn from the worshipper's instructions to the priests': the regulations for handling each offering. This may seem the dustiest corner of Leviticus, yet it glows with quiet glory. The God who is a consuming fire orders his worship down to the disposal of ashes, because nothing about approaching him is trivial.

The towering image is the perpetual fire (6:13). The altar on which fire came out from before the LORD (9:24) was never to go cold: the visible sign that atonement was always available and the door to God never closed. It foreshadows the lasting power of Christ's sacrifice, though with a difference: the fire never went out because Israel never stopped sinning, while Christ "offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins" (Heb 10:12). The one offering that need never be repeated has made the endless fire unnecessary, yet the devotion it symbolised burns brighter than ever in hearts set aflame by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Restitution for Sins Against a Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: Wrongs against a neighbour are breaches of faith against the LORD, put right with restitution plus a fifth before the guilt offering.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wrongs Against People Are Breaches of Faith Against God

The neighbour is to be repaid on the very day the guilt is realised.
verseByVerse.examples: The neighbour was paid before God was approached. A Christian who has wronged someone puts it right as part of coming back to God, not as an optional extra afterwards.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "If anyone sins and commits a breach of faith against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in a matter of deposit or security, or through robbery, or if he has oppressed his neighbor or has found something lost and lied about it, swearing falsely—in any of all the things that people do and sin thereby— if he has sinned and has realized his guilt and will restore what he took by robbery or what he got by oppression or the deposit that was committed to him or the lost thing that he found or anything about which he has sworn falsely, he shall restore it in full and shall add a fifth to it, and give it to him to whom it belongs on the day he realizes his guilt. And he shall bring to the priest as his compensation to the LORD a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD, and he shall be forgiven for any of the things that one may do and thereby become guilty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every offence in the list is committed against a person, and the verse calls all of them a breach of faith against the LORD. Cheating a neighbour over a deposit is not merely a civil matter with a religious dimension; it is an act against God, done to a man.

The remedy has two halves in a fixed order. First, restore in full, add a fifth, and pay it on the day he realizes his guilt. Not when convenient. Then the guilt offering.

The man is paid before God is approached. There was no arrangement in Israel for making peace with heaven while the defrauded person was still out of pocket, which is why Zacchaeus, the moment grace reached him, started calculating (Luke 19:8), and why Jesus told people to leave the gift at the altar and be reconciled to a brother first (Matt. 5:23-24). In both cases the grace comes first; the repaying is its fruit.
verseByVerse.note: Leviticus 6:1–7 is 5:20–26 in the Hebrew numbering (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Fire That Never Goes Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-13: The law of the burnt offering: the fire must never go out, and the priest changes his clothes to carry out the ashes.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Fire Nobody Was Allowed to Let Die

The altar never goes cold, and the ashes are carried out in working clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Somebody shovelled out yesterday's fire every morning. Unseen, repeated work in a church is service to God, and he sees it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the burnt offering. The burnt offering shall be on the hearth on the altar all night until the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it. And the priest shall put on his linen garment and put his linen undergarment on his body, and he shall take up the ashes to which the fire has reduced the burnt offering on the altar and put them beside the altar. Then he shall take off his garments and put on other garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place. The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and he shall arrange the burnt offering on it and shall burn on it the fat of the peace offerings. Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One instruction is repeated three times in five verses (vv. 9, 12, 13). In chapter 9 fire will come from before the LORD onto this altar, and Israel's job is to keep it alight: through every festival and every ordinary Tuesday, the altar never goes cold.

The mechanics are given with odd care. The priest removes the ashes in linen, then changes into other garments to carry them outside the camp. The holy garments are for the altar; the ash run is done in working clothes.

Somebody had to shovel out yesterday's fire before today's offering, every morning, in a country that never saw him do it. Most of what keeps worship going has always looked like that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-23 — The Priests and the Grain Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-23: The priests eat the grain offering in a holy place, and the high priest offers his own, morning and evening, wholly burned.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priest Is Also a Worshipper

The men fed by the offerings bring one that feeds nobody.
verseByVerse.examples: No office, however holy, exempts a man from needing grace, and those who lead God's people bring their own need to him first.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law of the grain offering. The sons of Aaron shall offer it before the LORD in front of the altar. And one shall take from it a handful of the fine flour of the grain offering and its oil and all the frankincense that is on the grain offering and burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the rest of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place. In the court of the tent of meeting they shall eat it. It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it as their portion of my food offerings. It is a thing most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering. Every male among the children of Aaron may eat of it, as decreed forever throughout your generations, from the LORD's food offerings. Whatever touches them shall become holy." The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "This is the offering that Aaron and his sons shall offer to the LORD on the day when he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half in the evening. It shall be made with oil on a griddle. You shall bring it well mixed, in baked pieces like a grain offering, and offer it for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. The priest from among Aaron's sons, who is anointed to succeed him, shall offer it to the LORD as decreed forever. The whole of it shall be burned. Every grain offering of a priest shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests' share of the grain offering counts as their most sacred food. Then a striking provision: from the day of his anointing, the high priest brings his own flour, twice daily, and unlike the people's grain offering it is wholly burned.

The men who live off the offerings of others bring one that feeds nobody, every day of their lives. Nothing about the priesthood exempts a priest from being a worshipper. Hebrews draws the contrast with our great High Priest: Israel's high priests offered daily, first for their own sins, but Jesus has no need to, since he offered up himself once for all (Hebrews 7:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 24-30: The sin offering is most holy and its holiness spreads; any sin offering whose blood is brought into the tent is burned, not eaten.
verseByVerse.theology:
Holiness Running the Other Way

Whatever touches the sin offering is made holy.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: contact with this offering spread holiness. Now: Christ, touched by sinners, made them clean instead of being made unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the LORD; it is most holy. The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. In a holy place it shall be eaten, in the court of the tent of meeting. Whatever touches its flesh shall be holy, and when any of its blood is splashed on a garment, you shall wash that on which it was splashed in a holy place. And the earthenware vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken. But if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, that shall be scoured and rinsed in water. Every male among the priests may eat of it; it is most holy. But no sin offering shall be eaten from which any blood is brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it shall be burned up with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The emphasis falls on contagion: splashed garments washed, an earthenware pot broken, a bronze one scoured.
