Here holiness travels outward. In most of Leviticus contact spreads uncleanness: touch a corpse and you are unclean. The sin offering runs the other way. What touches it is made holy, and its pot cannot simply be reused because something has happened to it that cannot be scrubbed off.

And the one exception: any sin offering whose blood is brought into the tent is burned, not eaten. The offerings that go furthest in are the ones nobody shares. Chapter 16 will show why.

6.theology:
The perpetual fire. The unceasing flame signified the constant availability of atonement and the constant need of a sinful people, a need answered once for all in Christ.

Daily devotion. The morning wood pictures tending the heart's fire, which God kindles and the Spirit keeps alight. "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19). Older Reformed writers spoke of a daily putting to death of sin and a daily renewing of grace, and the morning wood is a fair picture of it.

Provision for ministers. Those who serve at the altar share in what is offered there.
6.examples:
Then: before dawn the priest removed the night's ashes and laid on fresh wood, guarding the flame God himself had kindled.

Now: we tend devotion daily by the Word, prayer and the Spirit, resting in the finished sacrifice that ended the need for endless offerings, even as our hearts burn within us (Luke 24:32).

7.title: The Portion of the Priests: Order in Holy Things
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"This is the law of the guilt offering. It is most holy.<sup>2</sup>In the place where they kill the burnt offering they shall kill the guilt offering, and its blood shall be thrown against the sides of the altar.<sup>3</sup>And all its fat shall be offered, the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails,<sup>4</sup>the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>5</sup>The priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering to the LORD; it is a guilt offering.<sup>6</sup>Every male among the priests may eat of it. He shall bring the fat with the breast, that the breast may be waved as a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>31</sup>The priest shall burn the fat on the altar, but the breast shall be for Aaron and his sons.<sup>32</sup>And the right thigh you shall give to the priest as a contribution from the sacrifice of your peace offerings.<sup>33</sup>Whoever among the sons of Aaron offers the blood of the peace offerings and the fat shall have the right thigh for a portion.<sup>34</sup>For the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed I have taken from the people of Israel, out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, as a perpetual due from the people of Israel.<sup>35</sup>This is the portion of Aaron and of his sons from the LORD's food offerings, from the day they were presented to serve as priests of the LORD.<sup>36</sup>The LORD commanded this to be given them by the people of Israel, from the day that he anointed them. It is a perpetual due throughout their generations."<sup>37</sup>This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering,<sup>38</sup>which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai, on the day that he commanded the people of Israel to bring their offerings to the LORD, in the wilderness of Sinai.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 completes the priestly handbook: the guilt offering, the peace offering, and the priests' portions. To modern ears these are dry logistics; to faith they show the beauty of ordered worship. The God who saves is the God who orders.

The peace offering is divided into thanksgiving, vow and freewill offerings (7:12–16), the thanksgiving eaten the same day, so that joy is not hoarded but shared while fresh. The breast and right thigh go to the priests (7:30–34), God's provision for those who serve. The ban on blood and fat is pressed again (7:22–27): blood belongs to God because the life is in it, the principle chapter 17 explains and Hebrews builds on when it speaks of the blood of Christ. And every portion reserved, every drop of blood withheld, every wave of the priest's hands points to the day when the perfect Priest would offer the perfect sacrifice and give his people the choicest portion of all: himself, in the bread and the cup of the new covenant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — The Guilt Offering and the Priests' Portions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-10: The guilt offering, and which priest receives which portion.
verseByVerse.theology:
Income Specified in Law

The priests' living is written into the offerings themselves.
verseByVerse.examples: A tribe with no land lived by written provision, and churches still owe a fair living to those who give their lives to teaching them.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the law of the guilt offering. It is most holy. In the place where they kill the burnt offering they shall kill the guilt offering, and its blood shall be thrown against the sides of the altar. And all its fat shall be offered, the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails, the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. The priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering to the LORD; it is a guilt offering. Every male among the priests may eat of it. It shall be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy. The guilt offering is just like the sin offering; there is one law for them. The priest who makes atonement with it shall have it. And the priest who offers any man's burnt offering shall have for himself the skin of the burnt offering that he has offered. And every grain offering baked in the oven and all that is prepared on a pan or a griddle shall belong to the priest who offers it. And every grain offering, mixed with oil or dry, shall be shared equally among all the sons of Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A short paragraph settles who gets what: the hide to the officiating priest, the cooked grain offerings to the one who presents them, the dry ones shared among Aaron's sons.

It reads like accountancy and does something important. Levi received no farmland, and the priests' whole income was specified in law rather than left to whoever turned up. Paul quotes the arrangement when arguing that gospel workers should be supported: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple?... In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Cor. 9:13-14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-21 — The Peace Offering: Thanksgiving and Vows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 11-21: Thanksgiving, vow and freewill peace offerings, with time limits for eating and a ban on eating while unclean.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gratitude That Cannot Be Stored

The thanksgiving offering is eaten the same day, and nothing may be kept to the third.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: gratitude had to be spent at once, in company. Now: thanks for what God has done is still meant to be told and shared with others.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that one may offer to the LORD. If he offers it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the thanksgiving sacrifice unleavened loaves mixed with oil, unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and loaves of fine flour well mixed with oil. With the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving he shall bring his offering with loaves of leavened bread. And from it he shall offer one loaf from each offering, as a gift to the LORD. It shall belong to the priest who throws the blood of the peace offerings. And the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning. But if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow offering or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day that he offers his sacrifice, and on the next day what remains of it shall be eaten. But what remains of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned up with fire. If any of the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offering is eaten on the third day, he who offers it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be credited to him. It is tainted, and he who eats of it shall bear his iniquity. "Flesh that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten. It shall be burned up with fire. All who are clean may eat flesh, but the person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of the LORD's peace offerings while an uncleanness is on him, that person shall be cut off from his people. And if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether human uncleanness or an unclean beast or any unclean detestable creature, and then eats some flesh from the sacrifice of the LORD's peace offerings, that person shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The distinctions matter. A thanksgiving offering is brought for something God has done; a vow offering discharges a promise; a freewill offering is brought for no stated reason at all.

Consider what the one-day rule does to a family. A whole animal must be eaten before morning, far more than most households can manage. So the thanksgiving offering in effect forced a party: neighbours are called in, and they will want to know what is being celebrated. Gratitude for what God had done could not be conducted privately or stored. It had to be spent at once, in company, on people.

The meal of fellowship is closed to those not fit for it, the concern Paul brings to a very different table: Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord (1 Cor. 11:27). That warning, like this one, sends us to the cleansing God provides, not away from his table.

Leaven was banned from what was burned on the altar (2:11), but the leavened loaves of verse 13 were eaten at the meal, not burned.

What does “cut off from his people” mean? Interpreters differ: execution by the community, exclusion from the covenant people, or God’s own judgment, an early death or a line that dies out. The likeliest reading is that God himself would cut the person off; where the law means execution, it says so plainly.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-27: No fat and no blood, as permanent statutes.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Heaviest Penalty in the Dietary Law

Eating fat or blood cuts a person off from his people.
verseByVerse.examples: The reason for the ban waits until 17:11, but its seriousness was plain to everyone at once: life belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, You shall eat no fat, of ox or sheep or goat. The fat of an animal that dies of itself and the fat of one that is torn by beasts may be put to any other use, but on no account shall you eat it. For every person who eats of the fat of an animal of which a food offering may be made to the LORD shall be cut off from his people. Moreover, you shall eat no blood whatever, whether of fowl or of animal, in any of your dwelling places. Whoever eats any blood, that person shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reason is held back until 17:11, but the severity is already clear: of all the dietary rules in this book, fat and blood carry the heaviest penalty. When the first Christian council released Gentile converts from circumcision and the food laws, this is one of the four things they kept: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood (Acts 15:29).

Must Christians still avoid eating blood? The ban is older than Israel (Genesis 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it so that they could share a table with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29). Yet the New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Timothy 4:4). So most Christians hold that reverence for the life God gives remains, while meat not fully drained is not sin. And a blood transfusion is not eating at all: it gives life rather than taking it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 28-38: The wave offering and the priests' share, and the summary of the law of all the offerings.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Remarkable Provision, and a Provisional One

Seven chapters describe a single system for approaching God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priests stood daily, offering again. Now: Christ has offered one sacrifice and sat down.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, Whoever offers the sacrifice of his peace offerings to the LORD shall bring his offering to the LORD from the sacrifice of his peace offerings. His own hands shall bring the LORD's food offerings. He shall bring the fat with the breast, that the breast may be waved as a wave offering before the LORD. The priest shall burn the fat on the altar, but the breast shall be for Aaron and his sons. And the right thigh you shall give to the priest as a contribution from the sacrifice of your peace offerings. Whoever among the sons of Aaron offers the blood of the peace offerings and the fat shall have the right thigh for a portion. For the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed I have taken from the people of Israel, out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, as a perpetual due from the people of Israel. This is the portion of Aaron and of his sons from the LORD's food offerings, from the day they were presented to serve as priests of the LORD. The LORD commanded this to be given them by the people of Israel, from the day that he anointed them. It is a perpetual due throughout their generations." This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering, which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai, on the day that he commanded the people of Israel to bring their offerings to the LORD, in the wilderness of Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worshipper brings the portions with his own hands, and the summary closes the whole section: seven chapters, five offerings and the ordination rite, one system.

Stand back before the narrative resumes. Israel now has a way to approach God for devotion, for gratitude, for guilt known and unknown, for damage that needed repaying, and for ordinary fellowship, scaled from a bull to a bag of flour so that nobody was priced out. It is a remarkable provision, and, apart from the break of the exile, it ran for well over a thousand years, until the temple fell in AD 70.

The New Testament's verdict is not that it was primitive but that it was provisional. Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God (Heb. 10:11-12). The detail that carries the argument is the sitting. No chair stood among the tabernacle's furniture, because the work was never finished. He sat down.

7.theology:
The order of worship. God's careful regulation of holy things reflects that he is "not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Cor 14:33).

The sanctity of blood. The life is in the blood, and the blood belongs to God: the foundation of atonement, fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ.

The sacrifice of thanksgiving. The todah (thanksgiving) offering becomes, in Christ, the continual sacrifice of praise (Heb 13:15).
7.examples:
Then: the reconciled Israelite shared a thanksgiving feast the same day, and the priests received their portion.

Now: we offer the sacrifice of praise through Christ, support those who serve God's people, and marvel that the blood once forbidden as food is now, in Christ, the cup of salvation, received in bread and wine at his table.

8.title: The Ordination of Aaron: Consecrated by Blood and Oil
8.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments and the anointing oil and the bull of the sin offering and the two rams and the basket of unleavened bread.<sup>3</sup>And assemble all the congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting."<sup>4</sup>And Moses did as the LORD commanded him, and the congregation was assembled at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>5</sup>And Moses said to the congregation, "This is the thing that the LORD has commanded to be done."<sup>6</sup>And Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water.<sup>7</sup>And he put the coat on him and tied the sash around his waist and clothed him with the robe and put the ephod on him and tied the skillfully woven band of the ephod around him, binding it to him with the band.<sup>8</sup>And he placed the breastpiece on him, and in the breastpiece he put the Urim and the Thummim.<sup>9</sup>And he set the turban on his head, and on the turban, in front, he set the golden plate, the holy crown, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>10</sup>Then Moses took the anointing oil and anointed the tabernacle and all that was in it, and consecrated them.<sup>11</sup>And he sprinkled some of it on the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all its utensils and the basin and its stand, to consecrate them.<sup>12</sup>And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him.<sup>13</sup>And Moses brought Aaron's sons and clothed them with coats and tied sashes around their waists and bound caps on them, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>14</sup>Then he brought the bull of the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull of the sin altar and consecrated it to make atonement for it.<sup>16</sup>And he took all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat, and Moses burned them on the altar.<sup>17</sup>But the bull and its skin and its flesh and its dung he burned up with fire outside the camp, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>18</sup>Then he presented the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram.<sup>19</sup>And he killed it, and Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>20</sup>He cut the ram into pieces, and Moses burned the head and the pieces and the fat.<sup>21</sup>He washed the entrails and the legs with water, and Moses burned the whole ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering for the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>22</sup>Then he presented the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram.<sup>23</sup>And he killed it, and Moses took some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot.<sup>24</sup>Then he presented Aaron's sons, and Moses put some of the blood on the lobes of their right ears and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the big toes of their right feet. And Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>25</sup>Then he took the fat and the fat tail and all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat and the right thigh,<sup>26</sup>and out of the basket of unleavened bread that was before the LORD he took one unleavened loaf and one loaf of bread with oil and one wafer and placed them on the pieces of fat and on the right thigh.<sup>27</sup>And he put all these in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons and waved them as a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>28</sup>Then Moses took them from their hands and burned them on the altar with the burnt offering. This was an ordination offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>29</sup>And Moses took the breast and waved it for a wave offering before the LORD. It was Moses' portion of the ram of ordination, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>30</sup>Then Moses took some of the anointing oil and of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments, and also on his sons and his sons' garments. So he consecrated Aaron and his garments, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.<sup>31</sup>And Moses said to Aaron and his sons, "Boil the flesh at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and there eat it and the bread that is in the basket of ordination offerings, as I commanded, saying, 'Aaron and his sons shall eat it.'<sup>32</sup>And what remains of the flesh and the bread you shall burn up with fire.<sup>33</sup>And you shall not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are completed, for it will take seven days to ordain you.<sup>34</sup>As has been done today, the LORD has commanded to be done to make atonement for you.<sup>35</sup>At the entrance of the tent of meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, performing what the LORD has charged, so that you do not die, for so I have been commanded."<sup>36</sup>And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses.
8.overview:
From the laws of sacrifice we turn to the consecration of those who will administer them. Chapters 8–10 tell the ordination of Aaron and his sons, their first ministry, and the catastrophe that follows. Chapter 8 is the seven-day ceremony of installation, carried out by Moses, who here acts as presiding priest: the mediator who installs the mediators.

Aaron is washed, clothed not in his own righteousness but in robes provided for him, anointed with oil, and marked with blood: the whole man consecrated by sacrifice. He could not appoint himself; everything was done to him by another.

All of it anticipates Christ. Many Christians have seen its pattern at his baptism, when the Spirit descended like a dove and the Father spoke (Matthew 3:16–17), the anointing Peter later describes, and Hebrews confirms that Jesus, like Aaron, was called by God to be High Priest (Hebrews 5:4–6). Yet the contrast is greater still: Aaron needed blood for his own sin; Christ needed no cleansing, but shed his own blood to consecrate his people. With the ear that perfectly heard the Father, the hands that only did good, the feet that never strayed, wholly consecrated, he makes us "a kingdom, priests to his God" (Rev 1:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-5: The whole congregation is gathered, because the ordination is public.

Verses 6-9: Aaron and his sons are washed, then Aaron is clothed in the high priest's garments.

Verses 10-13: The tabernacle is anointed first, then Aaron's head.
verseByVerse.theology:
Anointed

Aaron is washed, robed and anointed by another, in front of everyone.
verseByVerse.examples: The priesthood was installed in public, before the people it would serve. Leaders in the church, too, are called and recognised openly, not self-appointed.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments and the anointing oil and the bull of the sin offering and the two rams and the basket of unleavened bread. And assemble all the congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting." And Moses did as the LORD commanded him, and the congregation was assembled at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And Moses said to the congregation, "This is the thing that the LORD has commanded to be done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven chapters of instruction end and the narrative resumes. The design given in Exodus 29 is now carried out, and the first thing the text insists on is the audience.

The whole nation is called to watch men become priests. Israel needs to see who has been appointed, by whose authority, and at what cost, because a priesthood that installs itself is answerable to nobody. The New Testament says the same of the same office: no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was (Heb. 5:4).
verseByVerse.note: Moses follows the instructions of Exodus 29 point by point.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water. And he put the coat on him and tied the sash around his waist and clothed him with the robe and put the ephod on him and tied the skillfully woven band of the ephod around him, binding it to him with the band. And he placed the breastpiece on him, and in the breastpiece he put the Urim and the Thummim. And he set the turban on his head, and on the turban, in front, he set the golden plate, the holy crown, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Washing comes before a single garment goes on. Whatever else ordination is, it begins with a man being cleaned by somebody else.

Exodus tells us what was engraved on the golden plate: Holy to the LORD (Ex. 28:36). Aaron wore those words on his forehead, where everyone could read them and he could not. A man was declared holy by an inscription he could never see for himself.

The Urim and Thummim were most likely sacred lots kept in the breastpiece, by which the high priest asked God for a yes or no (Num 27:21; 1 Sam 14:41). They disappear after the early monarchy; God now guides through his completed word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses took the anointing oil and anointed the tabernacle and all that was in it, and consecrated them. And he sprinkled some of it on the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all its utensils and the basin and its stand, to consecrate them. And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him. And Moses brought Aaron's sons and clothed them with coats and tied sashes around their waists and bound caps on them, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The oil touches objects first: the tabernacle, the altar seven times, the basin. Only then is it poured on Aaron.

The root behind anointed gives mashiach, messiah. Priests, kings and prophets were anointed, and each anointing was a small advance payment on a title that would belong to one man who held all three offices at once.

Then Aaron's sons are clothed. The office is not his alone and does not end with him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-21 — The Sin Offering and Burnt Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-21: Before the new priests serve anyone, a bull and a ram die for them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priest Needed What He Was Appointed to Administer

The sin offering comes first, then the burnt offering.
verseByVerse.examples: Guilt was dealt with before devotion was expressed. Christians still come to God in that order: forgiven first, then offering themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought the bull of the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull of the sin offering. And he killed it, and Moses took the blood, and with his finger put it on the horns of the altar around it and purified the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar and consecrated it to make atonement for it. And he took all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat, and Moses burned them on the altar. But the bull and its skin and its flesh and its dung he burned up with fire outside the camp, as the LORD commanded Moses. Then he presented the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram. And he killed it, and Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar. He cut the ram into pieces, and Moses burned the head and the pieces and the fat. He washed the entrails and the legs with water, and Moses burned the whole ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering for the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men about to be the nation's mediators must first stand where any guilty Israelite stands, hands pressed on an animal dying in their place. Then the ram, wholly consumed. Guilt is dealt with before devotion is expressed.

Nothing about ordination made Aaron less of a sinner. He needed the remedy he was appointed to administer, and that he needed it first is what Hebrews seizes on in describing a better priest: He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself (Heb. 7:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 22-24: The ram of ordination, with blood put on the right ear, thumb and toe.

Verses 25-30: The priests' hands are filled and the portions waved; oil and blood are sprinkled on the men and their garments.
verseByVerse.theology:
Ear, Thumb, Toe

Blood is put on the faculties a priest uses, and on his new clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the new vestments were splashed with blood on their first day. Now: what we hear, do and walk toward belongs to the one who bought us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he presented the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram. And he killed it, and Moses took some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. Then he presented Aaron's sons, and Moses put some of the blood on the lobes of their right ears and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the big toes of their right feet. And Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the strangest gesture in the ceremony, and the three points are not random. The ear hears God's word. The thumb does the work; no hand grips anything without it. The big toe is what a man stands and walks on. Hearing, working, going: the blood is applied to the faculties a priest will actually use.

Consecration is not an inward mood but a claim on the parts of a person that do things. Paul asks the same by the mercies of God: present your bodies as a living sacrifice (Rom. 12:1). Not your sentiments but your body, the thing that turns up places and handles things, offered because it has already been bought.
verseByVerse.note: The right side was the side of strength and honour in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he took the fat and the fat tail and all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat and the right thigh, and out of the basket of unleavened bread that was before the LORD he took one unleavened loaf and one loaf of bread with oil and one wafer and placed them on the pieces of fat and on the right thigh. And he put all these in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons and waved them as a wave offering before the LORD. Then Moses took them from their hands and burned them on the altar with the burnt offering. This was an ordination offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. And Moses took the breast and waved it for a wave offering before the LORD. It was Moses' portion of the ram of ordination, as the LORD commanded Moses. Then Moses took some of the anointing oil and of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments, and also on his sons and his sons' garments. So he consecrated Aaron and his garments, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses then takes the portions back from their hands and burns them (v. 28). The Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest is to fill his hands, and here it is acted out: a man was made a priest by having his hands filled with something he then gave away.

Then oil and blood together, on the men and on their clothes. Those vestments were the finest work in Israel, gold thread and blue and scarlet, and on the day they were first worn they were splashed with sacrificial blood. The garments that made a priest look holy were permanently marked with the evidence of what holiness had cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-36 — Seven Days at the Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 31-36: Seven days at the door of the tent, and Aaron and his sons do all that the LORD commanded.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sentence Laid Down Before It Detonates

A week at the threshold ends in full obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: The ordination took a week of waiting at the threshold. Some of God's best preparation of his servants looks like staying put.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Aaron and his sons, "Boil the flesh at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and there eat it and the bread that is in the basket of ordination offerings, as I commanded, saying, 'Aaron and his sons shall eat it.' And what remains of the flesh and the bread you shall burn up with fire. And you shall not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are completed, for it will take seven days to ordain you. As has been done today, the LORD has commanded to be done to make atonement for you. At the entrance of the tent of meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, performing what the LORD has charged, so that you do not die, for so I have been commanded." And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last instruction is about staying put. The ceremony is not a morning's event but a week, and for that week Aaron and his sons live at the threshold of the tent, going nowhere, repeating the offerings each day.

The chapter ends with a sentence Leviticus uses like a refrain: they did all the things that the LORD commanded. Chapters 8 and 9 turn on that clause, and chapter 10 opens with two men who did something the LORD had not commanded. The narrator lays the contrast down before it detonates; the only priest who would never break that refrain is the one Aaron foreshadowed.

8.theology:
Priesthood conferred from outside. Aaron is washed, robed, anointed and atoned for by another; in the same way we are made priests by grace.

Whole-life consecration. Blood on ear, hand and foot claims the entire person for God, as Christ claims every faculty of those he saves.

The anointing of the Spirit. The oil poured on Aaron foreshadows the Spirit who anointed Christ at his baptism and now anoints his people (1 John 2:20; Acts 10:38).
8.examples:
Then: for seven days Moses washed, robed, anointed and blooded Aaron and his sons, setting apart Israel's priesthood with fearful reverence.

Now: Christ is our consecrated High Priest, and by his blood and Spirit he makes us "a royal priesthood" (1 Pet 2:9), our whole lives set apart for God.

9.title: The Glory Appears: Fire from Heaven
9.text: <sup>1</sup>On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel,<sup>2</sup>and he said to Aaron, "Take for yourself a bull calf for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and offer them before the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And say to the people of Israel, 'Take a male goat for a sin offering, and a calf and a lamb, both a year old without blemish, for a burnt offering,<sup>4</sup>and an ox and a ram for peace offerings, to sacrifice before the LORD, and a grain offering mixed with oil, for today the LORD will appear to you.'"<sup>5</sup>And they brought what Moses commanded in front of the tent of meeting, and all the congregation drew near and stood before the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you."<sup>7</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "Draw near to the altar and offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people, and bring the offering of the people and make atonement for them, as the LORD has commanded."<sup>8</sup>So Aaron drew near to the altar and killed the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself.<sup>9</sup>And the sons of Aaron presented the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and put it on the horns of the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar.<sup>10</sup>But the fat and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver from the sin offering he burned on the altar, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>11</sup>The flesh and the skin he burned up with fire outside the camp.<sup>12</sup>Then he killed the burnt offering, and Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar.<sup>13</sup>And they handed the burnt offering to him, piece by piece, and the head, and he burned them on the altar.<sup>14</sup>And he washed the entrails and the legs and burned them with the burnt offering on the altar.<sup>15</sup>Then he presented the people's offering and took the goat of the sin offering that was for the people and killed it and offered it as a sin offering, like the first one.<sup>16</sup>And he presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the rule.<sup>17</sup>And he presented the grain offering, took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar, besides the burnt offering of the morning.<sup>18</sup>Then he killed the ox and the ram, the sacrifice of peace offerings for the people. And Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar.<sup>19</sup>But the fat pieces of the ox and of the ram, the fat tail and that which covers the entrails and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver—<sup>20</sup>they put the fat pieces on the breasts, and he burned the fat pieces on the altar,<sup>21</sup>but the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded.<sup>22</sup>Then Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and he came down from offering the sin offering and the burnt offering and the peace offerings.<sup>23</sup>And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and when they came out they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people.<sup>24</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
9.overview:
The seven days of preparation are over, and the eighth day dawns. Everything drives toward one promised moment: "that the glory of the LORD may appear to you" (9:6). All the offerings, all the blood, all the careful ritual aim at this: that sinners might behold the glory of God and live.

And the glory comes. Fire from God's presence consumes the offering. This is heaven's amen, God's visible acceptance of the sacrifice: the God who is a consuming fire consumes the substitute and spares the people. They answer in the only fitting way: "when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces" (9:24). Joy and awe belong together here, the worship of people who have seen the fire fall and lived.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: On the eighth day the priesthood begins its work, and Moses gives the order of the day: atonement first, for the priest and then for the people.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the man who will stand between God and the people must first be covered himself. Every human mediator in Israel was a sinner in need of the sacrifice he offered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: everything since Exodus 25 led to this one day. Now: we come to God through a priest who never had to offer anything for himself, and so his whole work is for us.

verseByVerse.quote: On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel, and he said to Aaron, "Take for yourself a bull calf for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and offer them before the LORD. And say to the people of Israel, 'Take a male goat for a sin offering, and a calf and a lamb, both a year old without blemish, for a burnt offering, and an ox and a ram for peace offerings, to sacrifice before the LORD, and a grain offering mixed with oil, for today the LORD will appear to you.'" And they brought what Moses commanded in front of the tent of meeting, and all the congregation drew near and stood before the LORD. And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you." Then Moses said to Aaron, "Draw near to the altar and offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people, and bring the offering of the people and make atonement for them, as the LORD has commanded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel. The week at the door is over. This is the first day the priesthood actually works.

And Moses tells them why they are doing it: for today the LORD will appear to you. Everything since Exodus 25 has been arranged so that a nation of former slaves can survive the presence of God in their camp. Today he arrives.

But before that comes an order which the New Testament will never stop pointing at: Offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people. For yourself first. Aaron cannot carry anyone else's guilt until his own has been dealt with, and the sequence is stated so plainly that it becomes the hinge of the argument in Hebrews for why we needed a different priest, one holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, who had no sins of his own to clear out of the way first (Heb. 7:26-27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-14: Aaron makes his own sin offering and burnt offering, step by step, with his sons handing him the blood and the pieces.
verseByVerse.theology: In Leviticus the careful procedure is itself the message: God is approached in the way he has given, not in a way we invent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the whole day rested on Aaron doing exactly what he was told. Now: our peace with God rests on what Christ did exactly as the Father willed, not on how well we perform our worship.

verseByVerse.quote: So Aaron drew near to the altar and killed the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself. And the sons of Aaron presented the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and put it on the horns of the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar. But the fat and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver from the sin offering he burned on the altar, as the LORD commanded Moses. The flesh and the skin he burned up with fire outside the camp. Then he killed the burnt offering, and Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar. And they handed the burnt offering to him, piece by piece, and the head, and he burned them on the altar. And he washed the entrails and the legs and burned them with the burnt offering on the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator slows down to record each step in deliberately unhurried prose: blood on the horns of the altar, the fat burned, the flesh and skin taken outside the camp. A man in new clothes is carefully doing what he was told, in order, while a nation watches, and the whole weight of the day rests on his getting it right.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-24 — The People's Offerings, and the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 15-21: The people's offerings follow in their order: sin, burnt, grain, then peace.

Verses 22-24: Aaron blesses the people, the glory appears, and fire consumes the offering.
verseByVerse.theology: The fire is God's answer. It shows that he has accepted the sacrifice offered in his appointed way, and so has accepted the people for whom it was offered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people knew they were accepted because they saw the fire fall. Now: we know we are accepted because God raised Jesus from the dead, his public sign that the sacrifice was received.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he presented the people's offering and took the goat of the sin offering that was for the people and killed it and offered it as a sin offering, like the first one. And he presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the rule. And he presented the grain offering, took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar, besides the burnt offering of the morning. Then he killed the ox and the ram, the sacrifice of peace offerings for the people. And Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar. But the fat pieces of the ox and of the ram, the fat tail and that which covers the entrails and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver— they put the fat pieces on the breasts, and he burned the fat pieces on the altar, but the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin dealt with, then total consecration, then the gift of ordinary produce, and last of all the shared meal, because the peace offering is the one Israel eats. The order runs from guilt removed to a family sitting down to dinner in God's presence, and that is the shape of the whole book compressed into one morning.

One detail is easy to miss: the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded. Even on the greatest day of his life, the measure of Aaron's action is not his instinct but his instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and he came down from offering the sin offering and the burnt offering and the peace offerings. And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and when they came out they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Aaron lifts his hands toward the people and blesses them, and comes down. He and Moses go into the tent, and come out, and bless the people again.

Many Christians have seen here a picture of our own High Priest. Jesus lifted up his hands and blessed his disciples as he was carried up into heaven (Luke 24:50–51), and Hebrews says that, having entered the true holy place, he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him (Hebrews 9:28).

This is what the whole book has been building toward: not the fire as spectacle, but the fire as answer. God had specified an offering; the offering was made exactly as specified; and God came out and took it. The shout and the faces in the dust are the response of people who have just watched heaven accept something on their behalf.

In the very next chapter the same sentence returns: And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them (10:2). The words are the same and the outcome is the opposite, and the difference is not the intensity of the fire but whether what it fell on had been authorised.

Then, centuries later, in a house in Jerusalem, divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them (Acts 2:3). Fire came down and settled on people, and they were not consumed. The difference between Leviticus 9 and Acts 2 is not that God had become less holy. It is that by then the offering had already been made, once, outside a city wall, and accepted; so when the fire came to rest on human beings, it came to dwell in them, not to judge them.

9.theology:
The goal of worship is glory. All the offerings aim at the appearing of God's glory (9:6, 23). That glory is now seen "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6).

Acceptance through a substitute. The fire from heaven seals God's acceptance of the sacrifice. The judgment that the altar pictured fell, at the last, on Christ, and because it fell on him it need never fall on those who trust him.
9.examples:
Then: Israel saw the fire fall, and shouted and fell on their faces.

Now: Because the fire of judgment fell on Christ, we behold God's glory not in terror but in worship. The right response to grace is still both: glad praise and humble awe before the God who accepts us in his Son.

10.title: Nadab and Abihu: Unauthorized Fire
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them.<sup>2</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD has said: 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.'" And Aaron held his peace.<sup>4</sup>And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said to them, "Come near; carry your brothers away from the front of the sanctuary and out of the camp."<sup>5</sup>So they came near and carried them in their coats out of the camp, as Moses had said.<sup>6</sup>And Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation; but let your brothers, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled.<sup>7</sup>And do not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting, lest you die, for the anointing oil of the LORD is upon you." And they did according to the word of Moses.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD spoke to Aaron, saying,<sup>9</sup>"Drink no wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations.<sup>10</sup>You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean,<sup>11</sup>and you are to teach the people of Israel all the statutes that the LORD has spoken to them by Moses."<sup>12</sup>Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his surviving sons: "Take the grain offering that is left of the LORD's food offerings, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, for it is most holy.<sup>13</sup>You shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your due and your sons' due, from the LORD's food offerings, for so I am commanded.<sup>14</sup>But the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed you shall eat in a clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you, for they are given as your due and your sons' due from the sacrifices of the peace offerings of the people of Israel.<sup>15</sup>The thigh that is contributed and the breast that is waved they shall bring with the food offerings of the fat pieces to wave for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as a due forever, as the LORD has commanded."<sup>16</sup>Now Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it was burned up! And he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the surviving sons of Aaron, saying,<sup>17</sup>"Why have you not eaten the sin offering in the place of the sanctuary, since it is a thing most holy and has been given to you that you may bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD?<sup>18</sup>Behold, its blood was not brought into the inner part of the sanctuary. You certainly ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as I commanded."<sup>19</sup>And Aaron said to Moses, "Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the LORD have approved?"<sup>20</sup>And when Moses heard that, he approved.
10.overview:
The same fire that fell in blessing now falls in judgment. Before the smoke of acceptance has cleared, Aaron's own sons offer "unauthorized fire" (10:1), and the holy fire that consumed the sacrifice consumes them.

Most readers recoil: was the punishment not too severe? The question deserves to be felt, and the chapter does not hide the cost; it shows a father who loses two sons in a moment. Its answer is that God had just come to live among sinners, and he would be approached as he had said, not as they pleased: they offered fire "which he had not commanded" (10:1). The wonder is not that Nadab and Abihu died, but that any of us live.

The chapter also ends in mercy. A grieving father who cannot bring himself to eat the sin offering gives his reason, and is told he is right. The same God who will not be trifled with makes room for a broken heart. Christians come to him by the one way he has opened, the new and living way through Christ's flesh (Heb 10:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: Two of Aaron's sons die before the LORD, and their father is forbidden even to mourn them in public.
verseByVerse.theology: The same fire that accepted the offering in chapter 9 now judges presumption. God's holiness is the reason for both: it is life to those who come his way and danger to those who do not.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Aaron had to let God be right on the worst day of his life. Now: a believer may grieve openly and still trust, for our High Priest has wept beside a grave himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD. Then Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD has said: 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.'" And Aaron held his peace. And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said to them, "Come near; carry your brothers away from the front of the sanctuary and out of the camp." So they came near and carried them in their coats out of the camp, as Moses had said. And Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation; but let your brothers, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled. And do not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting, lest you die, for the anointing oil of the LORD is upon you." And they did according to the word of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The happiest day becomes the most terrible: the same fire that had blessed now kills. Moses explains it: "Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified." The nearer a person stands to God (and no one stood nearer than these priests), the more seriously God's holiness must be honoured. He will not be treated as common or worshipped however we please.

This is the sober truth that stands beside all the grace of Leviticus. Yes, God has flung open a way to himself; but he is still the God who is "a consuming fire" (Heb 12:29), and we come with reverence and awe, not casual familiarity. And then: "Aaron held his peace." It is faith bowing before God, saying with silence something like what Job said in words: "the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:21). But it is not the silence of a man who felt little, as the next verses show.

The bodies are carried out by Aaron's cousins, and to Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar, Moses says: do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, do not tear your clothes, do not step outside the entrance, lest you die. These were Israel's customary signs of grief: Aaron may not mourn his own sons.

Why? Not because the grief was wrong. Israel is expressly given what Aaron is denied: "let your brothers, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled." The nation may weep. The father may not. Two reasons stand together. "The anointing oil of the LORD is upon you": they have only just been ordained (chs 8-9); to walk out now would be to desert the post God had just given them. And deeper: for the priests to take up the public signs of mourning would be a public protest, a way of saying before all Israel that God's verdict on the strange fire was wrong. They must stand in the hour of their own bereavement and let God be right.

So read verse 3 again. "Aaron held his peace" is the silence of a father with two dead sons and a command not to weep. Israel had a high priest who was not permitted to weep at a tomb. We have a High Priest who wept at one: standing at the grave of his friend, knowing he was about to raise him, Jesus wept (John 11:35). The priest who could not mourn points us to the Priest who could, and who would himself bear on the cross the fire of God’s judgment, so that the fire which fell on Nadab and Abihu need never fall on us.

What was the “unauthorized fire”? The text says only that it was fire which he had not commanded them. Most likely they took coals from somewhere other than the altar (cf. 16:12), or offered incense at a time and in a way God had not prescribed; the warning against drink in verse 9 suggests they may also have been drunk.

Does this establish the regulative principle of worship? The Reformed tradition holds that God may be worshipped only in the ways he commands in Scripture (Deut 12:32; Matt 15:9; Westminster Confession 21.1). Others hold the normative principle: whatever Scripture does not forbid is allowed. The death of Nadab and Abihu shows that God cares how he is worshipped, and the regulative principle is the safer course: the elements of worship are reading and preaching the word, prayer, singing, and the sacraments, while circumstances such as time and place are left to wisdom. Faithful Christians differ here, and both sides agree on the chapter's main lesson: worship is shaped by what pleases God, not by what pleases us.

Does their death mean Nadab and Abihu were lost for ever? Scripture does not say. It records a judgment in this life on a public sin at a decisive moment, much like the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira at the start of the church (Acts 5:1–11), and leaves their eternal state with God. Such sudden judgments are rare in Scripture and come mostly at new beginnings, as warnings written down for all who come after (1 Corinthians 10:11). The warning is real; so is the way of approach God has opened in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Unauthorized fire” can be rendered “strange fire” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-11 — Distinguish the Holy from the Common
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-11: God speaks to Aaron alone, a rare thing in Leviticus, and the subject is a clear head for holy work.
verseByVerse.theology: The priest's essential work was to tell the holy from the common and to teach God's people to see the difference.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: what the priest discerned, he taught. Now: pastors and parents still do this work, and need clear heads and a steady diet of Scripture to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Aaron, saying, "Drink no wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations. You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean, and you are to teach the people of Israel all the statutes that the LORD has spoken to them by Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The timing suggests the warning may be connected to what had just happened: careless, perhaps intoxicated, worship. But the reason God gives opens up the whole calling of the priest: they must be clear-headed "to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean," and "to teach the people" all of God's statutes. This is the heartbeat of Leviticus. When a people can no longer tell these things apart, holiness itself is lost (Ezek 22:26). Recovering them, learning to call holy what God calls holy, is still the work of God's word in his people, training us "to distinguish good from evil" (Heb 5:14).

Must Christians abstain from wine before worship or ministry? This was for priests on duty. Scripture does not require total abstinence (Ps 104:15; John 2:1–11), but it forbids drunkenness and bids us be filled with the Spirit instead (Eph 5:18), and elders must not be a drunkard (1 Tim 3:3). The principle remains: a clear head for holy things.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-20 — Grief and Grace at the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 12-15: Life at the altar goes on: the surviving priests are to eat their portion.

Verses 16-20: A rule is not kept, Moses is angry, and Aaron at last speaks.
verseByVerse.theology: The law was never a machine. The holy God who judged presumption also weighs the heart of a grieving man.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a grieving father's reason was accepted. Now: in seasons of loss, when ordinary duties are beyond us, we may tell God so honestly and expect to be understood.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his surviving sons: "Take the grain offering that is left of the LORD's food offerings, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, for it is most holy. You shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your due and your sons' due, from the LORD's food offerings, for so I am commanded. But the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed you shall eat in a clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you, for they are given as your due and your sons' due from the sacrifices of the peace offerings of the people of Israel. The thigh that is contributed and the breast that is waved they shall bring with the food offerings of the fat pieces to wave for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as a due forever, as the LORD has commanded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With two bodies just carried out of the camp, Moses turns to the surviving priests and tells them to eat their dinner.

It sounds almost brutal until you see what it is doing. The offerings are still holy; the priests are still priests; the arrangement God made has not been suspended because a disaster has happened inside it. Aaron is being told that his sons' sin has not disqualified the office or contaminated the food. Life at the altar goes on, and he is to sit down and eat as the law provides.

There is a particular mercy in the detail your sons and your daughters with you. The family that has just lost two of its men is named, together, as the people who will eat this. Grief does not put a household outside the provision of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it was burned up! And he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the surviving sons of Aaron, saying, "Why have you not eaten the sin offering in the place of the sanctuary, since it is a thing most holy and has been given to you that you may bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD? Behold, its blood was not brought into the inner part of the sanctuary. You certainly ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as I commanded." And Aaron said to Moses, "Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the LORD have approved?" And when Moses heard that, he approved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rule had not been kept, and Aaron's answer is the only thing he says in the whole chapter. Its key is such things as these have happened to me: the grief finally surfacing. In verse 3 he held his peace; here, sixteen verses later, a father who was forbidden to tear his clothes or let his hair down says the one sentence he is allowed.

His argument is not a technicality. When the priests ate the sin offering, they were acting for the people before God, confident that he had accepted it. Aaron is saying that he could not act with that confidence on the day God had killed his sons for presumption. To go through the motions would have been the very sin the day had just punished.

Moses approved, and that shows something about God which the rest of the chapter might have hidden. This is the same chapter in which fire came out and killed two men for doing what was not commanded, and it ends with a man not doing what was commanded, giving his reason, and being told he was right. The law was never a machine. It was always administered by a God who knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Ps. 103:14), and who does not break a bruised reed (Isa. 42:3).

Both things stand in the same twenty verses and neither cancels the other. He is a consuming fire, and he makes room for a father who cannot eat.

10.theology:
The holiness of God. God must be approached on his terms, not ours, and the greater the privilege, the greater the responsibility: those brought nearest must honour him most.

The only way. There is one acceptable approach to the Father, and it is Christ (John 14:6), who bore the judgment we deserved.
10.examples:
Then: Aaron's sons were consumed, and their father bowed in silence before the holiness of God.

Now: we are warned against casual, self-styled worship, and we are also shown a God who hears the honest grief of his servants.

11.title: Clean and Unclean: A People Set Apart
11.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying to them,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, These are the living things that you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth.<sup>3</sup>Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat.<sup>4</sup>Nevertheless, among those that chew the cud or part the hoof, you shall not eat these: The camel, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>5</sup>And the rock badger, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>6</sup>And the hare, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>7</sup>And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed but does not chew the cud, is unclean to you.<sup>8</sup>You shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses; they are unclean to you.<sup>9</sup>"These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat.<sup>10</sup>But anything in the seas or the rivers that does not have fins and scales, of the swarming creatures in the waters and of the living creatures that are in the waters, is detestable to you.<sup>11</sup>You shall regard them as detestable; you shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall detest their carcasses.<sup>12</sup>Everything in the waters that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you.<sup>13</sup>"And these you shall detest among the birds; they shall not be eaten; they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,<sup>14</sup>the kite, the falcon of any kind,<sup>15</sup>every raven of any kind,<sup>16</sup>the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind,<sup>17</sup>the little owl, the cormorant, the short-eared owl,<sup>18</sup>the barn owl, the tawny owl, the carrion vulture,<sup>19</sup>the stork, the heron of any kind, the hoopoe, and the bat.<sup>20</sup>"All winged insects that go on all fours are detestable to you.<sup>21</sup>Yet among the winged insects that go on all fours you may eat those that have jointed legs above their feet, with which to hop on the ground.<sup>22</sup>Of them you may eat: the locust of any kind, the bald locust of any kind, the cricket of any kind, and the grasshopper of any kind.<sup>23</sup>But all other winged insects that have four feet are detestable to you.<sup>24</sup>"And by these you shall become unclean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>25</sup>and whoever carries any part of their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening.<sup>26</sup>Every animal that parts the hoof but is not cloven-footed or does not chew the cud is unclean to you. Everyone who touches them shall be unclean.<sup>27</sup>And all that walk on their paws, among the animals that go on all fours, are unclean to you. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>28</sup>and he who carries their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening; they are unclean to you.<sup>29</sup>"And these are unclean to you among the swarming things that swarm on the ground: the mole rat, the mouse, the great lizard of any kind,<sup>30</sup>the gecko, the monitor lizard, the lizard, the sand lizard, and the chameleon.<sup>31</sup>These are unclean to you among all that swarm. Whoever touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until the evening.<sup>32</sup>And anything on which any of them falls when they are dead shall be unclean, whether it is an article of wood or a garment or a skin or a sack, any article that is used for any purpose. It must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it shall be clean.<sup>33</sup>And if any of them falls into any earthenware vessel, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it.<sup>34</sup>Any food in it that could be eaten, on which water comes, shall be unclean. And all drink that could be drunk from every such vessel shall be unclean.<sup>35</sup>And everything on which any part of their carcass falls shall be unclean. Whether oven or stove, it shall be broken in pieces. They are unclean and shall remain unclean for you.<sup>36</sup>Nevertheless, a spring or a cistern holding water shall be clean, but whoever touches a carcass in them shall be unclean.<sup>37</sup>And if any part of their carcass falls upon any seed grain that is to be sown, it is clean,<sup>38</sup>but if water is put on the seed and any part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean to you.<sup>39</sup>"And if any animal which you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>40</sup>and whoever eats of its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries the carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening.<sup>41</sup>"Every swarming thing that swarms on the ground is detestable; it shall not be eaten.<sup>42</sup>Whatever goes on its belly, and whatever goes on all fours, or whatever has many feet, any swarming thing that swarms on the ground, you shall not eat, for they are detestable.<sup>43</sup>You shall not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, and you shall not defile yourselves with them, and become unclean through them.<sup>44</sup>For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy. You shall not defile yourselves with any swarming thing that crawls on the ground.<sup>45</sup>For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy."<sup>46</sup>This is the law about beast and bird and every living creature that moves through the waters and every creature that swarms on the ground,<sup>47</sup>to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean and between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten.
11.overview:
Now begins the section on clean and unclean (chs 11–15), opening with the food laws. To a modern reader the rules can seem arbitrary, and the text gives no reason for any single one of them. Readers have suggested hygiene, the avoidance of pagan worship, or a symbolism of order. This commentary thinks the clearest thread is the one the chapter itself keeps touching: many of the forbidden creatures live on flesh or carrion, and every rule about touching concerns carcasses, so the laws kept death away from the table of the living God. But the chapter's own emphasis falls less on the reason for each rule than on the rule itself: Israel was to be a people who could tell one thing from another, and who were visibly different at every meal.

The chapter ends with the refrain that will run through the rest of Leviticus: "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (11:44–45). God grounds it in redemption: "I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (11:45). Holiness is the grateful response of a redeemed people to their redeeming God. The verse notes on vv. 44-47 show what happened to the food laws and to that refrain in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-12: For land and water creatures the law gives a double test that anyone can apply.

Verses 13-23: Birds are handled by a list rather than a test, and winged insects are forbidden except the locust family.
verseByVerse.theology: The tests are simple enough for any Israelite to use at a market stall. God's holiness was not kept among the experts; it was to be practised by ordinary people in ordinary choices.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: every shopping trip trained Israel to tell one thing from another, the very skill God asked of the priests in 10:10. Now: Christians are trained in the same habit of discernment, though the choices now concern conduct rather than menus.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying to them, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, These are the living things that you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat. Nevertheless, among those that chew the cud or part the hoof, you shall not eat these: The camel, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the rock badger, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the hare, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed but does not chew the cud, is unclean to you. You shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses; they are unclean to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dietary laws arrive without a word of explanation for the individual rules, and the test for land animals is doubled: an animal must both part the hoof and chew the cud.

So four animals are named and disqualified precisely because they pass one test and fail the other: the camel, the rock badger and the hare chew but do not part the hoof; the pig parts the hoof but does not chew.

Sceptics point out that the hare is not a ruminant like the cow. True, but the law is describing what an ordinary observer sees, a creature that keeps chewing, and the hare does in fact eat its own droppings to digest its food a second time. Scripture classifies animals by appearance and use, not by the categories of modern zoology, and is not in error for doing so.

The reasons readers have proposed are weighed in the chapter overview. What the text itself gives, over and over, is not the reason but the test.
verseByVerse.note: Deuteronomy 14:3-21 repeats these food laws with small differences.

verseByVerse.quote: "These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat. But anything in the seas or the rivers that does not have fins and scales, of the swarming creatures in the waters and of the living creatures that are in the waters, is detestable to you. You shall regard them as detestable; you shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall detest their carcasses. Everything in the waters that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Detestable comes four times in three verses. The rule sweeps out shellfish, eels and every bottom-feeder at a stroke. An Israelite standing at a market stall did not need a priest. He needed only to look for fins and scales.

Why do Christians eat shellfish (11:10) yet still hold to the sexual laws of chapter 18? Because the New Testament itself draws the line. The food laws marked Israel off from the nations, and Jesus and the apostles lift them explicitly (see vv. 44-47). The sexual laws rest on creation (Genesis 2:24), were binding on the Canaanites too (18:24–25), and are repeated by the apostles (Romans 1:26–27; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11). That is following the apostles, not picking and choosing. Israel's civil penalties ended with Israel's state, and the gospel offers washing to every sinner: such were some of you.

verseByVerse.quote: "And these you shall detest among the birds; they shall not be eaten; they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, the kite, the falcon of any kind, every raven of any kind, the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind, the little owl, the cormorant, the short-eared owl, the barn owl, the tawny owl, the carrion vulture, the stork, the heron of any kind, the hoopoe, and the bat. "All winged insects that go on all fours are detestable to you. Yet among the winged insects that go on all fours you may eat those that have jointed legs above their feet, with which to hop on the ground. Of them you may eat: the locust of any kind, the bald locust of any kind, the cricket of any kind, and the grasshopper of any kind. But all other winged insects that have four feet are detestable to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Birds are handled not by criteria but by a list. Eagle, vulture, kite, falcon, raven, ostrich, nighthawk, sea gull, hawk, owl, cormorant, stork, heron, hoopoe, bat. The bat is here because the Hebrew word means winged creatures, not birds in the modern scientific sense. Many of them are birds of prey or scavengers: creatures that live on flesh, and on flesh that is already dead.

That fits the thread this commentary follows through the chapter: whatever feeds on death is kept away from the table of a people who worship the living God.

Then insects: "on all fours" is an everyday way of saying creatures that creep along the ground, and the locust family is the surprising exception. Centuries later a man would live in the wilderness on locusts and wild honey (Mark 1:6), and Mark's first readers would have recognised that John the Baptist was eating clean food, in the desert, off the land.
verseByVerse.note: The identity of many of these birds is uncertain (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24-47 — Uncleanness, Death, and 'Be Holy, for I Am Holy'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 24-43: The law moves from eating to touching, and from the altar into the kitchen.

Verses 44-47: The chapter closes with its reason: God's own holiness.
verseByVerse.theology: Uncleanness here is not sin. It comes from contact with death, and it is removed by washing and waiting, which taught Israel that death does not belong in God's presence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a dead mouse in the flour was a matter for God's law. Now: no corner of an ordinary day is too small for a Christian to live it before God.

verseByVerse.quote: "And by these you shall become unclean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening, and whoever carries any part of their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. Every animal that parts the hoof but is not cloven-footed or does not chew the cud is unclean to you. Everyone who touches them shall be unclean. And all that walk on their paws, among the animals that go on all fours, are unclean to you.
