Take the whole block of chapters together (food, childbirth, disease, discharge) and the cumulative message is unmistakable. There is no area of ordinary human life untouched by corruption, and none of it can be argued away as somebody's fault.

Which is precisely the problem the next chapter exists to solve. After five chapters showing that uncleanness reaches everywhere and never stops, Leviticus provides one day in the year when all of it, known and unknown, is dealt with at once.

15.theology:
Uncleanness is not guilt. The chapter blames no one. It describes the condition of mortal bodies in a fallen world, and so teaches humility without shame.

Guarding God's presence. The purity laws exist to protect the dwelling of God among his people (15:31), the very thing Israel could not live without.

The reversal in Christ. Under the law uncleanness spread by touch. In Christ it is holiness that spreads, and cleansing flows from him to us.
15.examples:
Then: ordinary bodily life made every Israelite unclean again and again.

Now: like the woman in the crowd, we come to Jesus as we are, and he does not shrink from us. He makes us clean, and calls us his own.

16.title: The Day of Atonement: The Heart of the Gospel
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before the LORD and died,<sup>2</sup>and the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat that is on the ark, so that he may not die. For I will appear in the cloud over the mercy seat.<sup>3</sup>But in this way Aaron shall come into the Holy Place: with a bull from the herd for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering.<sup>4</sup>He shall put on the holy linen coat and shall have the linen undergarment on his body, and he shall tie the linen sash around his waist, and wear the linen turban; these are the holy garments. He shall bathe his body in water and then put them on.<sup>5</sup>And he shall take from the congregation of the people of Israel two male goats for a sin offering, and one ram for a burnt offering.<sup>6</sup>"Aaron shall offer the bull as a sin offering for himself and shall make atonement for himself and for his house.<sup>7</sup>Then he shall take the two goats and set them before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>8</sup>And Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats, one lot for the LORD and the other lot for Azazel.<sup>9</sup>And Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for the LORD and use it as a sin offering,<sup>10</sup>but the goat on which the lot fell for Azazel shall be presented alive before the LORD to make atonement over it, that it may be sent away into the wilderness to Azazel.<sup>11</sup>"Aaron shall present the bull as a sin offering for himself, and shall make atonement for himself and for his house. He shall kill the bull as a sin offering for himself.<sup>12</sup>And he shall take a censer full of coals of fire from the altar before the LORD, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and he shall bring it inside the veil<sup>13</sup>and put the incense on the fire before the LORD, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is over the testimony, so that he does not die.<sup>14</sup>And he shall take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger on the front of the mercy seat on the east side, and in front of the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times.<sup>15</sup>"Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering that is for the people and bring its blood inside the veil and do with its blood as he did with the blood of the bull, sprinkling it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat.<sup>16</sup>Thus he shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and because of their transgressions, all their sins. And so he shall do for the tent of meeting, which dwells with them in the midst of their uncleannesses.<sup>17</sup>No one may be in the tent of meeting from the time he enters to make atonement in the Holy Place until he comes out and has made atonement for himself and for his house and for all the assembly of Israel.<sup>18</sup>Then he shall go out to the altar that is before the LORD and make atonement for it, and shall take some of the blood of the bull and some of the blood of the goat, and put it on the horns of the altar all around.<sup>19</sup>And he shall sprinkle some of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleannesses of the people of Israel.<sup>20</sup>"And when he has made an end of atoning for the Holy Place and the tent of meeting and the altar, he shall present the live goat.<sup>21</sup>And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins. And he shall put them on the head of the goat and send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a man who is in readiness.<sup>22</sup>The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area, and he shall let the goat go free in the wilderness.<sup>23</sup>"Then Aaron shall come into the tent of meeting and shall take off the linen garments that he put on when he went into the Holy Place and shall leave them there.<sup>24</sup>And he shall bathe his body in water in a holy place and put on his garments and come out and offer his burnt offering and the burnt offering of the people and make atonement for himself and for the people.<sup>25</sup>And the fat of the sin offering he shall burn on the altar.<sup>26</sup>And he who lets the goat go to Azazel shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp.<sup>27</sup>And the bull for the sin offering and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the Holy Place, shall be carried outside the camp. Their skin and their flesh and their dung shall be burned up with fire.<sup>28</sup>And he who burns them shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp.<sup>29</sup>"And it shall be a statute to you forever that in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict yourselves and shall do no work, either the native or the stranger who sojourns among you.<sup>30</sup>For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins.<sup>31</sup>It is a Sabbath of solemn rest to you, and you shall afflict yourselves; it is a statute forever.<sup>32</sup>And the priest who is anointed and consecrated as priest in his father's place shall make atonement, wearing the holy linen garments.<sup>33</sup>He shall make atonement for the holy sanctuary, and he shall make atonement for the tent of meeting and for the altar, and he shall make atonement for the priests and for all the people of the assembly.<sup>34</sup>And this shall be a statute forever for you, that atonement may be made for the people of Israel once in the year because of all their sins." And Aaron did as the LORD commanded Moses.
16.overview:
This chapter stands at the centre of Leviticus. Once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the high priest passed through the veil, the heavy curtain, into the Most Holy Place, carrying blood. Hebrews 9–10 is the New Testament's own commentary on the day.

The chapter answers one question: how can sinful people live with a holy God among them? Aaron may not come in "at any time" (v. 2); he comes in plain linen, offers first for his own sin, and then deals with the people's sin through two goats. One is killed and its blood is brought before God; the other carries the people's sins away into the wilderness. Sin must be both paid for and removed, and the verse notes trace how both were done at once on the cross, where Christ entered "once for all into the holy places... by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12). Our sin has been carried away, never to be brought up against us again; the blood is on the mercy seat; the veil is torn; the way is open. God is still holy, holy, holy, and yet we may come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — Before the Veil: How Aaron May Enter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The most solemn day of Israel's year opens not with ceremony but with a grave: "after the death of the two sons of Aaron" (v.1). Before anything else, God sets out who may come near, when, and how.
verseByVerse.theology: Access to God is God's gift. Nobody, not even the high priest, may decide for himself when and how to approach. The way in exists only because God opens it and describes it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: even the high priest had to atone for himself before he could act for anyone else. Now: our High Priest is "holy, innocent, unstained" and needs no sacrifice for himself (Heb. 7:26-27), so we can trust him entirely with ours.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before the LORD and died, and the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat that is on the ark, so that he may not die. For I will appear in the cloud over the mercy seat.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter is dated by a death. Nadab and Abihu had offered "unauthorized fire before the LORD" and were consumed (Lev 10:1-2); now their father is told plainly why the veil exists. It is not decoration but a barrier, a "keep out" sewn in blue and purple and scarlet, guarding the mercy seat, the golden lid of the ark, where God said "I will appear in the cloud." The Holy One cannot be approached on a whim, in a manner of our own choosing. The wonder of the gospel is not that God lowered the barrier but that he himself passed through it, and then, at the cross, tore it from top to bottom (Matt 27:51). The God who says "lest he die" is the God who would one day die so that we might live: there is terror here, and tenderness too.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew name of the day, Yom Kippur (23:27), comes from the same root as kapporet, the word for the mercy seat (see vv. 11-14).

verseByVerse.quote: But in this way Aaron shall come into the Holy Place: with a bull from the herd for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering. He shall put on the holy linen coat and shall have the linen undergarment on his body, and he shall tie the linen sash around his waist, and wear the linen turban; these are the holy garments. He shall bathe his body in water and then put them on. And he shall take from the congregation of the people of Israel two male goats for a sin offering, and one ram for a burnt offering.
verseByVerse.commentary: "But in this way": four words of pure grace. God does not only bar the door; he shows the way through it. Then the change of clothes. On other days the high priest blazed with gold and precious stones (Ex 28); today he puts on plain white linen, dressed like the humblest servant. The greater the day, the lower he stoops, and many have seen here a picture of our Lord, who "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7), laying aside his glory to do the work of atonement. The people supply the goats, for it is their sin being dealt with.

verseByVerse.quote: "Aaron shall offer the bull as a sin offering for himself and shall make atonement for himself and for his house. Then he shall take the two goats and set them before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats, one lot for the LORD and the other lot for Azazel. And Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for the LORD and use it as a sin offering, but the goat on which the lot fell for Azazel shall be presented alive before the LORD to make atonement over it, that it may be sent away into the wilderness to Azazel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Aaron can carry anyone else's sin, he must deal with his own. The mediator kneels as a sinner first, a quiet confession that no son of Aaron is clean enough to save. This is the flaw in the old priesthood that makes us long for a better one: a priest who has "no need... to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins" (Heb 7:27).

What is Azazel? The meaning of the word is uncertain. Later Jewish tradition made it a wilderness demon. Others take it as a place, or as “the goat that departs”. This commentary takes the likeliest reading to be the wilderness itself, the barren realm cut off from God's camp, to which the sins were sent away. Whatever the word means, the goat was not an offering to Satan or to anyone else: it was sent, not sacrificed. Its work was to carry Israel's sins out of the camp and out of sight, beyond return.
verseByVerse.note: The English word “scapegoat” comes from Tyndale's 1530 translation, which read Azazel as “the goat that escapes”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-19 — Within the Veil: Blood on the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the high priest passes through the veil, shielded by a cloud of incense "that he may not die" (v.13), and sprinkles the blood on and before the mercy seat. This is the heart of the day and of the whole book.
verseByVerse.theology: Here the chapter teaches propitiation: God's just anger at sin is turned away, not because it is ignored, but because a life is given in the sinner's place and God himself accepts it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: one man, once a year, sprinkled blood on a golden lid that no one else ever saw. Now: what was hidden behind the veil has been set out in public at the cross, and every believer may come to God through Christ, any day of the year.

verseByVerse.quote: "Aaron shall present the bull as a sin offering for himself, and shall make atonement for himself and for his house. He shall kill the bull as a sin offering for himself. And he shall take a censer full of coals of fire from the altar before the LORD, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and he shall bring it inside the veil and put the incense on the fire before the LORD, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is over the testimony, so that he does not die. And he shall take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger on the front of the mercy seat on the east side, and in front of the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cloud shrouds the mercy seat, for no man, not even Aaron, can gaze on the unveiled glory and live. The incense is a mercy: it hides him. Then he sprinkles the blood of his own bull "on the front of the mercy seat... seven times," seven being the number of completeness, atonement fully made. The ark below holds the tablets of the law Israel has broken; the blood falls above them, between the broken law and the God who gave it. That golden lid is the most important object in the world that day, because it is where wrath and mercy meet. Here is the gospel in shadow: the law accuses from beneath, the blood answers from above, and God looks down not on our sin but on the sprinkled blood.

Why blood? It is the first question many readers ask: how can killing an animal answer moral guilt? To Israel blood meant life: "the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls" (Lev 17:11). Sin is rebellion against the God of life, and it ends in death. The animal's death said, in a form no one could miss, that sin costs a life, and that God in mercy accepted a life given in the sinner's place. Yet an animal does not understand, consent or share our nature, and Hebrews says plainly that "it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins" (Heb 10:4). The sacrifices were God's appointed sign and promise, pointing to a willing human substitute who would give his own life.

The Hebrew word for the lid is kapporet, the place of covering or atonement. When Jewish scholars put the Old Testament into Greek they rendered it hilasterion, and that is the word Paul reaches for to describe what God did at the cross: whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith (Rom. 3:25). Many interpreters think Paul is calling Christ the mercy seat itself, since Hebrews uses the same word for the golden lid (Hebrews 9:5); others take it more generally as the means by which wrath is turned away. Either way, what the mercy seat showed in picture, Christ is in fact: the place where the blood answers the broken law.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering that is for the people and bring its blood inside the veil and do with its blood as he did with the blood of the bull, sprinkling it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat. Thus he shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and because of their transgressions, all their sins. And so he shall do for the tent of meeting, which dwells with them in the midst of their uncleannesses. No one may be in the tent of meeting from the time he enters to make atonement in the Holy Place until he comes out and has made atonement for himself and for his house and for all the assembly of Israel. Then he shall go out to the altar that is before the LORD and make atonement for it, and shall take some of the blood of the bull and some of the blood of the goat, and put it on the horns of the altar all around. And he shall sprinkle some of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleannesses of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The blood of the people's goat is carried where no Israelite could go, sprinkled where only God could see, "because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and... all their sins" (v.16). Not only the people are cleansed but the place. "Unclean" in Leviticus does not simply mean dirty, nor is it always sin. It marks whatever belongs to the realm of death and decay (a corpse, a disease, a bodily discharge) and so cannot come near the God of life without cleansing. Israel's sins and uncleannesses are pictured as polluting even the tent where God consents to dwell "in the midst of their uncleannesses," and once a year it had to be cleansed so that he could go on living among them. And while Aaron works, "no one may be in the tent of meeting" (v.17): atonement is lonely work. On our great Day of Atonement, at the cross, the Mediator too was utterly alone: all the disciples left him and fled (Mark 14:50), and on the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34), so that we might never be forsaken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-28 — Outside the Camp: Sin Carried Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blood has been presented; now sin must be removed. Two movements make one atonement: sin paid for by blood, and sin carried away by the living goat.
verseByVerse.theology: The second goat shows expiation, the removal of sin. Forgiveness does not only cancel a debt; it takes the guilt away from the sinner so that it no longer stands between him and God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel stood and watched their sin walk away into the wilderness. Now: when an old sin comes back to accuse you, you may answer that it has already been carried away, and God does not send for it again.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he has made an end of atoning for the Holy Place and the tent of meeting and the altar, he shall present the live goat. And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins. And he shall put them on the head of the goat and send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a man who is in readiness. The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area, and he shall let the goat go free in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary: Aaron presses both hands on the goat's head, not a light touch but a leaning weight, and speaks aloud every kind of sin: iniquities (the crookedness of the heart), transgressions (deliberate rebellions) and sins (the failures and misses). Three words to leave nothing out; a whole year of a whole nation's guilt named over one head. Israel did not merely hear that their sin was forgiven; they watched it walk away. So with your sin: your Saviour took it on his own head, for "the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isa 53:6), and carried it beyond recovery. It is not filed away. It is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Aaron shall come into the tent of meeting and shall take off the linen garments that he put on when he went into the Holy Place and shall leave them there. And he shall bathe his body in water in a holy place and put on his garments and come out and offer his burnt offering and the burnt offering of the people and make atonement for himself and for the people. And the fat of the sin offering he shall burn on the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary: With the sin borne away, the mood changes. Aaron washes, lays aside the plain linen and puts his glorious garments back on: the servant's work done, the splendour restored. Many have seen in it a picture of our Lord, who after his humiliation was "crowned with glory and honor" (Heb 2:9). Then come the burnt offerings, whole animals given up to God: once sin has been dealt with, worship can rise. The order never changes: first atonement, then adoration. We do not worship our way into acceptance; we are accepted, and so we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who lets the goat go to Azazel shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp. And the bull for the sin offering and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the Holy Place, shall be carried outside the camp. Their skin and their flesh and their dung shall be burned up with fire. And he who burns them shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary: Sin’s uncleanness clings to everything near it, so the remains of the sin offerings are burned outside the camp. The writer of Hebrews sees his Lord in that lonely fire beyond the gate: "So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured" (Heb 13:12-13). Golgotha was outside the city wall: the sin-bearer was cast out as unclean, treated as sin itself, so that the unclean might be brought in. The place of shame became the place of cleansing. The call to us is to go out to him there, willing to share his reproach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-34 — A Statute Forever: The Sabbath of Atonement
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God fixes the day in the calendar for ever. The people do nothing; the priest does everything; and "on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you" (v.30).
verseByVerse.theology: The people's part is to humble themselves and to rest. Their cleansing is something done for them, not something they achieve.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the day came round again every autumn. Now: there is no annual reckoning to wait for; a believer who sins comes back to God the same day, through the same finished sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall be a statute to you forever that in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict yourselves and shall do no work, either the native or the stranger who sojourns among you. For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins. It is a Sabbath of solemn rest to you, and you shall afflict yourselves; it is a statute forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is a strange pairing: "afflict yourselves" and "do no work." Israel must feel the weight of sin (this was the one fast day in the law, a day to humble the soul) and yet must lift not a finger toward its own cleansing. Both are the gospel. We come empty-handed, mourning our sin, bringing nothing; and we rest, because the work is the priest's, not ours. "You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins": not some, but all; not partly, but clean. And it is called "a Sabbath of solemn rest," the deepest rest of the year, because the deepest rest a soul can know is to be clean before God and to have contributed nothing but need. That rest has a name: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

How Jewish readers take it. Yom Kippur remains the holiest day of the Jewish year. Rabbinic tradition teaches that repentance, prayer and deeds of kindness now bring atonement, and the Mishnah (Yoma 8:9) adds that the day does not atone for wrongs against a neighbour until the wrongdoer has made peace with him. Both readings agree that sin is real, that cleansing is God's gift, and that it is received with humbled hearts. This commentary reads the day as a shadow fulfilled when Christ entered the holy places once for all by his own blood (Hebrews 9:11–12).
verseByVerse.note: “Afflict yourselves” may mean “fast” (ESV note). The seventh month is September–October.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest who is anointed and consecrated as priest in his father's place shall make atonement, wearing the holy linen garments. He shall make atonement for the holy sanctuary, and he shall make atonement for the tent of meeting and for the altar, and he shall make atonement for the priests and for all the people of the assembly. And this shall be a statute forever for you, that atonement may be made for the people of Israel once in the year because of all their sins." And Aaron did as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The atonement is total in its reach (sanctuary, tent, altar, priests, and "all the people of the assembly"), with nothing and no one left uncleansed. Yet one phrase exposes the system's limit: "once in the year." The yearly return of this day was God's own admission that the real atonement was still to come (Heb 10:1-4). The chapter ends with "once in the year"; the gospel answers with "once for all."

Do Christians keep the Day of Atonement? No, because what it pictured has been done: Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin (Hebrews 10:18). Jewish people still keep it as Yom Kippur, with prayer and fasting but without sacrifice, since the temple fell in AD 70. For the Christian the curtain is torn, and every day is a day of open access to God.

16.theology:
Propitiation. The blood on the mercy seat turns away God's just anger and satisfies his justice. Christ is the propitiation for our sins (Rom 3:25; 1 John 2:2), not someone else winning over an unwilling God, but God himself providing the sacrifice he requires.

Expiation. The living goat carries confessed sin away. Both goats are needed to show one atonement: Christ's death pays for sin and removes it.

A finished work. Aaron entered yearly with another's blood and went out again; Christ entered with his own and sat down (Heb 10:12). The veil torn at his death (Matt 27:51) leaves the way open for ever.
16.examples:
Then: once a year Israel waited outside while the high priest went in with blood, wondering whether he would come out alive.

Now: Christ is both the goat that died and the goat sent away, and he has come out of the sanctuary alive, never to die again. So we no longer wait outside. We draw near with confidence (Heb 10:19-22), resting on his own word from the cross: "It is finished" (John 19:30).

17.title: The Sanctity of Blood: Life Given for Life
17.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons and to all the people of Israel and say to them, This is the thing that the LORD has commanded.<sup>3</sup>If any one of the house of Israel kills an ox or a lamb or a goat in the camp, or kills it outside the camp,<sup>4</sup>and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it as a gift to the LORD in front of the tabernacle of the LORD, bloodguilt shall be imputed to that man. He has shed blood, and that man shall be cut off from among his people.<sup>5</sup>This is to the end that the people of Israel may bring their sacrifices that they sacrifice in the open field, that they may bring them to the LORD, to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and sacrifice them as sacrifices of peace offerings to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And the priest shall throw the blood on the altar of the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting and burn the fat for a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>So they shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to goat demons, after whom they whore. This shall be a statute forever for them throughout their generations.<sup>8</sup>"And you shall say to them, Any one of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice<sup>9</sup>and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it to the LORD, that man shall be cut off from his people.<sup>10</sup>"If any one of the house of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn among them eats any blood, I will set my face against that person who eats blood and will cut him off from among his people.<sup>11</sup>For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life.<sup>12</sup>Therefore I have said to the people of Israel, No person among you shall eat blood, neither shall any stranger who sojourns among you eat blood.<sup>13</sup>"Any one also of the people of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who takes in hunting any beast or bird that may be eaten shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth.<sup>14</sup>For the life of every creature is its blood: its blood is its life. Therefore I have said to the people of Israel, You shall not eat the blood of any creature, for the life of every creature is its blood. Whoever eats it shall be cut off.<sup>15</sup>And every person who eats what dies of itself or what is torn by beasts, whether he is a native or a sojourner, shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening; then he shall be clean.<sup>16</sup>But if he does not wash them or bathe his flesh, he shall bear his iniquity."
17.overview:
With chapter 17 we cross into the second half of Leviticus, which scholars often call the Holiness Code (chs 17–27) because its refrain is "be holy." The focus shifts from the sanctuary to the life of the people, holiness lived out in the world. And it begins, fittingly, with blood.

Why such reverence for blood? The chapter answers in one of the key verses on atonement in Scripture, 17:11, explained at vv. 10-16: blood is life, and God has given it on the altar so that a life may be given in place of a life forfeited. The blood on the altar is not magic, and atonement is God’s own gift. There is no bloodless gospel: at the cross the innocent died for the guilty. And the blood that once was forbidden to drink becomes, in Christ, the cup of the new covenant: "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt 26:28). The sanctity of blood in Leviticus 17 finds its everlasting meaning at Calvary, where the life of the Son of God was poured out to make atonement for our souls.
17.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The giving of a life in place of the forfeit life is the heart of the sacrificial system and of the cross.

Atonement as God's gift. God does not need to be talked round into mercy. He provides the sacrifice himself, from a heart already set on saving (John 3:16).

The blood that speaks mercy. Abel's blood cried out for justice; Christ's blood "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb 12:24).
17.examples:
Then: every time an Israelite drained an animal's blood, he was reminded that life belongs to God.

Now: each time we take the cup at the Lord's Supper we receive, with awe and thankfulness, what that blood pointed to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: All sacrifice is brought to one place, the entrance of the tent.
verseByVerse.theology: False worship thrives in private. By bringing every sacrifice to one door, God removed the hiding places where Israel's old idolatries could survive.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel worshipped at one altar, in full view. Now: a faith kept entirely private, out of the sight of other believers, is the faith most likely to drift; we need the fellowship of the church.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons and to all the people of Israel and say to them, This is the thing that the LORD has commanded. If any one of the house of Israel kills an ox or a lamb or a goat in the camp, or kills it outside the camp, and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it as a gift to the LORD in front of the tabernacle of the LORD, bloodguilt shall be imputed to that man. He has shed blood, and that man shall be cut off from among his people. This is to the end that the people of Israel may bring their sacrifices that they sacrifice in the open field, that they may bring them to the LORD, to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and sacrifice them as sacrifices of peace offerings to the LORD. And the priest shall throw the blood on the altar of the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting and burn the fat for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. So they shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to goat demons, after whom they whore. This shall be a statute forever for them throughout their generations. "And you shall say to them, Any one of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it to the LORD, that man shall be cut off from his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first half of the chapter closes a loophole. Bloodguilt sounds severe for killing an animal at home until verse 7 gives the reason: goat demons. The law is aimed not at butchery but at secret sacrifice. Israel may well have picked up habits in Egypt, and killing an animal out in the open field was how those habits were kept alive: a quiet offering, away from the tent, to something else.

The remedy is one place for every sacrifice: one altar, one door, in full view. Worship that no one else can see drifts, and God removes the privacy in which it drifts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-16 — The Life Is in the Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-16: The reason behind every blood prohibition in the book.
verseByVerse.theology: Blood belongs to God because life belongs to God, and he has set it apart for one purpose: atonement.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a meal could be a lesson in reverence. Now: Christians are free to eat, but not free to treat lightly the death of Christ by which they were bought.

verseByVerse.quote: "If any one of the house of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn among them eats any blood, I will set my face against that person who eats blood and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life. Therefore I have said to the people of Israel, No person among you shall eat blood, neither shall any stranger who sojourns among you eat blood. "Any one also of the people of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who takes in hunting any beast or bird that may be eaten shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth. For the life of every creature is its blood: its blood is its life. Therefore I have said to the people of Israel, You shall not eat the blood of any creature, for the life of every creature is its blood. Whoever eats it shall be cut off. And every person who eats what dies of itself or what is torn by beasts, whether he is a native or a sojourner, shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening; then he shall be clean. But if he does not wash them or bathe his flesh, he shall bear his iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 11 is one of the most important verses in the Old Testament, and three things are packed into it. First, blood is life: not a symbol of life but where life resides, so that spilling blood is spending a life. Second, the altar is a gift: I have given it for you. The sacrificial system is not something Israel devised to placate God; it is something God handed down to Israel so that they might live with him and not die. Third, the way it works is stated plainly: atonement happens by the life. Not by the ritual, not by the sincerity of the worshipper, but by a life given in place of a life forfeited.

The King James Version reads for the soul where the ESV has by the life; the Hebrew can be taken either way, and both say that a life given is what atones.

That is why blood may never be eaten. To consume it would be to treat as ordinary food the one thing God had reserved as the price of atonement.

Hebrews builds directly on this verse: under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins (Heb. 9:22). And Peter names what that price finally turned out to be: you were ransomed... not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet. 1:18-19).

There is one more turn, and Israel would have found it staggering. The book that forbids drinking blood on pain of being cut off points forward to the Christ who says whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life (John 6:54). His hearers were appalled, and by Leviticus 17 they had reason to be. He meant receiving him and his death by faith. Blood was forbidden because it was the means of atonement; in him it is offered, because he is the atonement, and the life in his blood is given to us rather than kept from us.

Does the ban on eating blood still bind? It was given to Noah before Israel (Gen 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it for the sake of fellowship with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29). But the New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Tim 4:4), and most Christians have concluded that the principle, reverence for the life God gives, remains, while eating meat that is not fully drained is not sin. The command concerns eating, not medicine; a blood transfusion gives life and does not break it.

18.title: Sexual Ethics: A People Called to Be Different
18.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, I am the LORD your God.<sup>3</sup>You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you. You shall not walk in their statutes.<sup>4</sup>You shall follow my rules and keep my statutes and walk in them. I am the LORD your God.<sup>5</sup>You shall therefore keep my statutes and my rules; if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the LORD.<sup>6</sup>"None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness. I am the LORD.<sup>7</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, which is the nakedness of your mother; she is your mother, you shall not uncover her nakedness.<sup>8</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; it is your father's nakedness.<sup>9</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, your father's daughter or your mother's daughter, whether brought up in the family or in another home.<sup>10</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son's daughter or of your daughter's daughter, for their nakedness is your own nakedness.<sup>11</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife's daughter, brought up in your father's family, since she is your sister.<sup>12</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's sister; she is your father's relative.<sup>13</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother's sister, for she is your mother's relative.<sup>14</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's brother, that is, you shall not approach his wife; she is your aunt.<sup>15</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law; she is your son's wife, you shall not uncover her nakedness.<sup>16</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife; it is your brother's nakedness.<sup>17</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and of her daughter, and you shall not take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter to uncover her nakedness; they are relatives; it is depravity.<sup>18</sup>And you shall not take a woman as a rival wife to her sister, uncovering her nakedness while her sister is still alive.<sup>19</sup>"You shall not approach a woman to uncover her nakedness while she is in her menstrual uncleanness.<sup>20</sup>And you shall not lie sexually with your neighbor's wife and so make yourself unclean with her.<sup>21</sup>You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech, and so profane the name of your God: I am the LORD.<sup>22</sup>You shall not lie with a male as with a woman; it is an abomination.<sup>23</sup>And you shall not lie with any animal and so make yourself unclean with it, neither shall any woman give herself to an animal to lie with it: it is perversion.<sup>24</sup>"Do not make yourselves unclean by any of these things, for by all these the nations I am driving out before you have become unclean,<sup>25</sup>and the land became unclean, so that I punished its iniquity, and the land vomited out its inhabitants.<sup>26</sup>But you shall keep my statutes and my rules and do none of these abominations, either the native or the stranger who sojourns among you<sup>27</sup>(for the people of the land, who were before you, did all of these abominations, so that the land became unclean),<sup>28</sup>lest the land vomit you out when you make it unclean, as it vomited out the nation that was before you.<sup>29</sup>For everyone who does any of these abominations, the persons who do them shall be cut off from among their people.<sup>30</sup>So keep my charge never to practice any of these abominable customs that were practiced before you, and never to make yourselves unclean by them: I am the LORD your God."
18.overview:
Chapter 18 sets out the boundaries of sexual conduct. It opens and closes not with rules but with a Person: "I am the LORD your God" (18:2, 30). Israel's sexual ethics are grounded in the character of God and the identity of his redeemed people, and the call is to be different from the cultures behind and ahead of them. The prohibitions guard the family and protect the vulnerable; they are the wisdom of a loving Maker who designed sexuality for covenant, faithfulness and joy. Sexual sin is never merely private, and the chapter ends with a sobering warning to Israel itself (vv. 24-30).

For the church the call stands. The Spirit now dwelling in believers renews desire and makes the body his temple (1 Cor 6:19), and the gospel points beyond every earthly union to the marriage of the Lamb. And for those who have failed (and who has not?), the same Christ who upholds the boundary also bore the punishment for our breaking it, and he washes every sinner who comes to him (1 Cor 6:11).
18.theology:
Holiness grounded in God. Sexual ethics flow from God's character and the identity of a redeemed people, not from arbitrary rule.

A people called to be different. Neither Egypt behind nor Canaan ahead is to shape God's people (18:3); the church too is called not to be conformed to this world (Rom 12:2).

The dignity of the body. God's boundaries protect persons and help them flourish; in Christ the body becomes a temple of the Spirit.
18.examples:
Then: Israel was called to be visibly different from Egypt and Canaan.

Now: the church faces the same fierce pressure to conform. We hold God's design as wisdom and gift, not a cage, and we offer the cleansing of Christ to all who have failed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-30 — Holiness in the Family and the Marriage Bed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-5: The reason for the chapter: who is speaking, and whom Israel is not to copy.

Verses 6-18: Forbidden relationships within the crowded household.

Verses 19-23: Five further commands, one of them not sexual at all.

Verses 24-30: The warning of the land.
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are shaped neither by the culture they came from nor by the one they are entering, but by the God who redeemed them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: these laws made the home safe for the women and the young. Now: churches and families are called to be places where the vulnerable are protected, and where those who have fallen find both truth and a way back.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, I am the LORD your God. You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you. You shall not walk in their statutes. You shall follow my rules and keep my statutes and walk in them. I am the LORD your God. You shall therefore keep my statutes and my rules; if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter names two cultures, Egypt behind and Canaan ahead, and Israel is to resemble neither. Before either, it names who is speaking: the LORD their God. So the chapter is first about belonging to him. These laws went against both cultures at once, and the people receiving them had spent four centuries in Egypt watching one of them.

Verse 5 promises life to the person who keeps these statutes. Paul quotes it twice (Rom. 10:5; Gal. 3:12) to show that the law offers life for perfect obedience, and that no sinner has ever earned it. One man did: Christ kept these statutes in our place, and by his obedience the many are made righteous (Rom. 5:19). So whoever has failed here comes back by confession, to a mercy already secured.

verseByVerse.quote: "None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness. I am the LORD. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, which is the nakedness of your mother; she is your mother, you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; it is your father's nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, your father's daughter or your mother's daughter, whether brought up in the family or in another home. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son's daughter or of your daughter's daughter, for their nakedness is your own nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife's daughter, brought up in your father's family, since she is your sister. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's sister; she is your father's relative. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother's sister, for she is your mother's relative. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's brother, that is, you shall not approach his wife; she is your aunt. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law; she is your son's wife, you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife; it is your brother's nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and of her daughter, and you shall not take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter to uncover her nakedness; they are relatives; it is depravity. And you shall not take a woman as a rival wife to her sister, uncovering her nakedness while her sister is still alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 6 gives the principle governing the whole list, and what it protects becomes clear once you picture the setting. The household in the ancient world was large, crowded and multi-generational (several couples, their children, unmarried relatives and servants under one roof), and the people most vulnerable inside it were the women and the young.

These laws make the home a place where a woman is safe from the men she lives among.

If you were abused within your own family, this chapter is on your side. God named these acts as wrongs, and the shame of them belongs to the one who did them, not to you. Seek safety and help at once, and tell someone who can protect you; abuse is never to be hidden or tolerated in the name of family or faith.

Deuteronomy 25:5–10 commands a man to marry his dead brother’s childless widow. That was a specific exception, to raise up an heir; this verse forbids marrying a brother’s wife while he lives, as Herod did (Mark 6:17–18).
verseByVerse.note: “Uncover nakedness” means sexual relations.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not approach a woman to uncover her nakedness while she is in her menstrual uncleanness. And you shall not lie sexually with your neighbor's wife and so make yourself unclean with her. You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech, and so profane the name of your God: I am the LORD. You shall not lie with a male as with a woman; it is an abomination. And you shall not lie with any animal and so make yourself unclean with it, neither shall any woman give herself to an animal to lie with it: it is perversion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five commands of different kinds, and one of them is not sexual at all.

The first, verse 19, forbids relations during a wife's monthly period. Is that moral law or purity law? Christians differ. Its close tie to chapter 15 leads most to treat it as part of the purity laws fulfilled in Christ, while some think it still teaches tender respect for a wife's body.

Verse 21: Canaanite religion included the burning of children, and the ban on it is placed here because it belongs to the same subject: what a society does with its offspring, and whether the vulnerable exist for the convenience of the powerful.

Verse 22 forbids male homosexual practice. It is not a mistranslation, no amount of context removes it, and the New Testament reaffirms it (Rom. 1:26-27; 1 Cor. 6:9-10).

How it is said matters too. It stands in a list which also forbids adultery and incest and regulates a man's conduct toward his own wife: a chapter addressed to everyone's sexuality, not to one group's. And the New Testament paragraph naming this sin names beside it the greedy, the drunkards, the revilers and the swindlers, and then says: and such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (1 Cor. 6:11).

That is not a description of who is beyond reach. It is a description of the sort of people the church has always been made of. Whatever else this chapter is, it is not a licence for anyone to feel clean by comparison.

Does the verse condemn people who experience same-sex attraction? The verse addresses an act. Every one of us carries desires bent by the fall that need Christ's mercy and the Spirit's renewal (Romans 7:18–25). Many believers who never chose these attractions walk in costly faithfulness, and deserve the church's friendship, not suspicion.

Child sacrifice to Molech was an abomination: killing the vulnerable for the sake of religion or gain. Abortion is not the same act, but it shares the same evil wherever an unborn child’s life is ended for another’s sake; God forms the child in the womb (Ps 139:13–16). For anyone who carries that grief, the washing of 1 Corinthians 6:11 is offered in full.

Why condemn same-sex intercourse from Leviticus 18:22 but eat shellfish (11:10)? The food laws were ceremonial: they marked Israel off from the nations, and the New Testament lifts them explicitly (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). The sexual laws of chapter 18 are moral: they rest on creation (Gen 2:24), the nations were judged for breaking them (18:24–25), and the New Testament repeats them (Rom 1:26–27; 1 Cor 6:9–11). Christians are not picking and choosing; they are following the apostles. The death penalty of 20:13 belonged to Israel’s civil law and ended with it, and the gospel offers washing to every sinner: such were some of you.

“Abomination” means what God detests; the word is also used of idolatry and dishonest scales (Deut 7:25; Prov 11:1). It names the act, not a person beyond redemption.
verseByVerse.note: The name Molech may be a deliberate mockery, joining the Hebrew melek, “king”, to the vowels of the word for “shame”.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not make yourselves unclean by any of these things, for by all these the nations I am driving out before you have become unclean, and the land became unclean, so that I punished its iniquity, and the land vomited out its inhabitants. But you shall keep my statutes and my rules and do none of these abominations, either the native or the stranger who sojourns among you (for the people of the land, who were before you, did all of these abominations, so that the land became unclean), lest the land vomit you out when you make it unclean, as it vomited out the nation that was before you. For everyone who does any of these abominations, the persons who do them shall be cut off from among their people. So keep my charge never to practice any of these abominable customs that were practiced before you, and never to make yourselves unclean by them: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with an image that should stop anyone using it as a weapon against outsiders: the land vomited out its inhabitants.

Canaan is not being cleared because God prefers Israelites but because of what has been done there, and God turns the same warning on Israel.

The land is not Israel's by right of blood; it will treat Israel as it treated those before them.

Centuries later it did, and Ezekiel named these very defilements as Jerusalem’s guilt (Ezek. 22:10-11). Yet the same prophet promised cleansing, a new heart, and God's own Spirit within, causing his people to walk in his statutes (Ezek. 36:25-27).

19.title: The Holiness Code: Love Your Neighbor
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.<sup>3</sup>Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father, and you shall keep my Sabbaths: I am the LORD your God.<sup>4</sup>Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves any gods of cast metal: I am the LORD your God.<sup>5</sup>"When you offer a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD, you shall offer it so that you may be accepted.<sup>6</sup>It shall be eaten the same day you offer it or on the day after, and anything left over until the third day shall be burned up with fire.<sup>7</sup>If it is eaten at all on the third day, it is tainted; it will not be accepted,<sup>8</sup>and everyone who eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned what is holy to the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from his people.<sup>9</sup>"When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, neither shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest.<sup>10</sup>And you shall not strip your vineyard bare, neither shall you gather the fallen grapes of your vineyard. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner: I am the LORD your God.<sup>11</sup>"You shall not steal; you shall not deal falsely; you shall not lie to one another.<sup>12</sup>You shall not swear by my name falsely, and so profane the name of your God: I am the LORD.<sup>13</sup>"You shall not oppress your neighbor or rob him. The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning.<sup>14</sup>You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God: I am the LORD.<sup>15</sup>"You shall do no injustice in court. You shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great, but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor.<sup>16</sup>You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people, and you shall not stand up against the life of your neighbor: I am the LORD.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall reason frankly with your neighbor, lest you incur sin because of him.<sup>18</sup>You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.<sup>19</sup>"You shall keep my statutes. You shall not let your cattle breed with a different kind. You shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed, nor shall you wear a garment of cloth made of two kinds of material.<sup>20</sup>"If a man lies sexually with a woman who is a slave, assigned to another man and not yet ransomed or given her freedom, a distinction shall be made. They shall not be put to death, because she was not free;<sup>21</sup>but he shall bring his compensation to the LORD, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, a ram for a guilt offering.<sup>22</sup>And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering before the LORD for his sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven for the sin that he has committed.<sup>23</sup>"When you come into the land and plant any kind of tree for food, then you shall regard its fruit as forbidden. Three years it shall be forbidden to you; it must not be eaten.<sup>24</sup>And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, an offering of praise to the LORD.<sup>25</sup>But in the fifth year you may eat of its fruit, to increase its yield for you: I am the LORD your God.<sup>26</sup>"You shall not eat any flesh with the blood in it. You shall not interpret omens or tell fortunes.<sup>27</sup>You shall not round off the hair on your temples or mar the edges of your beard.<sup>28</sup>You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead or tattoo yourselves: I am the LORD.<sup>29</sup>"Do not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute, lest the land fall into prostitution and the land become full of depravity.<sup>30</sup>You shall keep my Sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary: I am the LORD.<sup>31</sup>"Do not turn to mediums or necromancers; do not seek them out, and so make yourselves unclean by them: I am the LORD your God.<sup>32</sup>"You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man, and you shall fear your God: I am the LORD.<sup>33</sup>"When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong.<sup>34</sup>You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.<sup>35</sup>"You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measures of length or weight or quantity.<sup>36</sup>You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.<sup>37</sup>And you shall observe all my statutes and all my rules, and do them: I am the LORD."
19.overview:
If chapter 16 is the theological summit of Leviticus, chapter 19 is the heart of its teaching on how to live. It opens with the book's defining command, "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2), and then shows what that holiness looks like not in the sanctuary but in the field, the marketplace and the courtroom, in the way Israel treats the deaf, the blind, the poor, the foreigner and the neighbour. Echoes of the Ten Commandments sit beside gleanings for the poor, wages paid the same day and honest weights. Holiness turns out to be intensely practical: the love of God spilling over into the love of neighbour.

At the centre stands the verse Jesus would lift up as the second great commandment: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (19:18). "I am the LORD" punctuates the chapter like a drumbeat, grounding every social command in the character of God: to love your neighbour is to be like God; to cheat the poor is to deny him. The chapter refuses to separate worship from the way we treat people.
19.theology:
Practical holiness. God's holiness is reflected not in withdrawal from the world but in justice, generosity, honesty and love in everyday life.

Love fulfils the law. The command to love one's neighbour sits at the heart of these laws, and the New Testament calls it the fulfilment of them all.

The law kept for us. The One who gave this law also kept it perfectly. Jesus, the true neighbour, loved not himself but us, became poor that we might be rich, and pours his own love into our hearts by the Spirit so that we may love as we have been loved.
19.examples:
Then: an Israelite farmer reflected God’s holiness in everyday mercy: field edges left, wages paid, honest scales.

Now: holiness still wears work clothes. We honour God in how we treat employees, the vulnerable, the elderly and the stranger, loving our neighbour as ourselves because Christ first loved us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-37 — 'You Shall Be Holy, for I Am Holy'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-8: The call to be holy, applied first at home.

Verses 9-18: Holiness in the field, the workplace, the courtroom and the heart.

Verses 19-37: Holiness in the details of farming, mourning, old age, hospitality and trade.
verseByVerse.theology: Being holy means becoming like God, and this chapter shows that God's likeness is seen first in how we treat parents, the poor, workers, the disabled, neighbours and strangers.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: an Israelite farmer showed God's holiness by the corners he left unharvested. Now: a Christian shows it in the margins of an ordinary week: time, money and attention left over for someone in need.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy. Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father, and you shall keep my Sabbaths: I am the LORD your God. Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves any gods of cast metal: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence the whole book has been circling is addressed not to the priests but to all the congregation. Holiness is not for the clergy alone.

What follows is not what anyone expects. Look after your parents. Take a day off. That is the opening move of the holiness code, and it sets the tone for a chapter in which imitating God turns out to consist almost entirely of how you treat the people around you.

Note too that the mother is named first, reversing the usual order of the fifth commandment; it is a small touch, and probably not an accident. Only then comes the prohibition of idols, after the family and the day of rest.

What of the Sabbath for Christians? It is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a gift Christians gladly set apart for worship and rest. Many godly believers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (the classic Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist statements of faith), hold it as a binding Christian Sabbath; faithful Christians differ, and no one may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "When you offer a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD, you shall offer it so that you may be accepted. It shall be eaten the same day you offer it or on the day after, and anything left over until the third day shall be burned up with fire. If it is eaten at all on the third day, it is tainted; it will not be accepted, and everyone who eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned what is holy to the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rule about the peace offering, from chapter 7, interrupts the commands about daily conduct.

It sits here because worship and conduct are not being treated as separate subjects. The same paragraph that will shortly forbid slandering your neighbour also tells you not to keep sacrificial meat past its day. In Leviticus the way you handle the holy things and the way you handle people are one topic.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, neither shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. And you shall not strip your vineyard bare, neither shall you gather the fallen grapes of your vineyard. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not command a handout; he commands a margin. The corners are left standing, the dropped grapes are left lying, and the poor come and do the work of gathering them.

The difference matters. A man who receives a parcel is a recipient; a man who reaps a corner is a harvester. The provision is arranged so that the person in need keeps his dignity and his labour, and he never has to ask the landowner for anything.

This is the law under which Ruth, a Moabite widow, went into a field belonging to a man named Boaz, fed her mother-in-law, and met the relative who would marry her and buy back the family’s land. The whole book of Ruth happens inside these two verses.
verseByVerse.note: The same provision is repeated in 23:22 and Deuteronomy 24:19-22.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not steal; you shall not deal falsely; you shall not lie to one another. You shall not swear by my name falsely, and so profane the name of your God: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last command, against swearing falsely by God's name, links the other three to God himself. A false oath does not merely wrong the man who was deceived; it drags the name of God into the deception as a guarantor. Someone who swears by God and lies has made God a witness to his fraud.

That is why Jesus' instruction on oaths cuts where it does: let what you say be simply "Yes" or "No" (Matt. 5:37). The problem with an elaborate oath is that it implies your ordinary word could not be trusted.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not oppress your neighbor or rob him. The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning. You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wages overnight. Take that clause concretely. A day labourer is paid at the end of the day because he has no reserves. Hold his wages until morning, for perfectly ordinary reasons, and his family does not eat tonight. The law reaches into the gap between an employer's convenience and a worker's supper, and comes down on the side of the supper. James is still angry about it centuries later (James 5:4).

The deaf and the blind. Both crimes are undetectable. A deaf man does not know he has been cursed. A blind man who trips never learns that the obstacle was placed there deliberately. There is no possibility of being caught and no victim who can testify, which is exactly why the clause but you shall fear your God is attached. This is legislation for the moments when nobody is watching, and the only thing that enforces it is the fear of God in the person concerned.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall do no injustice in court. You shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great, but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor. You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people, and you shall not stand up against the life of your neighbor: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In court the even-handedness is the point, and it cuts both ways. Favouring the powerful is the obvious corruption. Favouring the poor because they are poor is named here as the same crime: a sentimental verdict is still a false one, and a court that decides cases on sympathy has stopped being a court.

Slander and standing against a neighbour's life belong together. Talk is placed alongside bloodshed, because a reputation destroyed in conversation and a man destroyed in court are closer to each other than we like to think.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall reason frankly with your neighbor, lest you incur sin because of him. You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reason frankly. The alternative offered to hatred is not silence. It is speech: going to the man and telling him plainly what he has done. And the warning attached is sharp: if you say nothing, you incur sin because of him. Swallowing a grievance is not presented here as the meek option. It is presented as a way of becoming guilty yourself.

The New Testament reaches for the command to love your neighbour more than any other sentence in the book. Asked which commandment was the greatest, Jesus gave two, and the second was this one (Matt. 22:39). Paul says the whole law is fulfilled in it (Gal. 5:14). James calls it the royal law (James 2:8).

And it is placed immediately after verse 17, which is the part everyone forgets. Loving your neighbour, in the verse that defines it, includes telling him the truth to his face. The alternative to frank speech is not kindness. It is hatred kept hidden in the heart.

Does “as yourself” command self-love? It assumes the care that all people already have for themselves (Eph 5:29) and turns it outward. It is not a command to build self-esteem first. And Jesus answers “who is my neighbour?” with the Samaritan: anyone in need whom I can help (Luke 10:29–37).
verseByVerse.note: “Neighbor” here first means a fellow Israelite; verse 34 widens the same love to the foreigner.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall keep my statutes. You shall not let your cattle breed with a different kind. You shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed, nor shall you wear a garment of cloth made of two kinds of material. "If a man lies sexually with a woman who is a slave, assigned to another man and not yet ransomed or given her freedom, a distinction shall be made. They shall not be put to death, because she was not free; but he shall bring his compensation to the LORD, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, a ram for a guilt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering before the LORD for his sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven for the sin that he has committed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rules on mixing kinds look arbitrary, and no reason is given, and the honest thing is to say so rather than invent one. The best that can be said is that they belong with the food laws: a nation being trained, in a hundred daily particulars, to keep distinct things distinct.

Then a case of a very different weight: a man who sleeps with a slave woman promised to another. She is not free, so the law of adultery does not apply as it would to a free woman, and the text does not pretend otherwise, but it refuses to let the matter drop. There is an inquiry, and the man brings a guilt offering, and he is not excused because the woman was a slave.

Neither of them is put to death, which also spares the woman, who as a slave may have had little power to refuse. In many ancient codes a slave woman was treated as property, and an offence involving her was a matter of damages owed to her owner. Here the offence is against God and requires atonement.

Do Christians cherry-pick by ignoring the mixed-fabric law? These laws were signs of Israel’s separateness, fulfilled in Christ, who has broken down the dividing wall (Eph 2:14–15). The moral laws of this chapter, love your neighbour, honest weights, no slander, are repeated in the New Testament; the symbolic laws are not.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come into the land and plant any kind of tree for food, then you shall regard its fruit as forbidden. Three years it shall be forbidden to you; it must not be eaten. And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, an offering of praise to the LORD. But in the fifth year you may eat of its fruit, to increase its yield for you: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Four years of tending something you may not touch. It trains patience and teaches that the tree is God’s before it is yours, and the reason given at the end is agricultural (to increase its yield for you), which is God attaching a practical benefit to an act of restraint.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not eat any flesh with the blood in it. You shall not interpret omens or tell fortunes. You shall not round off the hair on your temples or mar the edges of your beard. You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead or tattoo yourselves: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This cluster is aimed at the religion of the surrounding nations, and the phrase for the dead explains all of it. These are funeral practices. The neighbouring cultures cut themselves in mourning to appease or attract the attention of the gods of the dead, and Israel is forbidden to do it, not because self-decoration is inherently wicked, but because these particular acts said something untrue about death and about who governs it.

Are tattoos sin today? The command forbade marking the body in mourning rites for the dead, a pagan practice (Deut 14:1). It is not repeated in the New Testament. Christians should think carefully about what they put on bodies that belong to the Lord (1 Cor 6:19–20), but a tattoo is a matter of wisdom and conscience, not a breach of this law.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute, lest the land fall into prostitution and the land become full of depravity. You shall keep my Sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary: I am the LORD. "Do not turn to mediums or necromancers; do not seek them out, and so make yourselves unclean by them: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ban on making a daughter a prostitute covers both the cult prostitution of Canaan and the trafficking of a child by her own father for money, and beside it stand the Sabbaths. The two sit side by side deliberately. A society that sells its daughters and a society that keeps its Sabbaths are being contrasted, and the second is offered as the alternative to the first. What a nation does with its rest and what it does with its vulnerable are connected.

Then mediums and necromancers, who consult the dead. Israel is not to go looking for information from that quarter, and the reason is the same as for the mourning marks: it treats the dead, rather than the living God, as the place to go for answers.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man, and you shall fear your God: I am the LORD. "When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rising before the grey head puts respect for the old into a single action. It is not a feeling about the elderly but a movement, made with the body, in a room, when someone comes in. And the same clause is attached again: you shall fear your God, because nobody can legislate for whether a man rises from his seat.

In verses 33-34 the command of verse 18 returns with the neighbour redefined: love him as yourself, now said of a foreigner. And the reason given is memory. A people who know from the inside what it is to be an alien in someone else's country are forbidden to treat anyone as an outsider in theirs.

Does this settle immigration policy? It binds how God’s people treat the foreigner among them: with love, justice and hospitality (Matt 25:35; Heb 13:2). It does not lay down a nation’s laws of entry; that is for governments to decide justly. But the church must never treat foreigners with contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measures of length or weight or quantity. You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. And you shall observe all my statutes and all my rules, and do them: I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends where a great deal of practical righteousness actually lives: in honest trade. A merchant with two sets of weights, a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling, could rob an entire town by a fraction at a time, and never be caught, and never break a law anyone could see him breaking. Proverbs returns to this repeatedly: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD (Prov. 11:1).

Look at what has been assembled. Holiness, the word that in this book has meant blood and veils and a fire nobody could approach, is spelled out for ordinary Israelites as: feed the poor without humiliating them, pay your workers before dark, tell the truth in court, do not exploit the disabled, say the hard thing to a brother's face rather than nurse it, stand up when an old man enters the room, love the foreigner because you remember being one, and keep honest scales: all of it said to a people reminded, at the close, that the LORD brought them out of Egypt.

Which is why nobody should be surprised at what God was like when he became man. The Holy One, when he finally walked about in a human body, spent his time with the poor, the disabled, the foreigners and the despised, not because he had set this chapter aside, but because he was the only one who ever kept it. He kept it for us, and his obedience is counted as ours (Rom. 5:19); so the reader this list convicts has a way back in confession, and the Spirit he gives grows this very love in us (Gal. 5:22).

20.title: Penalties for Violations: The Seriousness of Sin
20.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Say to the people of Israel, Any one of the people of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn in Israel who gives any of his children to Molech shall surely be put to death. The people of the land shall stone him with stones.<sup>3</sup>I myself will set my face against that man and will cut him off from among his people, because he has given one of his children to Molech, to make my sanctuary unclean and to profane my holy name.<sup>4</sup>And if the people of the land do at all close their eyes to that man when he gives one of his children to Molech, and do not put him to death,<sup>5</sup>then I will set my face against that man and against his clan and will cut them off from among their people, him and all who follow him in whoring after Molech.<sup>6</sup>"If a person turns to mediums and necromancers, whoring after them, I will set my face against that person and will cut him off from among his people.<sup>7</sup>Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, for I am the LORD your God.<sup>8</sup>Keep my statutes and do them;
