I am the LORD who sanctifies you.<sup>9</sup>For anyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death; he has cursed his father or his mother; his blood is upon him.<sup>10</sup>"If a man commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.<sup>11</sup>If a man lies with his father's wife, he has uncovered his father's nakedness; both of them shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.<sup>12</sup>If a man lies with his daughter-in-law, both of them shall surely be put to death; they have committed perversion; their blood is upon them.<sup>13</sup>If a man lies with a male as with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.<sup>14</sup>If a man takes a woman and her mother also, it is depravity; he and they shall be burned with fire, that there may be no depravity among you.<sup>15</sup>If a man lies with an animal, he shall surely be put to death, and you shall kill the animal.<sup>16</sup>If a woman approaches any animal and lies with it, you shall kill the woman and the animal; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.<sup>17</sup>"If a man takes his sister, a daughter of his father or a daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees his nakedness, it is a disgrace, and they shall be cut off in the sight of the children of their people. He has uncovered his sister's nakedness, and he shall bear his iniquity.<sup>18</sup>If a man lies with a woman during her menstrual period and uncovers her nakedness, he has made naked her fountain, and she has uncovered the fountain of her blood. Both of them shall be cut off from among their people.<sup>19</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother's sister or of your father's sister, for that is to make naked one's relative; they shall bear their iniquity.<sup>20</sup>If a man lies with his uncle's wife, he has uncovered his uncle's nakedness; they shall bear their sin; they shall die childless.<sup>21</sup>If a man takes his brother's wife, it is impurity. He has uncovered his brother's nakedness; they shall be childless.<sup>22</sup>"You shall therefore keep all my statutes and all my rules and do them, that the land where I am bringing you to live may not vomit you out.<sup>23</sup>And you shall not walk in the customs of the nation that I am driving out before you, for they did all these things, and therefore I detested them.<sup>24</sup>But I have said to you, 'You shall inherit their land, and I will give it to you to possess, a land flowing with milk and honey.' I am the LORD your God, who has separated you from the peoples.<sup>25</sup>You shall therefore separate the clean beast from the unclean, and the unclean bird from the clean. You shall not make yourselves detestable by beast or by bird or by anything with which the ground crawls, which I have set apart for you to hold unclean.<sup>26</sup>You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine.<sup>27</sup>"A man or a woman who is a medium or a necromancer shall surely be put to death. They shall be stoned with stones; their blood shall be upon them."
20.overview:
Chapter 20 returns to many of the sins named in chapter 18 (child sacrifice to Molech, occult practices, sexual transgressions) and now attaches penalties, often death. It is among the most difficult chapters in the Bible. A reader troubled by it is not being impious, and the questions deserve answers, which the verse notes on vv. 9-16 try to give. Israel was a theocracy, a nation ruled directly by God through his law, set apart as the family from which the promised Saviour would come, and the severity reflects the holiness of the God who dwelt in their midst. Our discomfort can also expose how lightly we take sin.

Yet the chapter is not finally about death; it is about holiness and belonging. Twice it returns to the call to be holy (20:7, 26), and it ends with the reason: God has set Israel apart "that you should be mine." And the gospel shines through the severity. Sin does deserve death, "the wages of sin is death" (Rom 6:23), but Christ bore that death, becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13), so that we who deserved to be cut off might be made holy and brought near. The chapter that pronounces death over sin drives us to the cross, where the Son died the death our sin deserved, and where God's people are at last made truly his.
20.theology:
The seriousness of sin. The death penalties reveal how gravely God regards sin among his people.

Israel, not the church. These civil penalties belonged to Israel as a nation under God's direct rule; the church lives under grace and church discipline, not the sword.

Separated to be his own. God's purpose in setting Israel apart is fulfilled as Christ purifies "a people for his own possession" (Titus 2:14).
20.examples:
Then: Israel learned that sin against a holy God is deadly serious.

Now: we do not wield Israel's civil sword, but we can recover sin's true weight, and with it a deeper wonder at the grace that made us God's own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-27 — Penalties, and a People Set Apart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-16: Penalties for Molech worship, mediums, cursing a parent and the sexual offences of chapter 18, with the call to holiness set in the middle.

Verses 17-27: Lesser penalties, the warning of the land, and the reason for everything.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who demands holiness is the God who gives it. Even in a chapter of penalties, he says, "I am the LORD who sanctifies you."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a community that looked away was treated as complicit. Now: a church or family that ignores the abuse of a child is not neutral either; it must act to protect the vulnerable.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Say to the people of Israel, Any one of the people of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn in Israel who gives any of his children to Molech shall surely be put to death. The people of the land shall stone him with stones. I myself will set my face against that man and will cut him off from among his people, because he has given one of his children to Molech, to make my sanctuary unclean and to profane my holy name. And if the people of the land do at all close their eyes to that man when he gives one of his children to Molech, and do not put him to death, then I will set my face against that man and against his clan and will cut them off from among their people, him and all who follow him in whoring after Molech.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 18 listed the offences; chapter 20 attaches the penalties, beginning with Molech. The reason given is not only the act but its effect on the sanctuary.

Then a clause with teeth: if the people close their eyes, God will act himself. A community that looks away is not neutral. It is named alongside the offender.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a person turns to mediums and necromancers, whoring after them, I will set my face against that person and will cut him off from among his people. Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, for I am the LORD your God. Keep my statutes and do them; I am the LORD who sanctifies you.
verseByVerse.commentary: In the middle of a chapter of penalties comes the call of chapter 19, to consecrate yourselves, followed at once by I am the LORD who sanctifies you. The one who demands the holiness is named as the one who supplies it, as he now does by the Spirit he gives to all who are in Christ (1 Thess. 4:7-8). That clause is the only reason a chapter like this is bearable.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death; he has cursed his father or his mother; his blood is upon him. "If a man commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death. If a man lies with his father's wife, he has uncovered his father's nakedness; both of them shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them. If a man lies with his daughter-in-law, both of them shall surely be put to death; they have committed perversion; their blood is upon them. If a man lies with a male as with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them. If a man takes a woman and her mother also, it is depravity; he and they shall be burned with fire, that there may be no depravity among you. If a man lies with an animal, he shall surely be put to death, and you shall kill the animal. If a woman approaches any animal and lies with it, you shall kill the woman and the animal; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A modern reader cannot read this page without difficulty, and the difficulty should be faced honestly rather than explained away. These are capital sentences for sins that no Christian state today punishes with death, and no Christian should wish otherwise.

Several things are true at once. Israel was not a church; it was a nation, with a criminal code, and this was that code. As in every legal system, the severity of a sentence is a statement about how gravely the society regards the act.

Those civil penalties were given to one particular nation, in one land, under one covenant, and the New Testament does not carry them across. The church has no sword. Paul's instruction about the gravest sin in the Corinthian congregation was to put a man out of the fellowship, not to put him to death (1 Cor. 5:13), and even that was aimed at his restoration, which 2 Corinthians 2:5-8 may describe.

Two further facts help. A death sentence required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6), so private sins were rarely capital cases. And Numbers 35:31 forbids a ransom for a murderer's life, which suggests to many scholars that for other offences a ransom could replace death, so that these penalties marked the most the crime deserved. That reading is debated.

So why do Christians still call the acts of 20:13 sin, while dropping both the penalty and the food laws such as the ban on shellfish (11:10)? Because the New Testament sorts them. The food laws marked Israel off from the nations and are lifted explicitly (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). The sexual laws rest on creation (Genesis 2:24), bound the Canaanites too (18:24–25), and are repeated by the apostles (Romans 1:26–27; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11). The death penalty belonged to Israel’s civil law and ended with that nation’s state. Christians are not picking and choosing; they are following the apostles, and the gospel offers washing to every sinner: such were some of you.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man takes his sister, a daughter of his father or a daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees his nakedness, it is a disgrace, and they shall be cut off in the sight of the children of their people. He has uncovered his sister's nakedness, and he shall bear his iniquity. If a man lies with a woman during her menstrual period and uncovers her nakedness, he has made naked her fountain, and she has uncovered the fountain of her blood. Both of them shall be cut off from among their people. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother's sister or of your father's sister, for that is to make naked one's relative; they shall bear their iniquity. If a man lies with his uncle's wife, he has uncovered his uncle's nakedness; they shall bear their sin; they shall die childless. If a man takes his brother's wife, it is impurity. He has uncovered his brother's nakedness; they shall be childless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remaining cases carry lighter penalties, and that itself teaches something. Not everything in the list is punished alike: each offence was weighed.

And what carries across from all of it is the seriousness. The New Testament nowhere lowers the estimate of these sins; it raises it, tracing adultery back to the lustful look and murder back to anger (Matt. 5:21-28).

What changes is not the gravity of sin but who bears its sentence. Every death penalty in this chapter is a statement that these things deserve death, and the gospel does not dispute it. It reports that the sentence was carried out on someone else, who also kept the law we broke, his obedience counted as ours (Rom. 5:19). So the way back for anyone who has done these things is confession and the mercy God promised (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore keep all my statutes and all my rules and do them, that the land where I am bringing you to live may not vomit you out. And you shall not walk in the customs of the nation that I am driving out before you, for they did all these things, and therefore I detested them. But I have said to you, 'You shall inherit their land, and I will give it to you to possess, a land flowing with milk and honey.' I am the LORD your God, who has separated you from the peoples. You shall therefore separate the clean beast from the unclean, and the unclean bird from the clean. You shall not make yourselves detestable by beast or by bird or by anything with which the ground crawls, which I have set apart for you to hold unclean. You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine. "A man or a woman who is a medium or a necromancer shall surely be put to death. They shall be stoned with stones; their blood shall be upon them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word "separated" appears twice, and it carries the whole logic of the book. Holy means set apart. But Israel's distinctiveness was never an end in itself, and the final clause says what it was for: that you should be mine.

That is the note the New Testament picks up when it describes the church in the same terms: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession (1 Pet. 2:9), words from Exodus and Isaiah handed to scattered, ordinary believers.

The church is still set apart, and for the same reason: not to be admired for its separation, but to belong to him.

21.title: Holiness for the Priests: A Higher Standard
21.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them, No one shall make himself unclean for the dead among his people,<sup>2</sup>except for his closest relatives, his mother, his father, his son, his daughter, his brother,<sup>3</sup>or his virgin sister (who is near to him because she has had no husband; for her he may make himself unclean).<sup>4</sup>He shall not make himself unclean as a husband among his people and so profane himself.<sup>5</sup>They shall not make bald patches on their heads, nor shave off the edges of their beards, nor make any cuts on their body.<sup>6</sup>They shall be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God. For they offer the LORD's food offerings, the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy.<sup>7</sup>They shall not marry a prostitute or a woman who has been defiled, neither shall they marry a woman divorced from her husband, for the priest is holy to his God.<sup>8</sup>You shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God. He shall be holy to you, for I, the LORD, who sanctify you, am holy.<sup>9</sup>And the daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by whoring, profanes her father; she shall be burned with fire.<sup>10</sup>"The priest who is chief among his brothers, on whose head the anointing oil is poured and who has been consecrated to wear the garments, shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes.<sup>11</sup>He shall not go in to any dead bodies nor make himself unclean, even for his father or for his mother.<sup>12</sup>He shall not go out of the sanctuary, lest he profane the sanctuary of his God, for the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him: I am the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And he shall take a wife in her virginity.<sup>14</sup>A widow, or a divorced woman, or a woman who has been defiled, or a prostitute, these he shall not marry. But he shall take as his wife a virgin of his own people,<sup>15</sup>that he may not profane his offspring among his people, for I am the LORD who sanctifies him."<sup>16</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>17</sup>"Speak to Aaron, saying, None of your offspring throughout their generations who has a blemish may approach to offer the bread of his God.<sup>18</sup>For no one who has a blemish shall draw near, a man blind or lame, or one who has a mutilated face or a limb too long,<sup>19</sup>or a man who has an injured foot or an injured hand,<sup>20</sup>or a hunchback or a dwarf or a man with a defect in his sight or an itching disease or scabs or crushed testicles.<sup>21</sup>No man of the offspring of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall come near to offer the LORD's food offerings; since he has a blemish, he shall not come near to offer the bread of his God.<sup>22</sup>He may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy things,<sup>23</sup>but he shall not go through the veil or approach the altar, because he has a blemish, that he may not profane my sanctuaries, for I am the LORD who sanctifies them."<sup>24</sup>So Moses spoke to Aaron and to his sons and to all the people of Israel.
21.overview:
Chapters 21 and 22 raise the standard for those who draw nearest to God: the priests, who handle the holy things and stand between God and the people. To whom much is given, much is required.

The hardest part for modern readers is the rule that a priest with a physical defect may not offer at the altar (21:17–23). The verse notes explain that this was a picture, not a verdict on anyone's worth, and that such a priest kept his place in God's household. The picture points to Christ, the priest who is "holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens" (Heb 7:26), the flawless priest the law required and Aaron could never be, fit to enter the true sanctuary and offer the perfect sacrifice, which was himself. And because our standing rests on his wholeness and not ours, the blemished, the lame and the scarred are made priests to our God in him (1 Pet 2:9).
21.theology:
A higher standard for leaders. Those who draw nearest to God bear greater accountability; teachers in the church will be judged with greater strictness (James 3:1).

The unblemished priest. The demand for a flawless priest and sacrifice points to Christ, the spotless Lamb (1 Pet 1:19).

Grace for the blemished. In Christ the broken are welcomed and made priests, clothed in his perfection.
21.examples:
Then: Israel's priests kept a stricter holiness, a living parable of the perfection God requires.

Now: no believer is kept back from God by disability, illness or scars. We rest in Christ, who clothes blemished sinners in his own perfection, and a church should make its welcome as wide as his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-24 — The Holiness of the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-15: Priests, and the high priest above all, are kept back from contact with death.

Verses 16-24: A priest with a physical defect may not serve at the altar, though he still shares the holy food.
verseByVerse.theology: The priests' life was a living picture of the holiness of the God they served, who is the God of life and wholeness. The cost of that picture fell on real people, and the law softened it where it could.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a priest might have to stay away from a funeral he longed to attend. Now: ministers still carry costs others do not see, and their people can pray for them and bear with them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them, No one shall make himself unclean for the dead among his people, except for his closest relatives, his mother, his father, his son, his daughter, his brother, or his virgin sister (who is near to him because she has had no husband; for her he may make himself unclean). He shall not make himself unclean as a husband among his people and so profane himself. They shall not make bald patches on their heads, nor shave off the edges of their beards, nor make any cuts on their body. They shall be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God. For they offer the LORD's food offerings, the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy. They shall not marry a prostitute or a woman who has been defiled, neither shall they marry a woman divorced from her husband, for the priest is holy to his God. You shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God. He shall be holy to you, for I, the LORD, who sanctify you, am holy. And the daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by whoring, profanes her father; she shall be burned with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priest lives under tighter restrictions than anyone else in Israel, and the first concerns death.

Grief is not forbidden him. But the man who serves the living God at the altar cannot be continually in contact with death, and where an ordinary Israelite could attend any funeral, the priest could attend almost none.

The pagan mourning rites are forbidden, as in 19:27-28, because they say something untrue about death.

Verse 9 is the hardest line here: a priest’s daughter who turns to prostitution is to be burned. It probably includes the cult prostitution of Canaan’s shrines, which profaned her father’s office. Whether the burning was the means of death or, as with Achan, of the body after execution (Joshua 7:15, 25) is debated. And this was Israel’s civil law, which ended with that nation; the church answers such sin with the welcome of Christ, who sent a sinful woman away forgiven (Luke 7:47–50).

verseByVerse.quote: "The priest who is chief among his brothers, on whose head the anointing oil is poured and who has been consecrated to wear the garments, shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes. He shall not go in to any dead bodies nor make himself unclean, even for his father or for his mother. He shall not go out of the sanctuary, lest he profane the sanctuary of his God, for the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him: I am the LORD. And he shall take a wife in her virginity. A widow, or a divorced woman, or a woman who has been defiled, or a prostitute, these he shall not marry. But he shall take as his wife a virgin of his own people, that he may not profane his offspring among his people, for I am the LORD who sanctifies him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest's restrictions are tighter still: not even his parents. The man who bore the name of God on his forehead could not stand at his own mother's graveside, because the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him.

That sets the reader up for something the Gospels do without comment. Israel's high priest could not go near a corpse. And in Nain, Jesus came up and touched the bier of a widow's only son (Luke 7:14), and in a synagogue ruler's house he took her by the hand (Matt. 9:25), and at Bethany he stood at the tomb of a man four days dead and called a man out of it (John 11:39-44). The one who was holier than Aaron ever was walked straight up to the dead and touched them, because uncleanness did not pass from them to him. Life passed from him to them, and the dead sat up.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron, saying, None of your offspring throughout their generations who has a blemish may approach to offer the bread of his God. For no one who has a blemish shall draw near, a man blind or lame, or one who has a mutilated face or a limb too long, or a man who has an injured foot or an injured hand, or a hunchback or a dwarf or a man with a defect in his sight or an itching disease or scabs or crushed testicles. No man of the offspring of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall come near to offer the LORD's food offerings; since he has a blemish, he shall not come near to offer the bread of his God. He may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy things, but he shall not go through the veil or approach the altar, because he has a blemish, that he may not profane my sanctuaries, for I am the LORD who sanctifies them." So Moses spoke to Aaron and to his sons and to all the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last section is the one modern readers find hardest. A descendant of Aaron with a physical defect may not offer at the altar.

Two things need saying, and the second matters more than the first.

The first is what the rule is doing. Everything presented at that altar had to be unblemished; the animals are held to the same standard in the next chapter. The priest at the altar was himself a living picture of a whole and undamaged offering. So the rule is about the picture, not about the man’s worth: he simply cannot serve as that picture.

The second is verse 22, easy to miss: he is barred from serving and not from eating. He remains a priest, supported by the offerings, sharing the most holy food, belonging entirely to the household of God. What he loses is one task, not his place in the household.

And then the gospel does something startling with these very people. When Jesus told a parable about a banquet whose invited guests refused to come, the master's instruction was to go into the streets and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame (Luke 14:21): much of the list of Leviticus 21, carried through the door and seated at the table. The altar admitted only the unblemished; the kingdom has one unblemished man, Christ, and admits all the rest on his account.

22.title: Holy Offerings: Nothing Blemished for God
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons so that they abstain from the holy things of the people of Israel, which they dedicate to me, so that they do not profane my holy name: I am the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Say to them, 'If any one of all your offspring throughout your generations approaches the holy things that the people of Israel dedicate to the LORD, while he has an uncleanness, that person shall be cut off from my presence: I am the LORD.<sup>4</sup>None of the offspring of Aaron who has a leprous disease or a discharge may eat of the holy things until he is clean. Whoever touches anything that is unclean through contact with the dead or a man who has had an emission of semen,<sup>5</sup>and whoever touches a swarming thing by which he may be made unclean or a person from whom he may take uncleanness, whatever his uncleanness may be—<sup>6</sup>the person who touches such a thing shall be unclean until the evening and shall not eat of the holy things unless he has bathed his body in water.<sup>7</sup>When the sun goes down he shall be clean, and afterward he may eat of the holy things, because they are his food.<sup>8</sup>He shall not eat what dies of itself or is torn by beasts, and so make himself unclean by it: I am the LORD.'<sup>9</sup>They shall therefore keep my charge, lest they bear sin for it and die thereby when they profane it: I am the LORD who sanctifies them.<sup>10</sup>"A lay person shall not eat of a holy thing; no foreign guest of the priest or hired worker shall eat of a holy thing,<sup>11</sup>but if a priest buys a slave as his property for money, the slave may eat of it, and anyone born in his house may eat of his food.<sup>12</sup>If a priest's daughter marries a layman, she shall not eat of the contribution of the holy things.<sup>13</sup>But if a priest's daughter is widowed or divorced and has no child and returns to her father's house, as in her youth, she may eat of her father's food; yet no lay person shall eat of it.<sup>14</sup>And if anyone eats of a holy thing unintentionally, he shall add the fifth of its value to it and give the holy thing to the priest.<sup>15</sup>They shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, which they contribute to the LORD,<sup>16</sup>and so cause them to bear iniquity and guilt, by eating their holy things: for I am the LORD who sanctifies them."<sup>17</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons and all the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of the house of Israel or of the sojourners in Israel presents a burnt offering as his offering, for any of their vows or freewill offerings that they offer to the LORD,<sup>19</sup>if it is to be accepted for you it shall be a male without blemish, of the bulls or the sheep or the goats.<sup>20</sup>You shall not offer anything that has a blemish, for it will not be acceptable for you.<sup>21</sup>And when anyone offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering from the herd or from the flock, to be accepted it must be perfect; there shall be no blemish in it.<sup>22</sup>Animals blind or disabled or mutilated or having a discharge or an itch or scabs you shall not offer to the LORD or give them to the LORD as a food offering on the altar.<sup>23</sup>You may present a bull or a lamb that has a part too long or too short for a freewill offering, but for a vow offering it cannot be accepted.<sup>24</sup>Any animal that has its testicles bruised or crushed or torn or cut you shall not offer to the LORD; you shall not do it within your land,<sup>25</sup>neither shall you offer as the bread of your God any such animals gotten from a foreigner. Since there is a blemish in them, because of their mutilation, they will not be accepted for you."<sup>26</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>27</sup>"When an ox or sheep or goat is born, it shall remain seven days with its mother, and from the eighth day on it shall be acceptable as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>28</sup>But you shall not kill an ox or a sheep and her young in one day.<sup>29</sup>And when you sacrifice a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the LORD, you shall sacrifice it so that you may be accepted.<sup>30</sup>It shall be eaten on the same day; you shall leave none of it until morning: I am the LORD.<sup>31</sup>"So you shall keep my commandments and do them: I am the LORD.<sup>32</sup>And you shall not profane my holy name, that I may be sanctified among the people of Israel. I am the LORD who sanctifies you,<sup>33</sup>who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD."
22.overview:
Chapter 22 turns from the holiness of the priests to the holiness of the offerings they handle. God will not be honoured with the maimed, the diseased or the second-rate: "to be accepted it must be perfect; there shall be no blemish in it" (22:21). Yet even the finest animal in Israel's flocks was still only an animal, unable truly to take away sin, and the demand for perfection points beyond every spotless lamb to the one perfect Lamb. Where every Israelite searched his flock for a flawless lamb, God searched all heaven and earth and provided his own Son, the perfect sacrifice God required and the perfect sacrifice God provided.

Malachi would later rebuke priests who broke this very law, and to give God less than our best is still to despise his name. The searching question comes home to our own hearts: do we give God the first and best, or the leftovers? The prime of our strength, or the dregs of our exhaustion? But the God who accepted the poor man's handful of flour does not despise the offering of the weary who have little left to give (Mark 12:43–44), and in Christ even our imperfect worship is made acceptable.
22.theology:
Without blemish. The demand for a flawless offering sets a standard no earthly lamb could meet, and points to Christ, who alone met it.

God deserves our best. To offer the maimed or leftover is to despise God's name; he is worthy of our first and finest.

The LORD who sanctifies. Holiness is God's gift and work, grounded in redemption and applied by the Spirit (22:32).
22.examples:
Then: an Israelite searched his flock for a flawless animal.

Now: we bring God our best, not our leftovers, yet we rest our acceptance not on our flawed offerings but on the one spotless Lamb.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-9: A priest who is unclean must wait, bathe and see the sun go down before he eats the holy offerings.

Verses 10-16: Who in a priest's household may eat the holy food (not a guest or a hired worker, but a bought slave and a daughter come home), and what happens after an honest mistake.
verseByVerse.theology: Holy things belong to God and to those he brings into his household. Access to them rests on belonging, not on rank, wages or a professional exemption.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: priests had no exemption from the rules they enforced. Now: pastors and church leaders need the same grace, and the same accountability, as everyone they serve.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons so that they abstain from the holy things of the people of Israel, which they dedicate to me, so that they do not profane my holy name: I am the LORD. Say to them, 'If any one of all your offspring throughout your generations approaches the holy things that the people of Israel dedicate to the LORD, while he has an uncleanness, that person shall be cut off from my presence: I am the LORD. None of the offspring of Aaron who has a leprous disease or a discharge may eat of the holy things until he is clean. Whoever touches anything that is unclean through contact with the dead or a man who has had an emission of semen, and whoever touches a swarming thing by which he may be made unclean or a person from whom he may take uncleanness, whatever his uncleanness may be— the person who touches such a thing shall be unclean until the evening and shall not eat of the holy things unless he has bathed his body in water. When the sun goes down he shall be clean, and afterward he may eat of the holy things, because they are his food. He shall not eat what dies of itself or is torn by beasts, and so make himself unclean by it: I am the LORD.' They shall therefore keep my charge, lest they bear sin for it and die thereby when they profane it: I am the LORD who sanctifies them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The men who administer the system are subject to it. There is no professional exemption: a priest with a skin condition waits outside the same as anybody else, and the penalty for eating while unclean is being cut off from my presence. Yet the paragraph closes on grace: the LORD himself sanctifies them.

verseByVerse.quote: "A lay person shall not eat of a holy thing; no foreign guest of the priest or hired worker shall eat of a holy thing, but if a priest buys a slave as his property for money, the slave may eat of it, and anyone born in his house may eat of his food. If a priest's daughter marries a layman, she shall not eat of the contribution of the holy things. But if a priest's daughter is widowed or divorced and has no child and returns to her father's house, as in her youth, she may eat of her father's food; yet no lay person shall eat of it. And if anyone eats of a holy thing unintentionally, he shall add the fifth of its value to it and give the holy thing to the priest. They shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, which they contribute to the LORD, and so cause them to bear iniquity and guilt, by eating their holy things: for I am the LORD who sanctifies them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line is drawn around the household, not around blood relations. A hired man who works on the premises every day may not eat; a purchased slave who lives there may. What decides it is belonging, not employment. Israel's servant laws trouble modern readers, and rightly ask for care; here at least the bought slave is counted as family at the holy table, ahead of the hired man.

And there is real care in the case of the daughter. A woman whose marriage has ended and who has returned to her father's house is explicitly restored to the provision she grew up with. She does not fall between two households.

Repaying the value plus a fifth is the rule already given for holy things in 5:16. Even an honest mistake with holy things carries a cost.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 17-25: Nothing blemished may be offered, whether as a vow, a freewill offering or a peace offering.

Verses 26-33: Small mercies for animals, and the closing reason for it all: the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt is the one who makes them holy.
verseByVerse.theology: God is worthy of the best, and he is also kind: the same laws that demand perfect offerings stop to protect a newborn animal and its mother.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God would not be worshipped with what was going spare. Now: the time, money and energy we give him can be our first and best, even when there is not much of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons and all the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of the house of Israel or of the sojourners in Israel presents a burnt offering as his offering, for any of their vows or freewill offerings that they offer to the LORD, if it is to be accepted for you it shall be a male without blemish, of the bulls or the sheep or the goats. You shall not offer anything that has a blemish, for it will not be acceptable for you. And when anyone offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering from the herd or from the flock, to be accepted it must be perfect; there shall be no blemish in it. Animals blind or disabled or mutilated or having a discharge or an itch or scabs you shall not offer to the LORD or give them to the LORD as a food offering on the altar. You may present a bull or a lamb that has a part too long or too short for a freewill offering, but for a vow offering it cannot be accepted. Any animal that has its testicles bruised or crushed or torn or cut you shall not offer to the LORD; you shall not do it within your land, neither shall you offer as the bread of your God any such animals gotten from a foreigner. Since there is a blemish in them, because of their mutilation, they will not be accepted for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temptation in any farming community is obvious: an animal has broken its leg and is worth nothing at market, so give that one to God. The law shuts the door on worship funded by whatever was going spare.

Centuries later Malachi found Israel's priests doing precisely that, and the sarcasm is withering: When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil? And when you offer those that are lame or sick, is that not evil? Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor? (Mal. 1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "When an ox or sheep or goat is born, it shall remain seven days with its mother, and from the eighth day on it shall be acceptable as a food offering to the LORD. But you shall not kill an ox or a sheep and her young in one day. And when you sacrifice a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the LORD, you shall sacrifice it so that you may be accepted. It shall be eaten on the same day; you shall leave none of it until morning: I am the LORD. "So you shall keep my commandments and do them: I am the LORD. And you shall not profane my holy name, that I may be sanctified among the people of Israel. I am the LORD who sanctifies you, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ban on killing a mother and her young on one day is a small mercy: nothing in the sacrificial system required it. It is there because God cares for his creatures, the same care that later forbids taking a bird and her young together, and muzzling the ox that treads the grain (Deut. 22:6; 25:4).

The chapter's reason is grace already given: the LORD who sanctifies them is the one who brought them out of Egypt to be their God.

The demand for an unblemished offering ran for well over a thousand years, and no animal could ever fully meet what it pointed to. Then John the Baptist stood on a riverbank, looked at Jesus walking toward him, and said Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! (John 1:29).

Peter uses the vocabulary of this chapter for him: a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet. 1:19). Every inspection Israel ever made of every animal it brought was a rehearsal for one examination, conducted, as it turned out, by a Roman governor who looked at him and said I find no guilt in him (John 18:38), and then handed him over anyway.

23.title: The Feasts of the LORD: A Rehearsal of Redemption
23.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, These are the appointed feasts of the LORD that you shall proclaim as holy convocations; they are my appointed feasts.<sup>3</sup>"Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation. You shall do no work. It is a Sabbath to the LORD in all your dwelling places.<sup>4</sup>"These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at the time appointed for them.<sup>5</sup>In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at twilight, is the LORD's Passover.<sup>6</sup>And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the LORD; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread.<sup>7</sup>On the first day you shall have a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>8</sup>But you shall present a food offering to the LORD for seven days. On the seventh day is a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work."<sup>9</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you and reap its harvest, you shall bring the sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest to the priest,<sup>11</sup>and he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD, so that you may be accepted. On the day after the Sabbath the priest shall wave it.<sup>12</sup>And on the day when you wave the sheaf, you shall offer a male lamb a year old without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And the grain offering with it shall be two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, a food offering to the LORD with a pleasing aroma, and the drink offering with it shall be of wine, a fourth of a hin.<sup>14</sup>And you shall eat neither bread nor grain parched or fresh until this same day, until you have brought the offering of your God: it is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.<sup>15</sup>"You shall count seven full weeks from the day after the Sabbath, from the day that you brought the sheaf of the wave offering.<sup>16</sup>You shall count fifty days to the day after the seventh Sabbath. Then you shall present a grain offering of new grain to the LORD.<sup>17</sup>You shall bring from your dwelling places two loaves of bread to be waved, made of two tenths of an ephah. They shall be of fine flour, and they shall be baked with leaven, as firstfruits to the LORD.<sup>18</sup>And you shall present with the bread seven lambs a year old without blemish, and one bull from the herd and two rams. They shall be a burnt offering to the LORD, with their grain offering and their drink offerings, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And you shall offer one male goat for a sin offering, and two male lambs a year old as a sacrifice of peace offerings.<sup>20</sup>And the priest shall wave them with the bread of the firstfruits as a wave offering before the LORD, with the two lambs. They shall be holy to the LORD for the priest.<sup>21</sup>And you shall make a proclamation on the same day. You shall hold a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a statute forever in all your dwelling places throughout your generations.<sup>22</sup>"And when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, nor shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner: I am the LORD your God."<sup>23</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>24</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall observe a day of solemn rest, a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets, a holy convocation.<sup>25</sup>You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall present a food offering to the LORD."<sup>26</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>27</sup>"Now on the tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. It shall be for you a time of holy convocation, and you shall afflict yourselves and present a food offering to the LORD.<sup>28</sup>And you shall not do any work on that very day, for it is a Day of Atonement, to make atonement for you before the LORD your God.<sup>29</sup>For whoever is not afflicted on that very day shall be cut off from his people.<sup>30</sup>And whoever does any work on that very day, that person I will destroy from among his people.<sup>31</sup>You shall not do any work. It is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwelling places.<sup>32</sup>It shall be to you a Sabbath of solemn rest, and you shall afflict yourselves. On the ninth day of the month beginning at evening, from evening to evening shall you keep your Sabbath."<sup>33</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>34</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, On the fifteenth day of this seventh month and for seven days is the Feast of Booths to the LORD.<sup>35</sup>On the first day shall be a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>36</sup>For seven days you shall present food offerings to the LORD. On the eighth day you shall hold a holy convocation and present a food offering to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>37</sup>"These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, which you shall proclaim as times of holy convocation, for presenting to the LORD food offerings, burnt offerings and grain offerings, sacrifices and drink offerings, each on its proper day,<sup>38</sup>besides the LORD's Sabbaths and besides your gifts and besides all your vow offerings and besides all your freewill offerings, which you give to the LORD.<sup>39</sup>"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the produce of the land, you shall celebrate the feast of the LORD seven days. On the first day shall be a solemn rest, and on the eighth day shall be a solemn rest.<sup>40</sup>And you shall take on the first day the fruit of splendid trees, branches of palm trees and boughs of leafy trees and willows of the brook, and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God seven days.<sup>41</sup>You shall celebrate it as a feast to the LORD for seven days in the year. It is a statute forever throughout your generations; you shall celebrate it in the seventh month.<sup>42</sup>You shall dwell in booths for seven days. All native Israelites shall dwell in booths,<sup>43</sup>that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God."<sup>44</sup>Thus Moses declared to the people of Israel the appointed feasts of the LORD.
23.overview:
Chapter 23 lays out Israel's sacred calendar, the appointed feasts of the LORD: fixed meetings between God and his people. First comes the weekly Sabbath; then Passover, Unleavened Bread and Firstfruits in the spring; Weeks fifty days later; and in the autumn Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Booths.

Taken together they are a year-long rehearsal of redemption, every feast a shadow, an outline drawn in advance, of the reality, which is Christ (Col 2:16–17). The spring feasts met their fulfilment at Christ's first coming, in the very season they marked: his death at Passover, his rising as the firstfruits, and the Spirit poured out at Pentecost. Of the autumn feasts, the Day of Atonement was fulfilled at the cross, while Trumpets and Booths look ahead to Christ's return and to God dwelling with his people for ever. The whole calendar tells the gospel in dates and seasons. Read with the New Testament open, feast after feast turns out to be about Christ.
23.theology:
Time belongs to God. The feasts are appointments God made, not festivals Israel invented, and they teach that the whole year is lived before him.

Shadow and substance. Each feast was a shadow pointing beyond itself to Christ, the substance (Col 2:17), and the order in which they were fulfilled was arranged by God, not by the people it happened to.

Hope still ahead. The calendar ends with God's people camping in joy, a picture of the day when he will dwell with them for ever.
23.examples:
Then: Israel kept the feasts, unknowingly rehearsing the gospel.

Now: Christians mark their weeks by the Lord’s Day, remember his death at his table, and wait for the final harvest, when God will make his home with his people for ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-44 — The Appointed Feasts of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-22: The Sabbath, then the spring feasts, from Passover to Weeks.

Verses 23-44: The autumn feasts of the seventh month: Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Booths.
verseByVerse.theology: The calendar is built around rest, remembrance and joy. God did not only command Israel's work; he commanded their holidays.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the feasts rehearsed Israel's redemption every year. Now: a Christian's diary can also be shaped by worship, with fixed times for gathering, remembering and rejoicing, received as gifts rather than burdens.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, These are the appointed feasts of the LORD that you shall proclaim as holy convocations; they are my appointed feasts. "Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation. You shall do no work. It is a Sabbath to the LORD in all your dwelling places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew word for the feasts, mo'adim, means appointed times, fixed meetings, and God calls them his own twice in one verse. These are not festivals Israel invented to commemorate its own history; they are appointments God made and expected to be kept, entered in a calendar he wrote.

And the first is not annual at all: the weekly Sabbath. The rhythm of Israel's worship begins with something available fifty-two times a year to every household in the land, requiring no journey, no animal and no priest. The most frequent appointment God kept with his people cost nothing at all.

Does the Sabbath bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exod 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary takes the Sabbath to be fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Heb 4:9–10), so no day binds the conscience (Rom 14:5), because Colossians places Sabbaths among the shadows; rest and gathering for worship on the Lord’s Day remain good gifts, gladly received. Faithful Christians differ here, and should bear with one another.

Must Christians keep these feasts? They were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17): Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7), and the Lord’s Supper has taken the Passover’s place. Keeping them is a matter of freedom, not obligation (Rom 14:5–6), and never a condition of standing with God (Gal 4:10–11).
verseByVerse.note: Israel's months were lunar; the first month (later called Nisan) fell in March–April.

verseByVerse.quote: "These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at the time appointed for them. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at twilight, is the LORD's Passover. And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the LORD; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall have a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work. But you shall present a food offering to the LORD for seven days. On the seventh day is a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Passover, on the fourteenth day of the first month, marked the night Israel came out of Egypt, kept every year since as a family meal with a lamb.

Paul states its fulfilment in a single sentence: For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7). And the Gospels place the crucifixion precisely here in the calendar, with John pausing to note that the soldiers did not break his legs, that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken" (John 19:36), the rule for the Passover lamb in Exodus 12:46.

Then comes Unleavened Bread, the seven days following, when no leaven (yeast) could be in the house. Paul takes it up in the same breath: Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump... Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:7-8).

A week of searching the house for crumbs, once a year, so that a nation would understand that a little evil, like a little yeast, works through the whole batch.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you and reap its harvest, you shall bring the sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest to the priest, and he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD, so that you may be accepted. On the day after the Sabbath the priest shall wave it. And on the day when you wave the sheaf, you shall offer a male lamb a year old without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD. And the grain offering with it shall be two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, a food offering to the LORD with a pleasing aroma, and the drink offering with it shall be of wine, a fourth of a hin. And you shall eat neither bread nor grain parched or fresh until this same day, until you have brought the offering of your God: it is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Firstfruits the timing matters: on the usual reading the day after the Sabbath is the first day of the week.

Paul's word for the resurrection is this feast's word: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20). One sheaf, lifted up early, on the first day of the week: and the whole point of a firstfruits offering is that it guarantees a harvest still standing in the field. It is not a sample. It is a promise about the rest.

Israel waved that sheaf every spring for centuries without knowing what it was rehearsing, and nobody in Israel ate from the new harvest until God had been given the first of it.

Which “Sabbath” is meant in verse 11? The Sadducees took it as the weekly Sabbath, so the firstfruits always fell on a Sunday; the Pharisees, as the first day of Unleavened Bread. Either way, Christ rose on the first day of the week, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor 15:20).
verseByVerse.note: The barley harvest came first, in early spring; the wheat harvest followed about seven weeks later, at the Feast of Weeks.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall count seven full weeks from the day after the Sabbath, from the day that you brought the sheaf of the wave offering. You shall count fifty days to the day after the seventh Sabbath. Then you shall present a grain offering of new grain to the LORD. You shall bring from your dwelling places two loaves of bread to be waved, made of two tenths of an ephah. They shall be of fine flour, and they shall be baked with leaven, as firstfruits to the LORD. And you shall present with the bread seven lambs a year old without blemish, and one bull from the herd and two rams. They shall be a burnt offering to the LORD, with their grain offering and their drink offerings, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And you shall offer one male goat for a sin offering, and two male lambs a year old as a sacrifice of peace offerings. And the priest shall wave them with the bread of the firstfruits as a wave offering before the LORD, with the two lambs. They shall be holy to the LORD for the priest. And you shall make a proclamation on the same day. You shall hold a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a statute forever in all your dwelling places throughout your generations. "And when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, nor shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven weeks and a day: this is the Feast of Weeks, which Greek-speaking Jews called Pentecost, from the word for fiftieth.

Fifty days after the resurrection, on the day this chapter appoints, the disciples were all together in one place when a sound like a mighty rushing wind filled the house (Acts 2:1-2). Luke did not choose that date. Leviticus did, many centuries earlier.

And the loaves waved at this feast are unlike anything else brought to that altar: two of them, and explicitly baked with leaven. Leaven has been banned from the offerings since chapter 2, and here it is required.

The likeliest reason is that this feast celebrates not the raw sheaf but the finished loaf, bread as people actually eat it. Which turns out to be exactly right for the day it was pointing at. At Pentecost the harvest gathered in was not sheaves of barley but three thousand ordinary people, forgiven but far from faultless.

Verse 22 is a gleaning law, dropped without transition into the middle of the festival calendar. Israel could not hold a harvest festival without being reminded, in the same paragraph, to leave part of the harvest standing for people who owned no field. Worship and care for the poor are commanded together.
verseByVerse.note: In later Jewish tradition the Feast of Weeks also came to celebrate the giving of the law at Sinai.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall observe a day of solemn rest, a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets, a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall present a food offering to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The autumn feasts begin, and the character of the calendar changes. No reason is given for the trumpets. There is no historical event attached and no ritual described beyond the noise and the rest. The day simply announces that the seventh month has arrived.

What makes it significant is what it announces. Nine days later comes the Day of Atonement. The trumpet is a warning sounded in advance of a reckoning, giving a nation time to prepare for it. That is a pattern Scripture keeps: the warning always comes first, and it comes early enough to act on.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Now on the tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. It shall be for you a time of holy convocation, and you shall afflict yourselves and present a food offering to the LORD. And you shall not do any work on that very day, for it is a Day of Atonement, to make atonement for you before the LORD your God. For whoever is not afflicted on that very day shall be cut off from his people. And whoever does any work on that very day, that person I will destroy from among his people. You shall not do any work. It is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwelling places. It shall be to you a Sabbath of solemn rest, and you shall afflict yourselves. On the ninth day of the month beginning at evening, from evening to evening shall you keep your Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Day of Atonement is set into the calendar here, with the ceremony itself already given in chapter 16. What this passage adds is what the people do while the high priest works.

Two commands, and they pull against each other: you shall afflict yourselves, and you shall not do any work. Fast, and rest.

Both halves are the gospel. Israel is to come empty-handed and mourning, bringing nothing, and then to sit still, because the work being done that day is the priest's and not theirs. It is the one fast commanded in the law, and it is also called a Sabbath of solemn rest.

And the warning attached is the sharpest given to any feast in the chapter: anyone who will not humble himself that day shall be cut off, and anyone who works I will destroy. There is no neutral way to spend the Day of Atonement.

Are these autumn feasts fulfilled at the cross or at Christ’s return? The Day of Atonement was fulfilled once for all at the cross (Heb 9:11–12, 24–26). Trumpets and Booths look ahead to the last trumpet (1 Thess 4:16) and God dwelling with his people (Rev 21:3). Some dispensational readers expect the feasts to be literally restored in a millennial kingdom; this commentary, holding the amillennial view, takes them as shadows whose substance is Christ, while gladly owning as brothers those who read the prophecies otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, On the fifteenth day of this seventh month and for seven days is the Feast of Booths to the LORD. On the first day shall be a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work. For seven days you shall present food offerings to the LORD. On the eighth day you shall hold a holy convocation and present a food offering to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you shall not do any ordinary work. "These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, which you shall proclaim as times of holy convocation, for presenting to the LORD food offerings, burnt offerings and grain offerings, sacrifices and drink offerings, each on its proper day, besides the LORD's Sabbaths and besides your gifts and besides all your vow offerings and besides all your freewill offerings, which you give to the LORD. "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the produce of the land, you shall celebrate the feast of the LORD seven days. On the first day shall be a solemn rest, and on the eighth day shall be a solemn rest. And you shall take on the first day the fruit of splendid trees, branches of palm trees and boughs of leafy trees and willows of the brook, and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God seven days. You shall celebrate it as a feast to the LORD for seven days in the year. It is a statute forever throughout your generations; you shall celebrate it in the seventh month. You shall dwell in booths for seven days. All native Israelites shall dwell in booths, that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God." Thus Moses declared to the people of Israel the appointed feasts of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last feast is the longest and the happiest. Once a year the whole nation moved out of its houses and camped. A settled people with vineyards and stone walls went back to living under leaves for a week, so that nobody could forget that this land had been a gift and their great-grandparents had crossed a desert with nothing.

Prosperity forgets, and the booths were built to stop it. Note that the command was given before they had a single house to move out of. God made a law against a forgetfulness that was still forty years away.

It is at this feast, on the last day of the feast, the great day, that Jesus stood up in the temple and shouted: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). By later Jewish custom the feast included a priest carrying water from the pool of Siloam to pour out at the altar, with prayers for rain and the words of Isaiah about drawing water from the wells of salvation (Isaiah 12:3). Jesus offered himself as the water.

The shape of the year: the spring feasts were each fulfilled at the first coming, in order, on the day appointed, and no human being arranged the timing. The autumn feasts open with a trumpet, pass through the day sin was dealt with, and end with God dwelling among his people in temporary shelters.

Scripture picks that last image up one final time, at the very end of everything: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people (Rev. 21:3), where dwell is the word for pitching a tent, the same word John used of the incarnation: the Word became flesh and dwelt, pitched his tent, among us (John 1:14). The feast that had Israel camping in the open for one week a year turns out to have been a rehearsal for God moving in permanently.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Booths is also called Tabernacles (ESV note); its Hebrew name is Sukkot.

24.title: The Lampstand, the Bread, and the Holiness of the Name
24.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel to bring you pure oil from beaten olives for the lamp, that a light may be kept burning regularly.<sup>3</sup>Outside the veil of the testimony, in the tent of meeting, Aaron shall arrange it from evening to morning before the LORD regularly. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations.<sup>4</sup>He shall arrange the lamps on the lampstand of pure gold before the LORD regularly.<sup>5</sup>"You shall take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it; two tenths of an ephah shall be in each loaf.<sup>6</sup>And you shall set them in two piles, six in a pile, on the table of pure gold before the LORD.<sup>7</sup>And you shall put pure frankincense on each pile, that it may go with the bread as a memorial portion as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>8</sup>Every Sabbath day Aaron shall arrange it before the LORD regularly; it is from the people of Israel as a covenant forever.<sup>9</sup>And it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place, since it is for him a most holy portion out of the LORD's food offerings, a perpetual due."<sup>10</sup>Now an Israelite woman's son, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the people of Israel. And the Israelite woman's son and a man of Israel fought in the camp,<sup>11</sup>and the Israelite woman's son blasphemed the Name, and cursed. Then they brought him to Moses. His mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.<sup>12</sup>And they put him in custody, till the will of the LORD should be clear to them.<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>14</sup>"Bring out of the camp the one who cursed, and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him.<sup>15</sup>And speak to the people of Israel, saying, Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin.<sup>16</sup>Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall stone him. The sojourner as well as the native, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.<sup>17</sup>"Whoever takes a human life shall surely be put to death.<sup>18</sup>Whoever takes an animal's life shall make it good, life for life.<sup>19</sup>If anyone injures his neighbor, as he has done it shall be done to him,<sup>20</sup>fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; whatever injury he has given a person shall be given to him.<sup>21</sup>Whoever kills an animal shall make it good, and whoever kills a person shall be put to death.<sup>22</sup>You shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native, for I am the LORD your God."<sup>23</sup>So Moses spoke to the people of Israel, and they brought out of the camp the one who had cursed and stoned him with stones. Thus the people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses.
24.overview:
Chapter 24 sets two images of continual ministry, the lampstand and the bread of the Presence, alongside a sobering account of judgment on blasphemy. The pairing seems jarring at first, but together they teach that the God who provides continual light and bread for his people will not have his name dishonoured.

Light and bread, set perpetually before the face of God (24:1–9), are signs of his provision for his people's life and sight, and of their place before him. Christ used both images of himself: he is the light which the darkness has not overcome (John 1:5), and the bread of life. We live by light and bread, and Christ is both. And the blasphemy case points to him too. Falsely charged with blasphemy, he bore the curse that falls on those who dishonour God’s name, so that we who have dishonoured God's name might hallow it and be made holy by it.
24.theology:
Christ the light. The continual lampstand points to Jesus, 'the light of the world' (John 8:12), and to his people who shine with borrowed light (Matt 5:14).

Christ the bread. The bread of the Presence points to Jesus, 'the bread of life' (John 6:35), who keeps us continually present and nourished before the Father.

The holiness of the Name. The judgment on the blasphemer enforces reverence for God's name, the name Jesus taught us to hallow (Matt 6:9).
24.examples:
Then: the priests tended the light and the bread, and Israel learned that the Name must never be cursed.

Now: we live by Christ our light and bread, kept continually before the Father, and we learn to speak God's name with reverence in a culture that uses it as a curse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The Lamp and the Bread of the Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: The lamp and the bread inside the Holy Place.
verseByVerse.theology: God's people were kept continually before him. The light never went out, and every tribe was represented at his table, week in and week out.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a priest trimmed the wicks every night in a room no one else saw. Now: much faithful service is hidden and repetitive, and God sees all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel to bring you pure oil from beaten olives for the lamp, that a light may be kept burning regularly. Outside the veil of the testimony, in the tent of meeting, Aaron shall arrange it from evening to morning before the LORD regularly. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations. He shall arrange the lamps on the lampstand of pure gold before the LORD regularly. "You shall take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it; two tenths of an ephah shall be in each loaf. And you shall set them in two piles, six in a pile, on the table of pure gold before the LORD. And you shall put pure frankincense on each pile, that it may go with the bread as a memorial portion as a food offering to the LORD. Every Sabbath day Aaron shall arrange it before the LORD regularly; it is from the people of Israel as a covenant forever. And it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place, since it is for him a most holy portion out of the LORD's food offerings, a perpetual due."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two permanent arrangements inside the Holy Place, and both are defined by the word regularly.

The lamp's oil was the finest grade. Somebody trimmed those wicks night after night, for centuries, in a room the public never entered.

Twelve loaves for twelve tribes: the whole nation, set out in bread, permanently in God's presence. Nobody was missing from that table, including the tribes that would later be lost to history.

The old loaves went to the priests, and centuries later David, a hungry fugitive with no right to it, ate that bread at Nob (1 Samuel 21:1–6), and when Jesus was challenged about his disciples picking grain on the Sabbath, that was the incident he cited (Mark 2:25-26). He used the holiest bread in Israel to argue that God’s law was never meant to stand in the way of human need; it was made with that need in view.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-23 — The Blasphemer, and Just Measure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-23: A rare narrative in Leviticus, and the laws it produced.
verseByVerse.theology: God's name is holy, and his justice is even-handed: the same law for foreigner and native, and penalties limited to the harm done.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the penalty could not exceed the damage. Now: when we are wronged, we may still seek justice, but Christ calls us to let go of revenge.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an Israelite woman's son, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the people of Israel. And the Israelite woman's son and a man of Israel fought in the camp, and the Israelite woman's son blasphemed the Name, and cursed. Then they brought him to Moses. His mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan. And they put him in custody, till the will of the LORD should be clear to them. Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Bring out of the camp the one who cursed, and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him. And speak to the people of Israel, saying, Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin. Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall stone him. The sojourner as well as the native, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death. "Whoever takes a human life shall surely be put to death. Whoever takes an animal's life shall make it good, life for life. If anyone injures his neighbor, as he has done it shall be done to him, fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; whatever injury he has given a person shall be given to him. Whoever kills an animal shall make it good, and whoever kills a person shall be put to death. You shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native, for I am the LORD your God." So Moses spoke to the people of Israel, and they brought out of the camp the one who had cursed and stoned him with stones. Thus the people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without warning comes a narrative, one of the few in the book. Two details stand out. The first is that they did not know what to do. There was no precedent, so they waited and asked rather than acting on instinct. The second is the ruling, stated twice (vv. 16, 22): one rule for sojourner and native. The case that produced it involved a man of mixed parentage, and the outcome is a principle of equal standing before the law: one code, no distinction by ancestry.

The formula "eye for eye" is almost always quoted as though it licensed revenge, and it did the opposite. In a world where an injury to a chief's son could cost a village, this rule set a ceiling: the penalty may not exceed the damage. One eye, not two; one tooth, not a family. It is a restraint on retaliation, administered by a court and not by the injured party.

That is what makes Jesus' handling of it so precise. You have heard that it was said, "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth." But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil (Matt. 5:38-39). He is not correcting the law. He is taking a rule that limits what a court may exact and telling his followers to go further still and surrender what they are owed, and then he did it himself, in front of a court, where when he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Pet. 2:23). The man of Leviticus 24 cursed the Name and was carried outside the camp and stoned. Christ was accused of blaspheming the Name (Mark 14:64), and led outside the city, and killed for it. The difference is that he had told the truth about who he was.

Was stoning for blasphemy fair? In Israel, cursing the name of the God who was the nation’s King was treason against the covenant itself. The penalty belonged to that civil law and ended with it; the church answers blasphemy with the word and discipline (1 Cor 5:12–13), and most Christians today agree that the state should not compel true worship.

25.title: The Jubilee: The Year of the LORD's Favor
25.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall keep a Sabbath to the LORD.<sup>3</sup>For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its fruits,<sup>4</sup>but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the LORD. You shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard.<sup>5</sup>You shall not reap what grows of itself in your harvest, or gather the grapes of your undressed vine. It shall be a year of solemn rest for the land.<sup>6</sup>The Sabbath of the land shall provide food for you, for yourself and for your male and female slaves and for your hired worker and the sojourner who lives with you,<sup>7</sup>and for your cattle and for the wild animals that are in your land: all its yield shall be for food.<sup>8</sup>"You shall count seven weeks of years, seven times seven years, so that the time of the seven weeks of years shall give you forty-nine years.<sup>9</sup>Then you shall sound the loud trumpet on the tenth day of the seventh month. On the Day of Atonement you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land.<sup>10</sup>And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan.<sup>11</sup>That fiftieth year shall be a jubilee for you; in it you shall neither sow nor reap what grows of itself nor gather the grapes from the undressed vines.<sup>12</sup>For it is a jubilee. It shall be holy to you. You may eat the produce of the field.<sup>13</sup>"In this year of jubilee each of you shall return to his property.<sup>14</sup>And if you make a sale to your neighbor or buy from your neighbor, you shall not wrong one another.<sup>15</sup>You shall pay your neighbor according to the number of years after the jubilee, and he shall sell to you according to the number of years for crops.<sup>16</sup>If the years are many, you shall increase the price, and if the years are few, you shall reduce the price, for it is the number of the crops that he is selling to you.<sup>17</sup>You shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God, for I am the LORD your God.<sup>18</sup>"Therefore you shall do my statutes and keep my rules and perform them, and then you will dwell in the land securely.<sup>19</sup>The land will yield its fruit, and you will eat your fill and dwell in it securely.<sup>20</sup>And if you say, 'What shall we eat in the seventh year, if we may not sow or gather in our crop?'<sup>21</sup>I will command my blessing on you in the sixth year, so that it will produce a crop sufficient for three years.<sup>22</sup>When you sow in the eighth year, you will be eating some of the old crop; you shall eat the old until the ninth year, when its crop arrives.<sup>23</sup>"The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine.
