For you are strangers and sojourners with me.<sup>24</sup>And in all the country you possess, you shall allow a redemption of the land.<sup>25</sup>"If your brother becomes poor and sells part of his property, then his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold.<sup>26</sup>If a man has no one to redeem it and then himself becomes prosperous and finds sufficient means to redeem it,<sup>27</sup>let him calculate the years since he sold it and pay back the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and then return to his property.<sup>28</sup>But if he does not have sufficient means to recover it, then what he sold shall remain in the hand of the buyer until the year of jubilee. In the jubilee it shall be released, and he shall return to his property.<sup>29</sup>"If a man sells a dwelling house in a walled city, he may redeem it within a year of its sale. For a full year he shall have the right of redemption.<sup>30</sup>If it is not redeemed within a full year, then the house in the walled city shall belong in perpetuity to the buyer, throughout his generations; it shall not be released in the jubilee.<sup>31</sup>But the houses of the villages that have no wall around them shall be classified with the fields of the land. They may be redeemed, and they shall be released in the jubilee.<sup>32</sup>As for the cities of the Levites, the Levites may redeem at any time the houses in the cities they possess.<sup>33</sup>And if one of the Levites exercises his right of redemption, then the house that was sold in a city they possess shall be released in the jubilee. For the houses in the cities of the Levites are their possession among the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>But the fields of pastureland belonging to their cities may not be sold, for that is their possession forever.<sup>35</sup>"If your brother becomes poor and cannot maintain himself with you, you shall support him as though he were a stranger and a sojourner, and he shall live with you.<sup>36</sup>Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God, that your brother may live beside you.<sup>37</sup>You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit.<sup>38</sup>I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to give you the land of Canaan, and to be your God.<sup>39</sup>"If your brother becomes poor beside you and sells himself to you, you shall not make him serve as a slave:<sup>40</sup>he shall be with you as a hired worker and as a sojourner. He shall serve with you until the year of the jubilee.<sup>41</sup>Then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and go back to his own clan and return to the possession of his fathers.<sup>42</sup>For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves.<sup>43</sup>You shall not rule over him ruthlessly but shall fear your God.<sup>44</sup>As for your male and female slaves whom you may have: you may buy male and female slaves from among the nations that are around you.<sup>45</sup>You may also buy from among the strangers who sojourn with you and their clans that are with you, who have been born in your land, and they may be your property.<sup>46</sup>You may bequeath them to your sons after you to inherit as a possession forever. You may make slaves of them, but over your brothers the people of Israel you shall not rule, one over another ruthlessly.<sup>47</sup>"If a stranger or sojourner with you becomes rich, and your brother beside him becomes poor and sells himself to the stranger or sojourner with you or to a member of the stranger's clan,<sup>48</sup>then after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him,<sup>49</sup>or his uncle or his cousin may redeem him, or a close relative from his clan may redeem him. Or if he grows rich he may redeem himself.<sup>50</sup>He shall calculate with his buyer from the year when he sold himself to him until the year of jubilee, and the price of his sale shall vary with the number of years. The time he was with his owner shall be rated as the time of a hired worker.<sup>51</sup>If there are still many years left, he shall pay proportionately for his redemption some of his sale price.<sup>52</sup>If there remain but a few years until the year of jubilee, he shall calculate and pay for his redemption in proportion to his years of service.<sup>53</sup>He shall treat him as a worker hired year by year. He shall not rule ruthlessly over him in your sight.<sup>54</sup>And if he is not redeemed by these means, then he and his children with him shall be released in the year of jubilee.<sup>55</sup>For it is to me that the people of Israel are servants. They are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
25.overview:
Chapter 25 unveils one of the most radical and beautiful institutions in Scripture: the Sabbath year and, every fiftieth year, the Jubilee. Every seventh year the land rested, and every fiftieth year liberty was proclaimed: Israelites in servitude were set free and family lands restored. A whole society was reset.

Beneath it lies one sentence: "The land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me" (25:23). Israel did not ultimately own the land; God did, and they were his tenants. So no debt could be permanent, no slavery perpetual and no family dispossessed for ever, because everything belonged to God, and God is a Redeemer. The Jubilee built grace into Israel’s buying and selling: a society shaped by the character of the God who sets people free.

The gospel is the true Jubilee. Our debt of sin, which we could never repay, is cancelled; our slavery is broken; our lost inheritance is restored; and we who were strangers are brought home to the family of God. What Christ began will be completed in the new creation, when the whole earth rests in the freedom of the children of God. The Jubilee trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, and fittingly, for our true Jubilee is bought by the blood of the cross. Liberty, at last, throughout the land.
25.theology:
The gospel as Jubilee. Liberty for captives, cancelled debts and restored inheritance are fulfilled in Christ, who announced that the year of the Lord's favour had come in him (Luke 4:21).

Everything belongs to God. We hold what we have as his tenants, and so we are not free to keep others in permanent poverty or bondage.

The kinsman-redeemer. The relative who buys back lost land and frees the enslaved points to Christ, who became our flesh and blood in order to redeem us (Heb 2:14-17).
25.examples:
Then: every fiftieth year slaves went free and families returned to their lost lands.

Now: those whom Christ has set free are made open-handed by his Spirit: slow to hold on to what others owe them, and quick to help a struggling family keep its footing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-22 — The Sabbath Year and the Year of Jubilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-7: The land's Sabbath every seventh year.

Verses 8-22: The fiftieth year, the Jubilee, and how it shaped every sale of land.
verseByVerse.theology: Rest and release are built into God's order. He provides for those who stop when he says stop, and he will not let his people's poverty become permanent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God answered the farmer's question, "What shall we eat?", with provision in advance. Now: resting one day in seven, or turning down work that would swallow every hour, is an act of trust that God will still provide.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall keep a Sabbath to the LORD. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its fruits, but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the LORD. You shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard. You shall not reap what grows of itself in your harvest, or gather the grapes of your undressed vine. It shall be a year of solemn rest for the land. The Sabbath of the land shall provide food for you, for yourself and for your male and female slaves and for your hired worker and the sojourner who lives with you, and for your cattle and for the wild animals that are in your land: all its yield shall be for food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land gets a Sabbath. The commandment about the seventh day is extended to the seventh year, and the logic is identical. Israel is asked to believe that provision does not depend on unbroken work, and to prove it by stopping: not for a day, which anyone can manage, but for a farming year, which means trusting God with the food supply.

Whatever grows untended belongs to everyone: the list runs past the household, past the workers, past the livestock, all the way down to the wild animals. In the year the owner stops owning, the field feeds whoever comes to it.

Does the Jubilee bind today? It was part of Israel’s civil law in the land, and it ended with Israel’s life as a nation under God’s direct rule. Jesus announced the true Jubilee, the year of the Lord’s favor (Luke 4:18–21): release for captives of sin. Its principles remain: the earth is the Lord’s, the poor are not to be left in permanent bondage, and generosity is a duty.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall count seven weeks of years, seven times seven years, so that the time of the seven weeks of years shall give you forty-nine years. Then you shall sound the loud trumpet on the tenth day of the seventh month. On the Day of Atonement you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land. And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan. That fiftieth year shall be a jubilee for you; in it you shall neither sow nor reap what grows of itself nor gather the grapes from the undressed vines. For it is a jubilee. It shall be holy to you. You may eat the produce of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jubilee begins on the Day of Atonement, the one day in the year when the nation's sin is dealt with. Liberty is proclaimed in the hours after the scapegoat is led away. Forgiveness in the sanctuary and release in the marketplace begin on the same day.

Over fifty years land piles up in fewer and fewer hands. Bad harvests and bad decisions bring debt, debt forces sales, and families slip from owning land to renting it and then to servitude. And every fiftieth year a horn sounded and the whole process reset. Land went back to the family that had lost it. People who had sold themselves walked home.

Was the Jubilee ever actually kept? The Old Testament never records one being celebrated, and it shows Israel neglecting the land’s Sabbath years (2 Chronicles 36:21) and breaking a solemn release of slaves (Jeremiah 34:8–17). The law stood, largely unkept, as a promise waiting for someone who would keep it, which is part of why Jesus’ words at Nazareth landed as they did.
verseByVerse.note: The word “jubilee” comes from the Hebrew yobel, the ram's horn blown to announce it.

verseByVerse.quote: "In this year of jubilee each of you shall return to his property. And if you make a sale to your neighbor or buy from your neighbor, you shall not wrong one another. You shall pay your neighbor according to the number of years after the jubilee, and he shall sell to you according to the number of years for crops. If the years are many, you shall increase the price, and if the years are few, you shall reduce the price, for it is the number of the crops that he is selling to you. You shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God, for I am the LORD your God. "Therefore you shall do my statutes and keep my rules and perform them, and then you will dwell in the land securely. The land will yield its fruit, and you will eat your fill and dwell in it securely. And if you say, 'What shall we eat in the seventh year, if we may not sow or gather in our crop?' I will command my blessing on you in the sixth year, so that it will produce a crop sufficient for three years. When you sow in the eighth year, you will be eating some of the old crop; you shall eat the old until the ninth year, when its crop arrives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is blunt about what is actually being sold: the number of the crops (v. 16).

Israel could not sell land permanently at all. Every land deal in the country was a lease with a known expiry date, and both parties could count the harvests remaining. A buyer near the jubilee paid little because he was buying few crops; a buyer just after it paid much.

The reason is verse 23, which governs the whole chapter. Israel did not own Canaan. Israel rented it, from a landlord who had strong views about how tenants treat each other.

Then the objection any farmer would raise: what shall we eat? God does not dismiss the question or rebuke the asking. He answers it with a promise of a triple harvest in the sixth year, given in advance of the obedience he is requesting.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-55 — Redemption of Land and of People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 23-38: How a poor family's land is bought back, and how the poor are to be helped without profit.

Verses 39-55: Israelites driven into servitude, their treatment and their release.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption is a family duty. When a relative falls into poverty, the nearest kinsman steps in, and behind every human redeemer stands the God who brought his people out of Egypt and calls them his own servants.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the aim of the law was that a struggling brother could go on living beside you. Now: helping someone in debt keep his home and dignity is still the shape of Christian love.

verseByVerse.quote: "The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me. And in all the country you possess, you shall allow a redemption of the land. "If your brother becomes poor and sells part of his property, then his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold. If a man has no one to redeem it and then himself becomes prosperous and finds sufficient means to redeem it, let him calculate the years since he sold it and pay back the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and then return to his property. But if he does not have sufficient means to recover it, then what he sold shall remain in the hand of the buyer until the year of jubilee. In the jubilee it shall be released, and he shall return to his property. "If a man sells a dwelling house in a walled city, he may redeem it within a year of its sale. For a full year he shall have the right of redemption. If it is not redeemed within a full year, then the house in the walled city shall belong in perpetuity to the buyer, throughout his generations; it shall not be released in the jubilee. But the houses of the villages that have no wall around them shall be classified with the fields of the land. They may be redeemed, and they shall be released in the jubilee. As for the cities of the Levites, the Levites may redeem at any time the houses in the cities they possess. And if one of the Levites exercises his right of redemption, then the house that was sold in a city they possess shall be released in the jubilee. For the houses in the cities of the Levites are their possession among the people of Israel. But the fields of pastureland belonging to their cities may not be sold, for that is their possession forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The redemption laws introduce a word that will matter enormously later. The Hebrew is go'el, the kinsman-redeemer, and redeeming is a family duty, not an optional kindness. When a relative is in trouble, the nearest able kinsman pays what is needed to buy back what was lost. Three things are required of him: he must be related, he must be willing, and he must be able. Ruth's story is this law in action: Boaz is her go'el.

And if no redeemer appears, the man is not abandoned: the property returns to him at the jubilee anyway. The law has a safety net.

Special provision follows for houses in walled cities, which may be redeemed only within a year, and for the Levites, whose houses may always be redeemed because the Levitical cities are their possession among the people of Israel (v. 33).
verseByVerse.note: The same word, go'el, is used of God himself as Israel's Redeemer (Isaiah 41:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother becomes poor and cannot maintain himself with you, you shall support him as though he were a stranger and a sojourner, and he shall live with you. Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God, that your brother may live beside you. You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to give you the land of Canaan, and to be your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The clause "fear your God" is again attached to conduct no court could police, and the reason follows in verse 38: the God who brought them out of Egypt and gave them the land. A lender who charged a desperate man interest would be doing something entirely legal in every surrounding nation.

And the stated aim is not repayment. It is that your brother may live beside you. The purpose of the law is that the man stays your neighbour, in the same street, on speaking terms.

Is charging interest sin? The law forbade profiting from a poor brother’s need (v. 36). It allowed interest from a foreigner in trade (Deut 23:20), and Jesus speaks of money with bankers earning interest (Matt 25:27). Commercial lending and borrowing are not sin; exploiting the desperate is.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother becomes poor beside you and sells himself to you, you shall not make him serve as a slave: he shall be with you as a hired worker and as a sojourner. He shall serve with you until the year of the jubilee. Then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and go back to his own clan and return to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves. You shall not rule over him ruthlessly but shall fear your God. As for your male and female slaves whom you may have: you may buy male and female slaves from among the nations that are around you. You may also buy from among the strangers who sojourn with you and their clans that are with you, who have been born in your land, and they may be your property. You may bequeath them to your sons after you to inherit as a possession forever. You may make slaves of them, but over your brothers the people of Israel you shall not rule, one over another ruthlessly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the hardest section. An Israelite driven by poverty into servitude is treated as a hired worker and freed at the jubilee, and the governing reason is stated twice: they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt.

That is why no Israelite may be held permanently. God has a prior claim on them. A people already bought out of slavery are not available to be owned, because they already belong to someone.

Verses 44-46 then permit the purchase of foreign slaves as permanent property, and it would be dishonest to soften it. The law regulated an institution that existed everywhere in the ancient world; it did not abolish it here. It did forbid, on pain of death, the kidnapping on which the Atlantic slave trade was built (Exodus 21:16), and it gave refuge to a slave who escaped a master (Deuteronomy 23:15–16). What Scripture does is plant within slavery a truth that eventually destroyed it: the insistence, running from Genesis 1 to Philemon, that a human being bears the image of God. When Paul finally wrote to a slave-owner about a runaway, he asked him to receive the man back no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother (Philem. 16), and slavery cannot last where that sentence is taken seriously.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a stranger or sojourner with you becomes rich, and your brother beside him becomes poor and sells himself to the stranger or sojourner with you or to a member of the stranger's clan, then after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him, or his uncle or his cousin may redeem him, or a close relative from his clan may redeem him. Or if he grows rich he may redeem himself. He shall calculate with his buyer from the year when he sold himself to him until the year of jubilee, and the price of his sale shall vary with the number of years. The time he was with his owner shall be rated as the time of a hired worker. If there are still many years left, he shall pay proportionately for his redemption some of his sale price. If there remain but a few years until the year of jubilee, he shall calculate and pay for his redemption in proportion to his years of service. He shall treat him as a worker hired year by year. He shall not rule ruthlessly over him in your sight. And if he is not redeemed by these means, then he and his children with him shall be released in the year of jubilee. For it is to me that the people of Israel are servants. They are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even when an Israelite sells himself to a wealthy foreigner the redemption right stands, and the chapter closes on the sentence underneath all of it: they are the LORD's servants, brought out of Egypt.

Now hold this chapter next to a Sabbath morning in Nazareth. Jesus stood up in the synagogue, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, and read: to proclaim liberty to the captives... to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor. Then he rolled it up, sat down, and said Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (Luke 4:18-21).

Isaiah's phrase is jubilee language, and what Jesus announced in that room was that the true Jubilee had begun.

Everything in this chapter turns out to be a picture of him and his work. Here are a people who cannot free themselves, and a kinsman who must be related to them, willing to act and able to pay. A debt is discharged with someone else's money, and captives walk home to a property they had forfeited, on a day that began with atonement. Knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18-19).

He became man so that he could be our kinsman, and the price he paid was not silver.

26.title: Blessings and Curses: The Covenant's Heart
26.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not make idols for yourselves or erect an image or pillar, and you shall not set up a figured stone in your land to bow down to it, for I am the LORD your God.<sup>2</sup>You shall keep my Sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary: I am the LORD.<sup>3</sup>"If you walk in my statutes and observe my commandments and do them,<sup>4</sup>then I will give you your rains in their season, and the land shall yield its increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit.<sup>5</sup>Your threshing shall last to the time of the grape harvest, and the grape harvest shall last to the time for sowing. And you shall eat your bread to the full and dwell in your land securely.<sup>6</sup>I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid. And I have broken the bars of your yoke and made you walk erect.<sup>14</sup>"But if you will not listen to me and will not do all these commandments,<sup>15</sup>if you spurn my statutes, and if your soul abhors my rules, so that you will not do all my commandments, but break my covenant,<sup>16</sup>then I will do this to you: I will visit you with panic, with wasting disease and fever that consume the eyes and make the heart ache. The sound of a driven leaf shall put them to flight, and they shall flee as one flees from the sword, and they shall fall when none pursues.<sup>37</sup>They shall stumble over one another, as if to escape a sword, though none pursues. 26.overview:
Chapter 26 brings the covenant to its solemn climax with blessings and curses, the two roads before the covenant people. Spoken to a people the LORD had already brought out of Egypt (26:13), they set faithfulness and its blessings, crowned by God walking among his people (26:12), against unfaithfulness and its escalating discipline, ending in exile. The form resembles the treaties of the ancient world, which also ended with blessings and curses, but the heart of it is the presence or absence of God himself. The judgments are sobering, "sevenfold" again and again (26:18, 21, 24, 28), but they are the discipline of a covenant Father, meant to bring his people back. And the chapter's last word is mercy: even in exile, confession will find a God who remembers his covenant (26:40–45), because the covenant rests finally not on Israel's obedience but on God's character. The God who threatens curse is the God who will not let his people go.

And the cross is where the curses and the blessings meet. Israel, and we with them, chose the road of unfaithfulness. But Christ bore the curse and kept the covenant we broke, his obedience counted as ours (Rom 5:19), "so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith" (Gal 3:14). The promise of verse 12 is fulfilled for ever when God dwells with his people (Rev 21:3).
26.theology:
The covenant's two roads. Blessing follows faithfulness and curse follows unfaithfulness, and the greatest blessing is God's own presence.

Mercy outlasts judgment. Even in exile, confession reopens the door, for the covenant rests on God's faithfulness, not ours: "I will for their sake remember the covenant" (26:45).

Christ bore the curse. Jesus "redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Gal 3:13), bearing the full covenant judgment, even the exile of being forsaken by God, so that the blessing might come to us.
26.examples:
Then: Israel was warned of discipline and exile, and promised that confession would meet a remembering God.

Now: a believer who has wandered need not wonder whether the door is still open. Confession meets the same remembering God, and in Christ the blessing is ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-46 — Blessing, Discipline, and Covenant Faithfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-13: The two commands on which the chapter hangs, and the blessings of faithfulness.

Verses 14-39: Five escalating rounds of discipline, ending in exile.

Verses 40-46: The way back.
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgments on his people are meant to bring them back, not to destroy them, and his covenant holds because of who he is.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was warned plainly and in advance. Now: God's warnings in Scripture are also mercies, given early enough for us to turn.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not make idols for yourselves or erect an image or pillar, and you shall not set up a figured stone in your land to bow down to it, for I am the LORD your God. You shall keep my Sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before either the blessings or the curses stand two commands: whom you worship, and when. Everything that follows in this chapter hangs on those two, which is a fair summary of the whole covenant: the right God, honoured at the right times, in the place he appointed.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you walk in my statutes and observe my commandments and do them, then I will give you your rains in their season, and the land shall yield its increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit. Your threshing shall last to the time of the grape harvest, and the grape harvest shall last to the time for sowing. And you shall eat your bread to the full and dwell in your land securely. I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid. And I will remove harmful beasts from the land, and the sword shall not go through your land. You shall chase your enemies, and they shall fall before you by the sword. Five of you shall chase a hundred, and a hundred of you shall chase ten thousand, and your enemies shall fall before you by the sword. I will turn to you and make you fruitful and multiply you and will confirm my covenant with you. You shall eat old store long kept, and you shall clear out the old to make way for the new. I will make my dwelling among you, and my soul shall not abhor you. And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, that you should not be their slaves. And I have broken the bars of your yoke and made you walk erect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessings begin with things anyone can see: harvests running into one another without a gap, and sleep without fear.

In the promise "I will walk among you," the word walk is the one used of God in Eden, moving about in the garden in the cool of the day. Everything the tabernacle was built to make possible is compressed into that sentence: not prosperity, not safety, but God at ease in the middle of his people. Paul quotes this promise to the church in Corinth, Gentiles and Jews together: we are the temple of the living God (2 Corinthians 6:16). In Christ it has begun to come true.

The blessings rest on what God had already done: he had broken their yoke and made them walk erect. Slaves stoop; he straightened their backs.

Does this promise health and wealth to obedient believers? These were the covenant terms for Israel as a nation in the land (Deut 28). Christ bore the curse of the law (Gal 3:13), and believers have every spiritual blessing in him (Eph 1:3), while being told to expect trouble in the world (John 16:33). It is no prosperity promise.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you will not listen to me and will not do all these commandments, if you spurn my statutes, and if your soul abhors my rules, so that you will not do all my commandments, but break my covenant, then I will do this to you: I will visit you with panic, with wasting disease and fever that consume the eyes and make the heart ache. And you shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it. I will set my face against you, and you shall be struck down before your enemies. Those who hate you shall rule over you, and you shall flee when none pursues you. And if in spite of this you will not listen to me, then I will discipline you again sevenfold for your sins, and I will break the pride of your power, and I will make your heavens like iron and your earth like bronze. And your strength shall be spent in vain, for your land shall not yield its increase, and the trees of the land shall not yield their fruit. "Then if you walk contrary to me and will not listen to me, I will continue striking you, sevenfold for your sins. And I will let loose the wild beasts against you, which shall bereave you of your children and destroy your livestock and make you few in number, so that your roads shall be deserted. "And if by this discipline you are not turned to me but walk contrary to me, then I also will walk contrary to you, and I myself will strike you sevenfold for your sins. And I will bring a sword upon you, that shall execute vengeance for the covenant. And if you gather within your cities, I will send pestilence among you, and you shall be delivered into the hand of the enemy. When I break your supply of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in a single oven and shall dole out your bread again by weight, and you shall eat and not be satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary: Then the reverse, at more than twice the length, in five escalating rounds; even drought is described as metal, a sky like iron and ground like bronze that will yield nothing. The escalation matters more than any individual item. The refrain is not I will destroy you but if you will not listen: each round is a door held open, another attempt to make them listen when gentler measures had failed.
verseByVerse.note: Deuteronomy 28 gives a longer list of covenant blessings and curses in the same pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if in spite of this you will not listen to me, but walk contrary to me, then I will walk contrary to you in fury, and I myself will discipline you sevenfold for your sins. You shall eat the flesh of your sons, and you shall eat the flesh of your daughters. And I will destroy your high places and cut down your incense altars and cast your dead bodies upon the dead bodies of your idols, and my soul will abhor you. And I will lay your cities waste and will make your sanctuaries desolate, and I will not smell your pleasing aromas. And I myself will devastate the land, so that your enemies who settle in it shall be appalled at it. And I will scatter you among the nations, and I will unsheathe the sword after you, and your land shall be a desolation, and your cities shall be a waste. "Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths as long as it lies desolate, while you are in your enemies' land; then the land shall rest, and enjoy its Sabbaths. As long as it lies desolate it shall have rest, the rest that it did not have on your Sabbaths when you were dwelling in it. And as for those of you who are left, I will send faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies. The sound of a driven leaf shall put them to flight, and they shall flee as one flees from the sword, and they shall fall when none pursues. They shall stumble over one another, as if to escape a sword, though none pursues. And you shall have no power to stand before your enemies. And you shall perish among the nations, and the land of your enemies shall eat you up. And those of you who are left shall rot away in your enemies' lands because of their iniquity, and also because of the iniquities of their fathers they shall rot away like them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth round is the worst, and Scripture does not look away from it. Two things should be said about a passage this dark.

The first is that it is meant to heal, not to take revenge. Verse 41 names the goal: that their uncircumcised heart, a heart closed to God, might be humbled. The purpose is not the ruin but the repentance it is meant to produce.

A Christian in hardship may wonder whether this is God’s curse on him. It is not. Christ bore the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13), and the troubles of a believer are the discipline of a Father who loves his children, never the punishment of an enemy (Hebrews 12:5–11).

The second is that all of it happened. This chapter was read in Israel for centuries as something that might happen, and then Assyria came, and then Babylon, and the land lay empty. And when the writer of Chronicles came to explain the exile, he reached back to these very verses: the land enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years (2 Chron. 36:21), making up the sabbath years Israel had never given it, exactly as verses 34-35 said it would.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers in their treachery that they committed against me, and also in walking contrary to me, so that I walked contrary to them and brought them into the land of their enemies—if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled and they make amends for their iniquity, then I will remember my covenant with Jacob, and I will remember my covenant with Isaac and my covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land. But the land shall be abandoned by them and enjoy its Sabbaths while it lies desolate without them, and they shall make amends for their iniquity, because they spurned my rules and their soul abhorred my statutes. Yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them, for I am the LORD their God. But I will for their sake remember the covenant with their forefathers, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the nations, that I might be their God: I am the LORD." These are the statutes and rules and laws that the LORD made between himself and the people of Israel through Moses on Mount Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all that, the chapter does something the reader has no right to expect. The way back is left open at the far end of the worst that could happen. And it is not a new covenant offered on better behaviour; it is the old one, remembered, with the patriarchs named in reverse order as though God were walking back up the family line to where the promise started.

Verse 44 is the sentence to take away from the chapter. Even in exile, even after five rounds of judgment that they brought on themselves and were warned about in advance, he does not break the covenant, and the reason given is not anything about them. It is for I am the LORD their God. The covenant holds because of who is keeping it.

That is exactly the logic Paul uses, looking at his own unbelieving nation and refusing to conclude that God had finished with them: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Rom. 11:29).

And it is why a believer can be sure of God's promises at all. A covenant that depended on Israel would have ended somewhere in the book of Judges. This one is held up from God’s side, by One who does not change his mind about the people he has bound himself to.

Does verse 42 mean a future national and territorial restoration for Israel? Dispensational readers hold that it does, with Romans 11:29 as support. Many Reformed readers answer that the return from Babylon fulfilled the promise of verses 40–45 in its first sense, and that the New Testament sees the covenant with Abraham fulfilled in Christ and his people (Gal 3:29); many of them also expect a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Rom 11:26), without a separate promise of land. Faithful Christians differ here. All agree that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2) and that for Jew and Gentile alike the way home is Christ.

27.title: Vows and Dedications: All Things Are His
27.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, If anyone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the valuation of persons,<sup>3</sup>then the valuation of a male from twenty years old up to sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary.<sup>4</sup>If the person is a female, the valuation shall be thirty shekels.<sup>5</sup>If the person is from five years old up to twenty years old, the valuation shall be for a male twenty shekels, and for a female ten shekels.<sup>6</sup>If the person is from a month old up to five years old, the valuation shall be for a male five shekels of silver, and for a female the valuation shall be three shekels of silver.<sup>7</sup>And if the person is sixty years old or over, then the valuation for a male shall be fifteen shekels, and for a female ten shekels.<sup>8</sup>And if someone is too poor to pay the valuation, then he shall be made to stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him; the priest shall value him according to what the vower can afford.<sup>9</sup>"If the vow is an animal that may be offered as an offering to the LORD, all of it that he gives to the LORD is holy.<sup>10</sup>He shall not exchange it or make a substitute for it, good for bad, or bad for good; and if he does in fact substitute one animal for another, then both it and the substitute shall be holy.<sup>11</sup>And if it is any unclean animal that may not be offered as an offering to the LORD, then he shall stand the animal before the priest,<sup>12</sup>and the priest shall value it as either good or bad; as the priest values it, so it shall be.<sup>13</sup>But if he wishes to redeem it, he shall add a fifth to the valuation.<sup>14</sup>"When a man dedicates his house as a holy gift to the LORD, the priest shall value it as either good or bad; as the priest values it, so it shall stand.<sup>15</sup>And if the donor wishes to redeem his house, he shall add a fifth to the valuation price, and it shall be his.<sup>16</sup>"If a man dedicates to the LORD part of the land that is his possession, then the valuation shall be in proportion to its seed. A homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver.<sup>17</sup>If he dedicates his field from the year of jubilee, the valuation shall stand,<sup>18</sup>but if he dedicates his field after the jubilee, then the priest shall calculate the price according to the years that remain until the year of jubilee, and a deduction shall be made from the valuation.<sup>19</sup>And if he who dedicates the field wishes to redeem it, then he shall add a fifth to its valuation price, and it shall remain his.<sup>20</sup>But if he does not wish to redeem the field, or if he has sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed anymore.<sup>21</sup>But the field, when it is released in the jubilee, shall be a holy gift to the LORD, like a field that has been devoted. The priest shall be in possession of it.<sup>22</sup>If he dedicates to the LORD a field that he has bought, which is not a part of his possession,<sup>23</sup>then the priest shall calculate the amount of the valuation for it up to the year of jubilee, and the man shall give the valuation on that day as a holy gift to the LORD.<sup>24</sup>In the year of jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought, to whom the land belongs as a possession.<sup>25</sup>Every valuation shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs shall make a shekel.<sup>26</sup>"But a firstborn of animals, which as a firstborn belongs to the LORD, no man may dedicate; whether ox or sheep, it is the LORD's.<sup>27</sup>And if it is an unclean animal, then he shall buy it back at the valuation, and add a fifth to it; or, if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold at the valuation.<sup>28</sup>"But no devoted thing that a man devotes to the LORD, of anything that he has, whether man or beast, or of his inherited field, shall be sold or redeemed; every devoted thing is most holy to the LORD.<sup>29</sup>No one devoted, who is to be devoted for destruction from mankind, shall be ransomed; he shall surely be put to death.<sup>30</sup>"Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD.<sup>31</sup>If a man wishes to redeem some of his tithe, he shall add a fifth to it.<sup>32</sup>And every tithe of herds and flocks, every tenth animal of all that pass under the herdsman's staff, shall be holy to the LORD.<sup>33</sup>One shall not differentiate between good or bad, neither shall he make a substitute for it; and if he does substitute for it, then both it and the substitute shall be holy; it shall not be redeemed."<sup>34</sup>These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai.
27.overview:
Leviticus closes not with the thunder of Sinai but with laws about vows: the voluntary dedication of persons, animals, houses and land to the LORD. After all the commanded offerings, the book ends with the offerings no one commands, the overflow of a grateful heart. Beneath it lies the truth that crowns the whole book: everything belongs to God. What we vow to him, we give back from what was already his.

It all points to Christ, who is both the One devoted wholly to God and the price of our redemption. He is the firstborn given to the Father, the One who could say, "I have come to do your will, O God" (Heb 10:7), holding nothing back; and he is the ransom by which we, who could never pay the price of our own redemption, are redeemed: "you were bought with a price" (1 Cor 6:20). The book that opened with the burnt offering, the picture of a life given wholly to God, closes with the same call turned toward us: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship" (Rom 12:1). Holy, holy, holy is the LORD, and all that we are and have is his.
27.theology:
All things belong to God. The tithe and the devoted thing confess that everything is the LORD's: "The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof" (Ps 24:1).

Voluntary consecration. Worship that begins with God's gift to us ends with our glad gift to him.

Christ our ransom. We could never pay our own redemption price; we were redeemed by "the precious blood of Christ" (1 Pet 1:19).
27.examples:
Then: a grateful Israelite might vow himself or his field, confessing that all he had was God's.

Now: we present our whole selves to God, not to buy his favour but because Christ first gave himself wholly for us. And a promise made to God in a crisis is worth keeping, or bringing honestly to him if it cannot be kept.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-34 — Vows, the Devoted Thing, and the Tithe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-25: The prices for redeeming what has been vowed: persons, animals, houses and land.

Verses 26-34: What cannot be vowed because it already belongs to God, and the tithe.
verseByVerse.theology: A vow to God is serious, and so is his kindness: the law fixes a price and then bends it for those who cannot pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a published price list protected the worshipper from being exploited at the sanctuary door. Now: churches should be just as careful that no one is pressured into giving, or shamed for giving little.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, If anyone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the valuation of persons, then the valuation of a male from twenty years old up to sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary. If the person is a female, the valuation shall be thirty shekels. If the person is from five years old up to twenty years old, the valuation shall be for a male twenty shekels, and for a female ten shekels. If the person is from a month old up to five years old, the valuation shall be for a male five shekels of silver, and for a female the valuation shall be three shekels of silver. And if the person is sixty years old or over, then the valuation for a male shall be fifteen shekels, and for a female ten shekels. And if someone is too poor to pay the valuation, then he shall be made to stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him; the priest shall value him according to what the vower can afford.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book ends with an appendix on vows, and it looks at first like an anticlimax after chapter 26. It is not. It is about what happens when somebody, moved by gratitude or desperation, promises God something, and then has to work out what that costs.

The sums are substantial: fifty shekels for a man in his prime.

These are not statements of human worth. They are a schedule of redemption prices, published in advance precisely so that nobody haggled over a person at the sanctuary door and no priest could set his own rate.

For anyone too poor to pay, here again is the provision that ran through the sin offering in chapter 5 and the cleansing of the leper in chapter 14. A fixed price, and then a clause that bends it to what the man actually has. Nobody in Israel was ever priced out of the sanctuary. It happens so often in this book that it stops looking like an exception and starts looking like the character of the God who gave the law.

Why are women valued less (vv. 3–7)? The valuations reflect the labour a person could give in an agrarian economy, which is why children and the elderly are valued less too. They are not a measure of worth before God, in whose image man and woman are made alike (Gen 1:27; Gal 3:28).
verseByVerse.note: A shekel was about 11 grams (2/5 ounce) of silver (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "If the vow is an animal that may be offered as an offering to the LORD, all of it that he gives to the LORD is holy. He shall not exchange it or make a substitute for it, good for bad, or bad for good; and if he does in fact substitute one animal for another, then both it and the substitute shall be holy. And if it is any unclean animal that may not be offered as an offering to the LORD, then he shall stand the animal before the priest, and the priest shall value it as either good or bad; as the priest values it, so it shall be. But if he wishes to redeem it, he shall add a fifth to the valuation. "When a man dedicates his house as a holy gift to the LORD, the priest shall value it as either good or bad; as the priest values it, so it shall stand. And if the donor wishes to redeem his house, he shall add a fifth to the valuation price, and it shall be his. "If a man dedicates to the LORD part of the land that is his possession, then the valuation shall be in proportion to its seed. A homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver. If he dedicates his field from the year of jubilee, the valuation shall stand, but if he dedicates his field after the jubilee, then the priest shall calculate the price according to the years that remain until the year of jubilee, and a deduction shall be made from the valuation. And if he who dedicates the field wishes to redeem it, then he shall add a fifth to its valuation price, and it shall remain his. But if he does not wish to redeem the field, or if he has sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed anymore. But the field, when it is released in the jubilee, shall be a holy gift to the LORD, like a field that has been devoted. The priest shall be in possession of it. If he dedicates to the LORD a field that he has bought, which is not a part of his possession, then the priest shall calculate the amount of the valuation for it up to the year of jubilee, and the man shall give the valuation on that day as a holy gift to the LORD. In the year of jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought, to whom the land belongs as a possession. Every valuation shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs shall make a shekel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same pattern extends to property. A vowed animal cannot be swapped for another, and land follows the jubilee calendar of chapter 25.

The added fifth appears throughout, and it does the same work every time: buying back what you gave away costs more than giving it did. A vow is a gift, not a loan.

verseByVerse.quote: "But a firstborn of animals, which as a firstborn belongs to the LORD, no man may dedicate; whether ox or sheep, it is the LORD's. And if it is an unclean animal, then he shall buy it back at the valuation, and add a fifth to it; or, if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold at the valuation. "But no devoted thing that a man devotes to the LORD, of anything that he has, whether man or beast, or of his inherited field, shall be sold or redeemed; every devoted thing is most holy to the LORD. No one devoted, who is to be devoted for destruction from mankind, shall be ransomed; he shall surely be put to death. "Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD. If a man wishes to redeem some of his tithe, he shall add a fifth to it. And every tithe of herds and flocks, every tenth animal of all that pass under the herdsman's staff, shall be holy to the LORD. One shall not differentiate between good or bad, neither shall he make a substitute for it; and if he does substitute for it, then both it and the substitute shall be holy; it shall not be redeemed." These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some things cannot be vowed at all, because they already belong to God. The firstborn of the animals is the LORD's: nobody can dedicate what was never his to give. And anything devoted (Hebrew herem, something handed over wholly to God, often for destruction) is beyond redemption entirely.

With the tithe of the flock there was to be no inspecting the animals to make sure the tenth one was the runt. The animal that happened to be tenth was the one that went.

The book stops in the middle of administrative detail, a strange place to end, until you measure the whole distance travelled. Leviticus opened with God calling out of a tent that nobody could enter, telling a nation how to come near without dying. It ends with rules about a man's field and a herdsman counting animals under his staff.

That downward movement is the point. Everything in the book runs one way: from the Most Holy Place outward, through the priests, through the camp, into the kitchen, the marketplace, the harvest and the ordinary working day. Holiness starts at the mercy seat and finishes among the livestock, and there is no point along that line where God is not interested.

The last word of Leviticus is Sinai. The people who received it were camped at the foot of the mountain, and everything in these twenty-seven chapters was arranged so that the God on top of it could live at the bottom of it, among them, without consuming them.

That arrangement held, with interruptions, for well over a thousand years, and was always temporary. And when it was finally replaced, it was replaced not by a better system but by a person, who did not come down the mountain to a tent but became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and in whom the whole book is answered: the offering, the priest, the blood, the mercy seat, the scapegoat, the jubilee trumpet and the lamb without blemish, all of it, in one man, once.

Can “devoted to destruction” justify a vow to kill a person, as Jephthah did? No. This concerns what God himself had placed under judgment, such as the Canaanites or an idolatrous town (Deut 13:15). The law forbids child sacrifice absolutely (18:21; Deut 12:31).

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Gal 6:6; 1 Cor 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.
